T° THE ELECTORS OF THE TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I think it is due to you that I should exOain why I have not allowed myself to be nominated for the present vacancy in the representation of your Ward. You" are well aware that my desire has not been to secure a seat in the Council,but to kill improper trading which had been so extensively practised for many years past. You are also aware that my sole object in retir- ing from your representation was to prevent Mr. Henry Roberts from creeping back into the Council before the issue of the Inquiry Reports and before he had satisfied the ratepayers that his company would never again trade with the Corporation while be was a member of it. Irumediately upon my nomination for the recent casual Bewsey vacancy, Mr. Henry Roberts retired. He has not so far been nominated for any other ward, but it is not unlikely that had I now stood and been returned for your ward, one of his many compact " friends still In the Council would have at once retired in his favour, and thereby necessitated a second resignation on my part. In view of this and of the honour you so gener- ously conferred upon me two years ago, I have felt that while you would appreciate and approve my recent action, it would not be fair to you to run any risk of the Inconvenience of a second contest in your ward, and so I have felt it best to stand aside in favour of Mr. Benson, and to wait and watch developments. With respectful sincerity, but without any hesitation, I desire to ask you to return Mr. Benson, who, as a large ratepayer,and a well-known and respected trades- man, has come forward as a loyal supporter of those principles which you so signally endorsed two years ago. He is to be opposed by Mr. A. J. Jolley, who was so ignominiously defeated on the purity issue in November 1902, when out of 1,096 votes recorded in the Fairfield Ward, he only received 158. tha balance (If 938 rotes being given to Non-Trading Candidates. I observe that Mr. Jolley calls the Non-Trading move- ment a" campaign of calumny," which is not compli- mentary to the great majority of the burgesses of Warrington, who have so emphatically endorsed the i movement. Like Mr. Henry Roberts n the anony- mons letters he has written to the Papers under the pseudonym 'A Ratepayer," 14c., Mr. Jolley does not mention a single instance of an incorrect statement made by a Non-Trader, I now challenge him to do so in regard to any charge I have ever made. I venture to say the challenge will not be accepted. I have made the most definite charges in regard to the considerable trading of John Buckley and Co., and the enormous trading of the Warring-on Slate Co., and every charge I have made has been proved to the hilt. The small com- pany of J. Buckley and Co, did a very large proportion of its whole carting business with the Corporation.whilst a considerable shareholder, who was also its Secretary, was in the Council. In regard to the Slate Company, the Non-Trading Commissioners' Report. page 13, con- tains a list of 15 large contracts recently let by the Coun- cil, amounting in all to £171,475. The Report proceeds : " In every one of these cases. the Warrington Slate Company, as sub-contractors, supplied materials in large quantities." The report further makes end establishes far more serious charges than ever were made in the agitation, as a reference tolthe Inquiry pro- ceedings will amply prove, ond yet Mr. A. J. Jolley has the assurance to come before you, and say what he was just as prepared to say. and in fact did say, before the Inquiry was held—that nothing has been proved; in fact this gentleman is the only party who has without any qualification defended improper company trading. He has condemned poor Aldtrman Sutton for re atively trivial trading, but he has not a word except of approval to say regarding the large direct and enormous indirect trading of Mr. Henry Roberts through the Warrington Slate Company. In this respect Mr. A. J, Jolley is entirely opposed to the views of Mr. Henry Roberts, who, we know, in 1900 was himself a Non-Trader. In a speech made before the General Purposes Committee (on November 26th, 1900) Mr. Roberts referred to the expulsion from the Manchester City Council of the then Lord Mayor- elect simply because he had been proved to have been supplying goods to that Corporation as a sub-contractor. Mr. Henry Roberts, who was Mayor at the time, said (I quote from the " Warringtoa Guardian " of November 28th, 19:i0) " after the publication of the occurrences at Mancheater every public man had been put upon his trial, and he was personally pleased that Mr. Forshaw had brought the matter forward. So far as he (Mr. Roberts) was personally concerned, neither he nor any member of nis family had any pecuniary interest what- ever, either directly or indirectly, in any contracts which the Warrington Slate Company had or might have with the Corporation, and this would continue as long as he remained a member of the T.:mar. Council." Mr. A. J. Jolley is the ettainpion as well as the apolo- gist of Mr. Henry Roberts ;he was a member of the Council when the above speech was made ; he has never yet objected to these Non-Trading professions I flag him now. as I have been in vain asking Mr. Henry Roberts for three years pest. why if (as the latter has so clearly set forth), it is wrong to take Ibis own and his familyallfive-eiglathe share of the pm tits accruing to the Warrington Slata Company directly n. indirectly from contracts which that company had or might have with the Corporation, It can by any kind of reasoning what- ever be right to take the live-eighths of the relatively larger profits accruing to the Slate Company from the enormous business the Company has received from the contractors to the Corporation as sub and sub sub-con- tractor? Will lidr.Jolley give a straightforward answer to this straightforward question ?—lf not, why not ? Two years ago, although I never personally can- vassed one of you, you returned me by such an over- whelming majority that Mr. Henry Roberts charged you with "temporary mental aberration." If you do not now sustain, in the person of Mr. Benson, the judg- ment you then recorded, Mr. Roberts will claim his insulting reference to you to have been proved. For the following reasons I ask you to specially oppose Mr. A. J Jolley • 1. Because he is an uncompromising supporter of all company trading 2. Because contractors once or twice removed (that is sub-contractors or sub-sub-contractors) and such friends of theirs as Mr. A. J, Jolley. voting in the selection of principal contractors, is bound to lead to a monopoly, as has been the case in Warrington. For some years the heavy building work of the Corpora- tion, for some reason or other, has been divided among only a few firms, and this despite the existence of apparently reasonable advertising provisions. 3. Because ill, not in the public interest that such sub and sub-sub-contracting should be done by a member of any Town Council or of any public body, and because by such methods our town is not likely to get the best value for its money. An Association was founded in June 1902, under the name of the British Cotton Growing Association, with the object of extending the Growth and Cultivation of Cotton in the British Colonies. Dependencies, and Protectorates. A guarantee fund of £50,000 was raised, to be spread over five years, and enquiries were commenced throughout. those portions of the British Empire where the conditions as to the possibilities of cotton growing were suitable. Experi- mental plantations were inaugurated, large quantities of seed were distributed, ginning and baling machinery was sent Out, advances were made to planters, and grants were made to various Colonies.

In October 1903, it being found that. the work was much larger than originally contemplated, it was decided to increase the guarantee fund to £lOO,OOO. The continued shortage in the supply of cotton in the earlier months ot 19 4 enabled speculatois to force up American cotton from Fd. per pound to 93. The majority of the Lancashire HMIs were, in consequence compeiled to run short time, entailing serious privations on the operatives and heavy losses on the employers. It being then felt that more rapid devtlopments in the work of the Association were necessary, it was decided to increase the find to £EOO,OOO, and lip petition His Majesty the King to grant a Royal Charter of Incorporation to the Association.
On August 27th, 190, the Charter was granted, and The British Cotton Growing Association was thereby incorporated, _ _ _ .

It is an admitted fit'ct that the world's consumption of eotton has overtaken the supply, and the danger of the situation is intensified by the fact that American require- ments have enormously increased in recent years, namely. from 2,500,030 bales in 1891 to 4,000,000 bales in 1902, and will no doubt go on increasing. It is estimated that the normal increase in the world's consumption of cotton is 400,030 bales per annum. It is therefore evident that unless new cotton fields are opened up in other parts of the world, most of the mills in this country will have per- manently to work short time, and many may be closed entirely. Even should the present American crop prove to be a favourable one, the efforts of the Association must be in no way relaxed, for future years are most doubtful, and with the increase in consumption it is almost certain that within a compasatively short period there will be another shortage. In 1901 and 1902 many cotton mills in this country were unable to run full time, owing to shortage of cotton. In 1 903 most of the Lancashire mills ran short time for a period ef four months, and it has been estimated that the spinners, manufacturers, and operativeslsuffered in that year a direct loss of £2,000,900, apart from the losses consequently entailed upon merchants and others Indirectly interested in the welfare of the cotton trade.

In the present year the majority of the mills have been compelled to run short time for sight months, and it is impossible to estimate the loss to the whole Empire of this serious diminution in the productive and earning power of the most important manufacturing industry of the world. It has been estimated that if all the cotton mills in this country were running three-quarters time instead of full time the loss would be not leas than £300,000 a week, or at the rate of £15,000,000 per annum. A prolonged continua- tion of such a serious position of aff sirs cannot be contem- plated with equanimity and the cotton trade, in which it is estimated that 10,000,000 of the population of this country are directly or indirect'y interested has serious losses facing It, which must sooner or later re-act on the prosperity of the whole of the country, and eventually on other parts of the Empire. The objects of the Assotiation are thus of national import- ance, closely affecting not only spinners, manufacturers, and operatives, or dyers, printers, bleachers, finishers, and other allied trades. Merchants, shippers, and distributors are suffering severely ; engineers, chemical manufacturers, colliery owners, machine makers, bankers, lawyers, stock- brokers, insuran'e companies, railway companies, and ship owners are affected by depression in the cotton trade. Owners of property,shopkeepers,brewers,provision merchants farmers, and in fact all wholesale and retail dealers in every branch of trade, and all producers are concerned in it directly or indirectly. Apart from the direct losses caused by short time in the cotton trade, the consequent abssnce of surplus capital for se-investment in new industries renders the question one of the gravest national importance. The only proposal which holds out any prospect of per- ,manent relief is the opening up of new cotton fields as soon

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

His Majesty's Birthday.—The King will next week have his usual birthday party at Sandringham, which of all places, both his Majesty and Queen Alexandra like best. It is full of the memories of their married life, and it is at his Norfolk home that the King likes to spend his birthday, surrounded by those nearest and dearest to him, and the party also invariably includes a few of his Majesty's oldest and most intimate friends. The day is spent in a very simple and homely fashion, as is customary at Sandringham except when the King and Queerore entertaining Royal visitors there. It is seldom that the Queen misses a visit to the kennels, which is part of the daily routine, as is also an inspec- tion of the gardens and grounds, all the walks at Sandringham being most carefully laid down, so as to present clean walking, even in the wettest seasons. The Visit of the King and Queen of Portugal.—The King of Portugal is a great favourite in this country, and her Majesty will extend a very warm welcome to Queen Arnelie, who is the eldest daughter of the Comtesse de Paris, with whom Queen Alexandra is upon terms of intimate friendship. Dorn Carlos is still a comparatively young man, having been born in 1863, and he married the beautiful Princess Am4lie of Orleans some three years before his accession to the throne in 1889. The King and Queen of Portugal will occupy the State apartments at Windsor Castle, which include several magnificent rooms. The suite was last occupied by the King and Queen of Italy in November last year, and before that by the Emperor and Empress of Germany in 1899. A Distinguished Sportswoman.—The Duchess of Bedford presided last week at the re-opening of Prince's Skating Rink, which is one of the haunts of smart Society. The Duchess cares more for natural history than she does for the pleasures of social life, but she has had much to do with the evolution of real ice skating. and the very fashionable and exclusive Rink at Hyde Park, is her own property. She is a thorough sportswoman and is as expert with the fly-rod as she is with the gun, and it is therefore not surprising that she prefers the country to town life. The daughter of Arch- bishop Tribe, of Lahore, she gained much of her experi- ence with the rifle in India, and the Duchess is as deadly at big game as she is among the grouse and pheasants. But unlike many people devoted to sport, her interest in the animal world is not confined to mere killing. The Duchess is a keen student of natural history. and is a fellow of the Zoological Society in Regent's Park. The Astor Family.—The Astor wedding was dis- tinguished by the presence of a vast throng of fashionable guests, and by the huge number and magnificence of the presents, but it was entirely free from'that ostentatious display which has marked the weddings of so many daughters of American million- aires, as though Mr. Astor is a British subject, all his wealth comes from America. The founder of the family John Jacob Astor, was the son of a butcher at Waldorf, in Germany. In 1779, when he was sixteen he joined his uncle in London, then a partner in Broadwoods, the well known piano manufacturers. Four years later he went to New York, where he! engage I in the fur trade. In this he was successful, and invested his profits in buying up land round New York, which, as the city spread, increased immeasurably in value, and oh his death in 1848, he left a fortune of five millions sterling. The present Mr. William Waldorf Astor, father of last week's bride is understood to be worth at least four times as much,cand this is by no means the whole of the Astor wealth, as his brother had a large share in the estate. The Winter Season.—The winter season in London promises to be a very busy one, in spite of the attrac- tions of hnnting parties, and country house entertain- ments. Sociologists tell us Ithat women of well-to-do classes show an increasing fondness for single blessed- ness,but nevertheless Society weddings are very numei- ous, and it ie no doubt owing to these that the leading shopkeepers are less loud in their complaints, than they have been, about the general want of money. One wedding they say, begets many,and Miss Pauline Astor who was last week married to Captain Spender-Clay was one of several of the bridesmaids who accompanied Lady Marjorie Greville to the altar, and have since entered upon wedded life. It is true that bribal outfits are lesselabomte than was formerly the rule, and even i where there is unlimited wealth, as n the case of Miss Astor, the trousseau bears the stamp of simplicity. It is no use having a huge number of dresses which must become more or less but of date before they are wanted and it is permissible now to wear a gown several times, whereas formerly it would have been allowed to appear only once or twice at Society functions. In spite how- ever of these economies there is a more cheerful note in shopland, and in London a busy time is expected before Christmas, and the general departure of the fashionable world, in search of warmer climates abroad. Concerning Muffs.—Where fashionable bridesmaids are concerned, muffs have now quite taken the place of the one time indispensable shower bouquets, and those carried by Miss Pauline Astor's ten maids" were particularly successful. The trails of roses and foliage, gave a light graceful appearance to the drawn brown chiffon, and unquestionably the idea of these semi- floral muffs is a most delightful one. Muffs for even- ing wear are another innovation. They are very large, and built to match the cloaks with which they are to be worn. They also shew floral decoration and the wearers generally are dispensing with gloves. New Headgear.—The overloaded millinery of the early autumn has disappeared, and in its place we have a very much more becoming and welcome simplicity. The shape is receiving the greatest attention, then a feather or a cluster of flowers is erranged,and perchance a band of velvet or a buckle added, and the creation is complete. One of the prettiest shapes for morning wear, or travelling, is the little Breton sailor, with its brim of rough-haired beaver, and its crown of felt, preferably all white, the sole trimming consisting of a band of black velvet.—For more dressy wear, the all- round, (smooth beaver hat, raised from the head by a velvet bandeau, a couple of ostrich_plumes falling at the back, and fastened in with a button or buckle, is very charming. There is an infinite variety of clasps,buttons, and buckles, for millinery purposes, and when of good quality, and well and carefully chosen, these add con- siderably to the beauty of a hat or toque. • Modes in Lamp and Candle Shades.—ln lamp shades there is little that is novel this winter,and the majority of housewives are remaining faithful to the pretty chiffon and lace specimens we have had with us so long. Drum shaped shades, built of vellum, ornamented with water-coloured sketches,and further adorned with ribbon and sequim embroidery, are in request among women who must always, and at any cost, be up-to-date, but they are by no means so successful as the old fashioned lace and chiffon shades. In the manufacture of candle shades fringe predominates.the fringe in some instances consisting of strings of amber colored or white beads, in others of tubes of glass, with pendent drops, both forming small hoops of silver or gilt. For electric light; flowers with their accompanying foliage form shades, and at the moment the leading flower is the pink chrysanthemum.

WHAT THE KIRK STONE SAW.
DY ITALLIWELL SUTC LI FFE, A.ntlior of "Apples of Discord," "The Elevent. Comtnandine-it," "A Tra.4edy in, Grey," &e.

They call the rls,e Wynya's Kirk. but churc!‘ It never was, ay.' of the 'dud timl are sacred to i'man rites. Just,: grey old pil!ar of stone, with a square hole in the middle. of it. this kirk, and it lies at the head of a little brawling stream that runs down from the moor through a coppice of brambles and mountain-ash It is here that the hillside lassies come on Michaelmas Eve if they want to consult the oracle on the question of their future husbands. The left. hand is thrust thronzh the hole, and the worshipper must chant a certain old-fashioned cradle-song in a low key, while she awaits jud;.ment; then she whispers the man's name, whoever he be. If the fingers grow warm, her choice is good, but if cold she will do well to set her heart elsewhere.

The moor lassies laugh as they enter the dingle, and joke one another about this or that sweetheart; but as the shade grows deeper, and there is no sound but the snapping of a twig underfoot or the call of a bird, they stop laughing, and press close against one another, and move tremulously under the spell of witchcraft. And generally, of course, there are sportive lads lurking behind the Kirk- Stone, who turn the mystery to frolic, and lau4h loudly at the crucial moment and then they -must needs make atonement for their blundering fun, and away they all go home again, the lassies not so frightened nor so conifortless as they were on their way up the dingle. Hetty Ratcliffe—old Squire Ratcliffe's daughter, of Ryecollar—was a good deal above the farm wenches and the working lads who used Wynyates Kirk as a meeting-place on Michaelmas Eve; it was not to be expected that she .hould have any such silly belief in the oracle, : II less a wish to meet any menfolk there. The last, Elio certainly had not, to her own belief; but, superstition she had in plenty, and the Kirk might be able to tell her what she tucst wanted to know just now. Young Royle was living at Hill House then, not a stone's throw from the old Sqi ire's door; the Squire hated young R.oyle, and the Squire's daughter loved him; and this was exactly where the whole trouble came in.

They were a good old yeoman stock, the Boyles, and Griff, the last of the breed, had a tidy bit of land when his father died, as well as the house and something put by in the chest upstairs. But Griff was what we call up here a "raflle-coppin " a jollyoboon comrade, with more spirit than sense, and a liking for strong waters that outran purse and discretion alike; he would rather play at fisticuffs for a--year than work for a day, and he could not keep his hands off Squire Ratcliffe 's game. Ryecollar. lies lower than Marshcotes and Ling Crag, and there were pheasants in plenty, as well as giouse and hares, on the upland edge of the estate; and the Squire hated young Royle, because he knew, as well as could be, that two good tables were being supplied, -day in and day out, at his own expense. _ _ _ _

The sun had gone down behind a red shoulder of the hills, on Michaelmas Eve, when the old Squire tramped into the hall. "I passed Griff Royle's door a while back, Hetty," he growled, strett\hing his well-turned legs before the fire. The girl reddened and fell to polishing a pewter mug that stood on the mantelshelf ; it was strange that her father should speak of Griff on the very night she meant to go to Wynyates Kirk. "Did you, father? " she stammered. "Yes—and the smell of my own pheasant came through the door." "Are you—are you sure it was your pheasant.? " "Do you think I don't know the smell of my own birds, cooked or uncooked? It was mine, I tell you. Young Griff is the worst poacher that ever went unhung, and I'll be even with him yet. He won't even stick to the seasons! Poach or shoot fair, a man has no right to take pheasants till October."
"Perhaps he'd forgotten the date. It's very near October now, father."

The Squire stared at her incredulously, then laughed a great laugh from his belly upwards. " Well, you were made so, you women. The Lord knows best, only He might have salted your tails with a pinch of sense. Get me a pint of home- breued, Hetty, and after that we'll have supper." Old Ratcliffe grew mellower as the evening wore on. Hetty glanced at the clock from time to time, and wondered if she could win free of the house before midnight; for go to the kirk she would, whatever the hour might be. Eleven struck from the clock in the corner, and the Squire began to chuckle contentedly to himself. His daughter scarcely noticed the cheery guffaw that put a climax to his musings; she was thinking that the other lasses would be leaving Wynyates Kirk now, and that the way was open for her as soon as she could escape from the house. "See here, Hetty, I'm in high feather to-night," broke in the Squire. "I am going my rounds, and it's ten to one I net a poacher or two. Shall I treat you like a man for once, lass, and bid you come with me? " "Yes, do, father ! " cried the • girl eagerly. There seemed a chance of slipping away to the Kirk at some point of the journey. "Well, you shall come. You're a good lass, as women go, and a bit of a change will do you no harm in the world. Run away upstairs and put a shawl or something over your head." She was away and back again in a moment. Her father had shouldered 11:s gun and was standing at the open door: he laughei like a boy as Hetty and he struck into the road. And Hetty, too, laughed a little, because she knew his errand. "Heart alive, Hetty, if only your mother could see us now ! " went on the Squire. "She was always too good for me by half, and maybe I didn't treat her over-well at times. She was your sort, Hetty, sick after trifles, and led by every fancy that could make a woman go mad for the moon. She kept herself scant of food, God knows, and that did all the mischief. Well, here we are at Job Wilkinson's; I'll give him an eye-opener." Squire Ratcliffe lifted his brawny fist and hammered at the door of the cottage. As this was of no avail, he shouted himself red about the gills; then pounded away again at the panels, until it seemed that either his fists or the door must soon give way.
- A night-capped head thrust itself out of the upper window. "Be durned to thee! who art 'a ? " growled a voice from under the nightcap. "The devil in breeches, my lad. I've come to fetch you."

A pause; then a surly muttering from above: "Oh, it's t' Squire, is't ? Aye, aye, tha'rt right; t' devil i' breeches, an' proper." "Well, get to bed again, Job. You are not at my eame, anyway; better luck next time." And the Squire, with a rollicking laugh, was half on his way to the next cottage.
They went the round of the hamlet, until Squire Ratcliffe had assured himself that one and all of his tenants were safe under roof.
"I've drawn every cover blank, Hefty, be hanged if I haven't," he observed, a trifle ruefully. "So you're coining back home to bed ? " sug- gested the daughter, with a fine air of innocence.

"No; I've a fancy to collar young Royle to- night. No use knocking him up, for he's as sure as rain to be somewhere about the woods. He's had a pretty run, but it's a very long lane that has no turning. You'd better go home, Hetty ; you're not fit for these all-night pranks." The Squire watched her turn the corner of the road; then chuckled afresh, with an impatient sigh cutting across the chuckle. "Well, well, she's a girl it does any man's heart good to father. God bless her, and keep her from going the way of her mother."

"The way of her mother" was just the grave, and jt always angered Squire Ratcliffe, big and sound of body, to think of folks being weak enough to drop into six-by-three of mould, when they might have had so much better a time by staying above ground.' To this day, fond as he had been of his wife, he was always a little angry with her for dying.

Heity; directly the corner was turned, ran straight to Hill House. The house was dark. She tried the door, and found it locked; then threw pebbles up at the window that she knew was Griff's. Last of all, she went round to the yard, where Tramp's kennel was, and called the spaniel by name. There was no answer; it was certain that Gruff was abroad in search of her ;ather's game. _ _
She halted a moment, wondering if she could do anything to give Gruff warninw. No. there were
too many places in which he tnight be at work, and the night was dark; it would be like seeking a needle in a haystack.

"Gruff, I wish you would be just a little steadier," she murmured fretfully, and went towards Wynvates Kirk, to learn what the oracle had to say about this same young swain and his wildness. It cost her an effort to enter the dingle. The stream plashed eerily amonc, its pebbles; the wind was like a dirge. But she struggled on. Half-way up the path something big and black got up under her feet, and scrambled away through the underbrush ; she was so startled that the sweat came out in beads on her forehead. Then she laughed at herself, as she remembered how fond the sheep were of :browsing.on the sweet "butter- grass " that fringed the stream.

But someone was before her at the Kirk. Her fears vanished in annoyance as she saw the squat, shapeless figure kneeling before the Stone. The devotee was too intent on her own business to hear the footfall behind her, too intent to heed that she had a listener; she whispered a name, and then Hetty's voice rang out, clear and sharp and scorn- ful, from the darkness of the glen.
"Who gave you leave, Meg Greenwood, to mak- free with Griff Royle's name? " cried the newe corner, white with anger.

She had recognised Meg—poor ugly Meg, with a face like a bit of knotty wood and a heart as sweet as kingcups—and it angered her that this farm-wench should be here on the self-same errand as herself. Besides, what did it mean? Had Griff stooped as low as this?

Meg Greenwood got up from her knees and stood staring at Hetty, her arms akimbo. "An' who gave thee leave to ax me about him ? " she demanded, with surly defiance. Hettv reddened and hung her head. "No one," she said, and yearned to be at her rival's throat. "Oh, tha'rt a pretty 'un, tha'rt 'vi' thy kiss- and-come-quick eye3f3 an' thy bonny red lips. But what's a' that, I'm asking thee? There's mony a soft heart lies under a roughened skin, an' that's what I'm telling thee, Hetty Ratcliffe." A silence fell between them.
"Did he—has be ever made love to you, Meg ? " asked the other anxiously. Her pride had clean gone in the need for present knowledge.

"Noan •' thy business," snarled Meg. Tkea, with a catch in her voice: "It's noan the likes o' me he speers after. He's niver done more nor throw me a' Good-day, Meg,' as he'd throw a bone to a dg. What's that getten to do wit? Does a lass wait to love till she's bidden ? "
"No, God knows she doesn't," murmured Hetty, glad to know that he was not Meg's, yet sick to learn if he were hers.
"Well, I'll leave thee to't," said Meg Green- wood, after a stupid pause. "Maybe tha'll ha' better luck,. but if iver tha plays him false I'll smash the face that has driven him to thee."

Hetty, watching her go down beside the talkative stream, was dimly conscious that here she had stumbled upon a love more unselfish, if not more passionate, than her own. Yet she wanted Gruff too badly to think much of Meg Greenwood, and presently she turned to the Kirk-Stone for guid- anne. _ _

Kneeling down, she put her right hand through the opening, and began to sing, in a low, full voice, the words of that old-world cradle-song which had come down from generation to genera• tion until its origin was lost:

Whisht thee, bairn! the wind is sleeping, Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'en; Dusk o'er Hug and bog is creeping, • Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'en. Whisht, thee, whisht! the night is falling, Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'en; Never heed the boggarts calling, Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'en. Whisht thee, bairn! thy mother's near thee, Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'en; Wind and boggarts mustna flair thee,, Nod, nod, nod and shut thy e'er,

She stopped • singing, and whispered 'jriff Royle," and waited tremblingly to hear the sequel. But Hetty Ratcliffe was too sensitive for this kind of ordeal • she imagined cold or heat in the fingers, one following the other, a hundred times in as many seconds. She was just going to turn away, in despair of receiving any clear message, when the fingers went very warm indeed; and small wonder, for a strong hand had grasped them from the other side.

- "They go hot if the man of your heart is meant for you, Hetty," came a rich, half-laughing voice. "Leave them awhile, dear, and see if they don't grow as warm as June sun on a hayrick." The girl wrenched her hlnd free, keeping back, first a cry of affright, and then an after-cry of joy. Young Royle emerged from the gloom and came close up to her. And then the hand went cold again, for Tramp, the spaniel, had crept to her side and pushed a loving nose into her palm. "And are you the man of my heart, think you? " said she, with a little laugh of scorn. "The same, and no other, sweetheart."

"Oh, indeed! And what makes you think that ? " "Just a ft,ncy. I heard you come up to the Kirk-Stone and begin to sing; and after that you whispered somebody's name, so loud that the somebody, if his ears were as sharp as a poacher's ought to be, could' hear it as plain as if you'd shouted it."

"It was only for fun," defiantly. "But I'm in earnest, and you're going to marry that somebody, Hefty." "Oh, I couldn't! He steals my father's game, and it must never be said that one of the Ratcliffes married a common thief! "
"He never stole anything—that somebody—but things that fly and swim; and they're free to all, as the moor-creed goes."
"But I don't love him-- "Nonsense I " "—mote than a very, very little. Not nearly enough to marry him." "Then what about the morning in Sear Wood, when you looked like the sunshine and told me—

"I want to go home. Shew me the way through the dingle, will you, Gruff? I am so afraid of slipping into the water by mistake." "There is no way at all through the dingle, Hetty, unless you pledge me your word that you'll marry me."
"Griff, I can't promise to-night. Let me go; I want to think about it."

"Thought and care bring the wrinkles. I can't let you go till you pr( mise." He dropped his bantering tone, and held her hand very tightly in his. "Hetty, girl, it's sick work waiting for your promise. There's nothing Ido but has you at the back of it. I'm a bit of a scamp, but will you take me and sin's it? "

How big and strong he was to have near one, felt Hetty, as she caught her breath and longed to let herself drop into his arms without more ado. Then, on a widen, she remembered Meg Green- wpod. "Did you hear someone else who came and whispered your name to-night ? " she asked quickly. "I couldn't help hearing." "And you heard what followed too?" "Yes."
"Did she speak the truth, Griff, when she said you'd never given her reason to love you? "
_ "Aye, that she did. Poor wench, I had never thought of such a thing—never, Hetty."
"I believe you," said Hetty after awhile. Then, with a swift drop into softness again: "I shouldn't like to think ill of you."

He .put both arms close about her. "Wilt you risk it, sweetheart?" he repeated. But she held out a little longer. "Suppose I said Yes,' Griff ? Would you try to give up the poaching? " Young Boyle made a grimace under cover of the darkness. The two passions had been brought into conflict at last, and it was hard to choose just at once. "I'll try, Hetty, I'll try my very best," he said at last. "But I'm afraid it's in the blood." "Really try? It would make such a difference to father, as well as to me." Then, with a woman's quick care of danger: "Father is after you to-night, Gruff; he .told ins so when I left him. Is it safe for you to be here?" "There's only one thing can make it unsafe, and that is No ' from you. Come, sweetheart!" And after that the night held a kindly veil oyer their doings, and the stream babbled loud enough to drown their words; and when Hefty freed her. self from the man of her heart she was not at all tired of his kisses, only she thought it was fitting she should seem so. All this beside the lichened Kirk; the Kirk remembered far-off Pagan days, before the creeds crept in, and to-day it could find a rough sTnpathy for these lusty men and women of the moors, who loved in the free old way and joyed in. the nakedness of heart to heart. "I must yet home," she declared, with a brisk air. "Griff. whatever would folks say if they

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
St. Clement's Mission.

Preaching at St. Clement's Mission on Sunday, the Rev: A. S. Cameron continued his addresses on the sub- ject" Do we believe ?" The life of Christ, said Mr. Cameron, should be the ideal of every Christian and, though they might fall short of their ideal, good Christians must cultivate humbleness, self-denial, and purity. They should deny themselves not only of sin- ful pleasures, but doubtful pleasures, and above all cultivate a pure and Godlike presence. Referring to the letters appearing in a London newspaper, he said many of the writers had made erroneous statements with reference to the creeds of - the Church. Creeds were simply the fences of the Church. What they (the Church of England) did teach was the way to the feet of Jesus, for had not our Saviour Christ said "Come unto Me all that travail qnd are heavy laden, and I will refresh you "? There was a large congregation. Memorial Service at Wycliffe Church. - -

At Wycliffe Church on Sunday morning a memorial service to the late Mr. Edward Pickavance, who for many years was an active member of the church, was conducted by the Rev. John Yonge. There was a large congregation and hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung. The choir rendered the anthem "Star of the Valley," which had been written by Mr. Alfred Corney and set to music by Mr. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. The soloist was Mrs. R. H. Pearson. The Rev. John Yonge based his sermon on the words " When thou passest through the waters I will be with thee" (Is. xliii 2) He said the late Mr. Pickavance had been a faithful, regular worshipper so long as health allowed, an earnest and diligent worker, a generous supporter and upholder a completely loyal member of the church. For many years he had been teacher of a numerous series of young men, and the Y.P.S. had been indebted to his generous hospitality oft many occasions. He favoured and helped •the formation of the P.S.A. and did what lay in his power to make it a success. He was a man whom they would greatly miss and not easily forget. At the even- ing service the anthem "The radiant morn hath passed away" was creditably interpreted. The Russian Outrage.

The recent Russian outrage in the North Sea formed the subject of a portion of the sermon delivered by the Rev. T. W. Barber at St. Paul's Church on Sunday morning. The outrage he said, had almost caused a conflagration, not only in Europe, but throughout the world. We hoped now, however, by the providence of God we had been mercifully delivered from a conflict with a Christian nation. Thanks were due to Him for having instilled the spirit of wisdom, counsel, and strength into the minds of the advisers of the Czar of all the Russias. Widows and orphans in Hull were mourning their loss that day, and as a congregation he was sure he was voicing their feelings when he said that their hearts went out in sympathy to the bereaved —the innocent victims of an unspeakable blunder. But a just retribution would be required. It was putting back the clock of time for an officer of the Czar to open a murderous fire in such circumstances and then steam away without the least sign of regret. As Englishmen and as Christians we viewed such conduct with aversion. Christianity and humanity had been shocked. Thank God we set a higher value upon life, even of the humblest, than was the case in Russia. At the evea- ing service the Dead March in "Saul "was played on the organ, the congregation standing in the meantime

div.head: *cline !IC .Society.—Open Meeting.
div.p: *cline !IC .Society.—Open Meeting.

An o-pen meeting of this society was held on Sunday, the church being crowded. Special interest centred in the service,ovving to the fact that Crosfleld's Prize Band was in attendance to accompany the hymns and render special selections. The band assembled near the Park gates, and marched along Sankey-street, Horsemarket- street and Bewsey-street, to Wycliffe Church. Mr. B. Farrar and Mr. R. Atkinson, secretary and treasurer res- pectively,headed the band, accompanied by Mr. Willett, Mr. Rigby and Mr.iVfoss,members of the Band Committee. By the time the band had taken its place accompanied by its able leader and conductor Mr. Halliwell, of Wigan, the beautiful sanctuary was crowded with over 1,000 people. Punakually at 3 o'clock, Mr. E. W. Bindloss the chairralllß announced the first hymn "0, God our help in ages past," which, accompanied by the band and organ, was heartily joined in by the great congrega- tion. bThe band rendered the following selections Memories of Mendelssohn, (arranged by Rimmer);recit, "Comfort ye," and chorus "And the Glory of the Lord" (Handel), and lastly the test piece at Crystal Palace • " Gems of Tschaikowsky ' (E. Swift) for which they won the first prize and cup. The last hymn "Onward Christian Soldiers," was sung with special heartiness. When the congregation were asked if they would like the band to attend at some future meeting, there were strong signs of approval. The Chairman expressed his great pleasure at seeing so large a gather- ing, and the pleasure it gave him to listen to the beautiful strains of the band. He made reference to the likelihood of a Peaceful and satisfactory settlement of the most deplorable event that had so recently taken place on the high seas. The Russian Fleet, through extreme carelessness,nervousness,or whatever the cause, had plunged bereaved ones into troeble and loss and brought a just cry of indignation from our country. That called for an agreement to all our demands at a very , early date. At this time :Christendom was thankful Ithat further war was averted. Mr. Wolstencroft, of Swinton, gave the address, which was listened to with rapt attention, his subject being " He is able to save." IThere were millions now and in past ages, he said, who I bore and had borne testimony to Christ's power to save. He referred to the black man who had tried Buddhism and other isims, but found none to satisfy him, until he found Christ. Christ saved from the inclination to do and go wrong : none were too sinful to be saved by the power of Christ ;and the Spirit of love. When Pro- fessor Darwin returned from a visit amongst the savages he declared Christianity would never succeed amongst them,but years after he had to acknowledge his mistake. The speaker com mem; ed Christ's great love to that large meeting. The President, Rev. John Young read the lesson. and the Secretary asked the meeting to join him in prayer for the widow and fatherless children of one of their brethren, who was killed at White Cross Works on Saturday morning. Afterwards the meeting passed a vote of condolence and sympathy with the widow and family. Mr. W. H. Payton,lllus.Bac.,as usual presided at the organ. A good collection was taken for the funds of the Brotherhood.

_ Spiritual Convention. A spiritual convention was held at Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street, on Saturday afternoon and even- ing, and attracted a fairly large congregation. Coun- cillor Brough presided. A lengthy programme was sub.- mated, solos being given by Mrs.Everness,Mrs. Dutton, Miss Bowyer, Messrs. H. and W. Bennett, W. White, and W. Knowles. Special hymns (three of which had been written by the pastor, the Rev. Alfred Barrett), and anthems were sung. Prayers were offered by Messrs. H. Thornton, J. Roscoe, T. Bold, Captain Langtan (Church Army), and the Pastor, while a lesson was read by Captain Langton. An address was given by the Rev. H. Wall. A public tea was afterwards provided. An open-air procession was formed in the evening, and paraded the principal streets of the town, headed by the pastor and the band of the Salvation Army. Short addresses were delivered en route by the Pastor,Captain Langton, and Mr. Hayes (Runcorn).—On returning to the church Mr. W. Carter (Darnton) delivered an address on " The true estimate of life." MI. H Thornton said their object in meeting that day was to try and deepen the work of Christ in the hearts of the people. He might venture to say that it had been his object in all his Christian life to strike a blow in favour of the Lord. People were being trained in all trades, and he thought they should also be trained in the great temperance work and also in the religious element of life. The IPastorl observed; that the convention had been organized for the upholding of the church, for the deepening of the spiritual life in the hearts of human beings and for bringing men to God.—The Chairman proposed a vote 0: thanks to all who had taken part in the proceedings, and said he hoped that some good result would come from them. (Applause.) The motion was carried, and the Chairman haring been thanked the meeting concluded.

div.head: PRETTY SKIRT.
div.p: A PRETTY SKIRT.

3iv e for the girl of limited means. The upper part of most Of the prettiest skirts this season is c.ither gauged, gathered, or tucked to fit the figure closely and therefoie renders the lining of that portion invisible. Many charm- ing skirts ready for fixing into . a band with material for the bodice can be bought in all sorts of material and colours, and as the smartest bodices are made in blouse form any gifi who has a slight knowledge of dressmak- ing can turn out a charming frock for at the most three pobnds, this amount, of course, in- cluding lining and some lace as a bodice

trimming. A pretty skirt is given in my sketch. It is made in that most charming of materials namely, chiffon velours of a most becoming tone of black. The skirt is made with two series of deep circular tucks, while very narrow tucks run vertically. A flounce of silk lace headed by a gauging is also used as a trimming, and a deep flounce of the material itself flows round the feet only enhanced by a couple of tucks just above the hem. A bodice to match this skirt would look well with a cape coming from either side of a boxpleat in front to form points on the shoulders and at tbe back. Similar silk lace to that used on the skirt should be used to soften the effect, and frills of the same lace should fall from the elbows of the loose and much tucked sleeves. To brighten the effect of the toilette a richly
CARACLILE COAT.

tiated ribbon sash could be worn fastened in a smart bow at the back with long ends falling on to the skirt at the back. Any coloured ribbon could be used which best becomes the complexion of the wearer, a brunette preferr- ing the richness of a full coloured orange and a blonde probably leaning to pink or pale blue as her fancy might tend. An alsatian ribbon bow to match is still worn in the hair, though the fashion is hardly a new one, and now that there is a vogue for twisting the hair in a wide plat round the head for the evening floral sprays or single flowers seeni to be preferred. Fur coats are quite one of the leading leatures of dress for street wear, and a very charming sample is given in my second illus- tration. The material of which it is made is grey caracole which is very fashionable. In this instance the smart coat i completed by a very becoming and simple toque hat of the same fur trimmed solely by a large white bird. Nothing could be simpler and yet more stylish than the mode depicted for the neck is finished by a stole tie of the caracole and the waist by a band of soft kid of the same tone of grey as the caracole. The sleeves are cut on the latest lines, for in this particular, as in Others, fashion varies from season to season. The coat also extends below the waist line, and this again is an important feature in this season's styles, for all the model French coats come well over the hips, but are confined at the waist by a belt of more or less elaboraticso.

A grey skirt must, of course, form part of th* toilette as any othcr would spoil the soft colour scheme. The coat could, Of course, be worn open as well as closed as the stole ends can be rinknotted and allowed to fall flatly at either side.

My Las' sketch depicts a fashionable hat made in soft brown chenille with a long para- dise plume bf creamy yellf)w sought in by a bow of orange coloured huroir velvet. In every way this Lthapeali emphasises the prevailing and Lest fashions for the colours are the most popular. There is, of course, a fear that when any strong and pronounced tone, such as orange, becomes universally popular it is the first hint' of its speedy demise, for it then becomes vulgarised by cheap and inartistic imitations. There is a hint already in the air that orange will be eventually super- seded by a particular tone of violet or helio- trope, or perhaps It may better be defined as a blending of the two. The colour is a particu- larly charming one and likely to suit everyone and I have seen 'some very effective hats of this colour in velvet, felt, and other materials. It could be used instead of orange in the hat I have depicted, the hat itself being of a deeper and darker tone than the ribbon and plume with which it is trimmed.

A FASHIONABLE HAT.

anew I had been here with you at thia time of night?" "Anything folks had to saw, Hetty, they could say to my face; and somebody's beauty would be spoilt in the telling. What made you come here to-night? Was it really the stuff about the Kirk- Stone ? "

She was a little ashamed of her superstition, w that realities loomed so big. "Yes, it was. I—l was bothered about you; I didn't see how you could go on living such a wild life if you loved toe. Griff, I've been as wretched as wretched lately."

"Well, and now?" "Ah, well, now it is different. What were you doing here?" "I came after' the' -pheasants, but those silly farm wenches and their lads nut sport out of the question. It gave me a sore heart, Hetty, to see them pairing off two by two. 7 "What—the pheasants, Griff ? " she put in deme'rely. "No, the lads and their•lasses. It felt hard to be left just by myself after they'd gone, and I had no spirit for anything except to lie in the bracken and sulk."

"Hush, Griff ! What was that?" cried die girl, clutching his arm. "A man coming through the dingle," said Royle quietly, after a pause. "And if it's the Squire, Hetty, I can't knock him down, can I, with things as they are between us? " "How can you jest about it?. If it is father, God help us!" Yes, they could see him now, swinging along the path towards them. The upland folk know the dark so well that they have learnt to use it as a candle. A few more strides, and the Squire was aware of the two figures in front of him. "Hallo! Royle, I'll be bound, by tile size of the man. Come, my lad, I've tried often enough, and now I've caught you. Who's that skulking behind the bush?"

Hefty might have escaped there and then, for the Squire had business to-night with none but Royle. But some instinct to keep close to her lover held her, and she stopped where she was, barely under shelter of the shrub. "Only a friend of mine, Squire; never mind smaller game," said Royle.

"I won't. You'll have to fight me, Royle of Hill House, and when I've knocked the flesh off your body I'll have your bones clapped in gaol for six months." Gruff was all fight in a moment. He forgot that it was Hetty-'s father who invited him to combat, and remembered only that there was a man of great bulk just ip front of him, anxious to fight him and able, apparently, to give him good game. Off went his coat, up went his shirt-sleeves to the shoulder; and he and Squire Ratcliffe were in and at one another with a will before the girl, crouch- ing under shelter, could move or speak.

She came out then and tried to rush between them. They were deaf, though, to anything out- side the thwack-thwack of give-and-take blows; it was a marvel that the girl was not crushed in her efforts to stop the fray. She stood off from them and waited for her chance; directly they fell back from one another after the first bout she came and gripped her father by the wrists. "You have fought enough, father," she cried, scarcely knowing what she said. The old Squire looked as if he had Feen a ghost. "Hetty I' In Satan's name, child, what are you doing here ? " "Letting Griff make me promise to marry him.' It was always a puzzle to her afterwards how sha found pluck to make her foolhardy confession. Squire Ratcliffe began to froth and stutter in his rage. "§o that's your game, Royle, is it? You rob me of my birds, you rob me of inv daughter-- you'll be asking for the breath in my lungs next! _
_ "I've tapped a little of that already," said Gt.:l'f quietly. _
_ The Squire snorted in disdain of the innuendo, and Hetty tried to get a word in, but the old man would not listen.
"Hearken to me, Squire," began Gruff, wiping the blood from his nose, because it had a tendency to trickle into his mouth as he talked,

"Listen to the wind, you God-forsaken will-o% the-wisp! You're a thieving race, you Royles, from father to son, and from son to the babe in the womb. You'd steal the seed from your neigh- bour's furrows, and sa,y that Heaven gave all men a right to grain that was dropped by the way." . •

"Come and tight, then, if you won't listen. We've first-rate fists, we Hill House folk, if we've nothing else." There was just a trace of softening in the Squire's face—the ghost of a grim chuckle that looked in at the corners of his mouth, and cams out again because the hospitality within was not of a first-rate order. "Aye, you can hammer; it's all you're good for. Come on," said he.
"Father, no!" The girl's voice was peremptory, her air defiant.

"And why not, baby? Who are you, to come between your father and a gaol-bird?" "Gaol-bird or honest, false or true, \I mean to marry Gruff Royle ; and I won't have father and son fighting together. See, father, what has he done so much amiss ? "

The Squire's face blackened as a new thought struck him; he had not had time :for it before. "What has he done amiss? " he cried brutally. "Nay, the dark and you and he know best, Hetty." Hetty clenched her hands together and her face went hard. "A Royle never thought so black a lie as that," she said proudly. The load was off old Ratcliffe's heart now. His brutality had been to try her, and there was no doubting the quick honesty of scorn lie had brought upon himself. "We never in this world stole a woman's honour, Squire. We have lived cheek by jowl, your folk and mine, these four hundred years; have you to learn that lesson yet?"
-Squire Ratcliffe looked from one to the other. It went sorely against the grain to own himself in the wrong. . _ _

"Curse you, lad," he cried irritably, "can't you see I was over-hasty? Hetty, run home and leave us to settle our quarrel, and you shall never hear another word about it. No, by Heaven you shan't! I'll not even ask how you came to be here to-night." "I will tell you without being asked, though you will laugh at me for iny pains. I came to ask the Kirk-Stone if I was to put Gruff out of my heart or not—and he was here." "On what business? " asked the Squire, with a twitching of the mouth. "A brace of pheasants, and perhaps a hare or two," put in Royle, still dabbing at his nose. . Then the Squire laughed outright. As his way was, his mood had shifted clean round. "That ever .we fathers should beget such children I One of you comes to steal my pheasants, and the other to inquire if she may marry tha man who stole them! See here, young folks, you're wanting to make a precious fool of me between you." "Well, my nose has paid for it, and we're quits." laughed Royle. "It's very nearly broken, Squire." "Ha, ha! It was a good smart stroke that, Royle; a really fine stroke, though I say it myself! You don't fight amiss for a youngster; perhaps we shall make a man of you one day—if only you'll drop the poaching." Hotly could scarce believe her ears, not under- standing that all along the Squire had been cherishing, a warm regard for his enemy's prowess; that brief spell of fight had named the old fellow's heart towards young Royle more than a lifetime of good works could have done. She crept to her father's side and cares.ed him silently. "There, there! " muttered the Squire, putting her way.. "He's only a good-for-nothing, Hetty, when all is said and done. Hoyle, you had one of my pheasants for supper last night; I sniffed it as I passed your front-door." "There you're wrong. It was one of old Squire Daneholine s ; I got it a fortnight since in the Saxilton Woods, and it ate like butter." Squire Ratcliffe slapped his thigh and laughed till the woods rang again. - "Good lad, good lad! Old Danehohne's a fool, and I've owed him a grudge this many a long day. Why don't you take all his game, and leave mine alone? " "So I will, Squire, if you'll make me yourrson," said Gruff promptly. "No, no! it's not to be heard of, though I do want that scrap of lr.nd of yours to round off the property. Come along, Hetty ; it's time we were in bed. Tell young Griff there to think no more of it, because your father will never be fool enough to let you." But old Squire Ratcliffe proved, in the end, to be more of a fool than he had reckoned upon. So the Kirk-Stone did its work well, after all. And the Boyles of Hill House are good fighting lad/ to this day, evary man of them, with a twist for poaching that a dash of Ratcliffe blood has done aothingto eradicate. rTtin END. 1

SIR A. K. WILSON.
TIE CRISIS PASSED.

Last week was a very trying time for the nation, which had to face a crisis unparalleled in modern times. "The Angel of Death has been abroad in the land.' You could almost hear the beating of his wings," to quote John Bright on a similar occasion. But fortunately the, crisis has passed, tided over by diplo- macy, and there is every prospect of peace with honour. Seldom has the nation shown a more solid front, animated only by one idea. War was ./not the desire of anyone, but it was felt by all that unless Russia granted our terms we .must take prompt action against the marauding Baltic Fleet. The story of how they fired upon the fishing smacks off the Dogger Bank is now ancient history, ingrained into the mind of every Briton, and it will be long before its effect will be forgotten. As soon as the news reached Mr. Balfour and Lord Lansdowne they proceeded to town, interviewed the King, and sent prompt representations to Russia. For a time it looked as though nothing could ward off war, especially as the Admiralty at St. Petersburg seemed in an aggressive rather than a conciliatory mood. We, however, showed our intention of prompt action, and the word went out to our three fleets—the Home Squadron under Sir A. K. Wilson in the Firth of Forth, the Channel Squadron under Lord Charles Beresford at Gibraltar, and the Mediterranean Squadron 'under Sir Compton Domville in the Adriatic and off Malta, together with the Cruiser Squadron and the torpedo flotilla. Lord Charles Beresford was the admiral nearest to Vigo, and he lost no time in coaling and clearing for action in case of emergencies. Whatever the ultimate outcome of the whole pitiable affair, it will undoubtedly add to the popularity of the Navy and reassure the nation with the knowledge that our first line of defence and offensive is ready when it is wanted. In the meantime the British demand for a full apology, adequate com- pensation, punishment of the guilty officers, and guarantees for the future was being entertained p.t St. Petersburg, and the Tsar ,wired at once in his own name to King
LORD BERESFORD. LORD BERESFORD'S FLAGSHIP.

div.head: PRIME MINISTER.
div.p: THE PRIME MINISTER.

Edward promising the first two., Then it .appeared as though a hitch had. arisen, but France. through M. Paul Cambon, the Am- -bassador in London,. laid itself out to aid a peaceful settlement and clear things up. Then it became evident that 'Admiral Rod- jestventsky was attempting to justify himself. He telegraphed from Vigo to the Tsar that he had been attacked by two Japanese torpedo-boats, • sheltered behind the fishing fleet. While regarding the idea as absurd, the British Government was bound to meet Russia so far as to agree to an "inter- national court." as outlined in Article 9 of the Hague Convention, the Russians stipu- lating to keep back the portion of the Baltic Fleet inculpated at Vigo till afterwards, giving guarantees for the future and promis- ing punishment, if the guilt were proved. On Friday these terms were placed before the now historic Cabinet meeting and agreed to. Mr. Balfour was due to speak in the evening at the meeting of the National Union , of Conservatives at Southampton, and there in a long speech he explained the whole state of the case, showing that we had obtained our terms in actual fact. He was received with great enthusiasm, as he went from point to point, showing that the Government did not intend to draw back one inch from their position. Meanwhile part of the Russian fleet is remaining at Vigo and part is con- tinuing its journey down the West Coast of Africa, while all arrangements are being made for the constitution of the Court of Inquiry at Vigo. In England, in addition to the inquest, there is ,being held a Board of Trade Inquiry, which will not itself apportion blame, but will report to .the International Court at Vigo. It has been a time of suspense, but it is 'to be trusted that the worst is now passed.
THE DEATH OF FIELD MARSHAL SIR HENRY NORMAN.

The death of Sir TI :v Norman. G.C.8., G.C.M.G., removes on', of our leading vete- rdris ; and London did homage to his memory last Saturday by tt:rning out to his funeral, which was hcid wi' h full militarN honoursf The dead Field was Governor 0. Chelsea Hospi- tal, and it was there that he
died at the age of seventy-eight —still in liar-

ness, so to speak. After service in the •chapel of the Hospital, the body was placed upon a gun-car- riage of the "si Battery, Royal Horse Artillery, and escorted to Brompton Cem- etery by the ist Life Guards and the 21st Lan- cers. Born in 1826, Sir Henry Norman entered the Indian Army at the ap of eighteen, and held. the proud record of hay ing been thanked five-and-twenty times in orders and despatches for his conduct in the field. Before the Mutiny he had gone through the Sikh War, the Peshawur Frontier War, and the Sonthal insurrection; and when the 'Mutiny broke out he became an acting Adju mnt-General, and distinguished himself bo

at Delhi and Lucknow, winning promotion alma decorations. Subsequently he became Assist- ant Military Secretary to the Duke of Cam- bridge, Military Secretary to the Government of India, member of the Viceroy's Council, and then of the Secretary for India's Council. In 1883 he became Governor of Jamaica, and five years later Governor of Queensland; and then, in 1893, when the Liberals had to ap- point a Viceroy of India in succession to Lord Lansdowne, upon Lord Cromer's refusal of the post, it was offered to and accepted by Sir Henry Norman. However, owing to the severe criticism which the appointment called forth, he cabled a withdrawal of his accept- ance from Queensland, and Lord Elgin wai appointed in his place. In 1901 the Gover- norship of Chelsea Hospital fell vacant and was given to him, and in the following year he received a Field Marshal's baton, on the same day as the Duke of Connaught.

THE RETIREMENT OF THE :BISHOP OF GLOUCESTER. It is announced that at the end of the present year, Dr. Ellicott, the octogenarian Bishop of Gloucester, will resign his See and retire into private life. Dr. Ellicott is a long way senior of the Lords Spiritual, senior indeed to the late Archbishop Canterbury: lnd it is known thal, if the late Earl of Beacons- field had had his way, he wOuld have been Primate of All England. Born in the same year as the late Queen Victoria, Dr. Ellicott was the last of Lord Palmerston's bishops and has held the See of Gloucester for over forty years. Appointed in 1863 to the com- bined Sees of . Bristol a n.d Glouces t e r, he resigned the former in 1897, but retained the lattlef. His retirement will sever many links with the past; and even at his advanced age it came as a surprise to many 'who had looked upon the hale and hearty old bishop as a good deal younger than many men twenty years his junior. Dr. Ellicott still rides a tricycle and can play a good game of billiards: and he was over seventy before he gave up his favourite sport of Alpine climbing. In his younger days the Bishop of Gloucester had a very distinguished career at Cambridge, where he was a Uni- versity Scholar and Members' Prizeman. A fellowship of his college, St. John's followed; and in 1843 he was ordained. Five years later he became Professor of Divinity at King's College London, where he remained until 1861, when he was appointed Hulsean Professor of Divinity at Cambridge and Dean of Exeter. Two years later followed the double bishopric.. Dr. Ellicott has writ- ten a great deal on theology and is the best known man in the Church crf England. His retirement will be regretted on every side ; but he has, indeed, earned his rest.
11IE JUGHT REV. Di. ELLICOTT.

div.head: MISS PAULINE ASTOR'S WEDDING.
div.p: MISS PAULINE ASTOR'S WEDDING.

One of the smartest weddings which London has witnessed for a long time took place on Saturday at St. Margaret's, Westminster, when Captain Spender Clay was married to Miss Pauline Astor, the only daughter of the multi-millionaire. Mr. William Waldorf Astor, who reckons his annual income by millions, derived from ground rents in New York, is an American by birth and made hi! money in the States, but some years age he renounced his American citizenship and became a naturalised Englishman. He bought Clivedon, which is one of the loveliest places in the country from the late Duke of West- minster, and has a magnificent- town house in Carlton House Terrace. Amongst his other purchases was the. Pall Mall Gazette," which is a great hobby of his. Miss Astor has two brothers, but she is, nevertheless, a great heiress and is, in addition, a very beautiful girl—beautiful out of the common, and not out of flattery to her wealth. The consequence is that her engagement has been rumoured times without number to all the eligibles of this and every other country. Her own choice, however, fell upon Captain Spender Clay, who recently resigned bill

CAPTAIN CLAY. MISS ASTOR. commission in the 2nd Life Guards. He, oa his side, is a very wealthy man and has a ,place near Lingfield. He first came into prominence some years back when Lord 'William Neville defrauded him of 'a large sum of money and was sent to penal ieivitude. The Bishop of London performed the ceremony, assisted by Canon Wilberforce, and 'a special programme of music was ,ar- ranged for the wedding. Over seven hundred invitations were issued and a great crowd of ',nests were present both at the church and At the reception in Carlton House Terrace. The bride was dressed in white satin, simply made, but trimmed with priceless lace. She was attended by eight bridesmaids, four English and four American, her special girl friends—Lady Sybil Grey, Miss Gladys Fellowes, Miss Dorothy Lawson, I\liss Lajeune, Miss Muriel White, Miss Caroline Drayton, and the two Misses Paul. They wore won- derful dresses of sunray-pleated chiffon, shaded from the most delicate pink at the waist to crimson at the hem, and the two little pages wore white satin cavalier suits. Captain Spender Clay was attended by Cap- tain de Crespigny as best man. The wedding presents, as may be imagined, were mag- nificent, and Mr. Astor rve his daughter some wonderful jewellery s

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
NORTHERN LEAGUE.
First Division.
SWINTON v. WARRINGTON.

This fixture was played off at Swinton on Saturday in beautiful weather before 6,000 spectators, several hundred of whom had journeyed from Warrington. Boardman, Naylor and Cooke were absentees fromAthe Warrington pack, but elicient substitutes were found in Morrison, Forster and Harmer. Teams and officials :

Swinton.—Dixon, back ; Gartrell, Valentine, Wall- work and Flynn, three-quarter backs; Kewin and Wil- liamson, hall, backs; Evans (captain), Barnett,Simister, Coletrup, Cheetham, Burrows, Yates and Pomfret. forwards.

Warrington.—Hallam, back; Fish; Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarter backs; Hockenhall and Davies, half-backs ; Thomas, Shurmrs, Preston, Belton, Forster, Jolley, Morrison and' Harper, for- wards.
Referee, Mr. J. Bruckshaw, Stockport. Touch judges Messrs. H. Lowe, Broughton, and J. Edwards, St. Helens.

IDickenson started for Warrington, and play for a time was of a fairly even character. Subsequently ScNinton from a free kick attacked, and poor fielding by Hallam placed the Warrington line in danger. Tile Swinton men time after time swooped down to the ; verge of the Wirepullers' line,but fine defence prevented ; a score, Valentineand tiewin being each tackled within ; a few inches of the goal-line. From a break away by 1 Wairington, Dnies put in a good run, and passing to 1 Harris, the last-named scored at the corner. Preston failed at goal. At half-time the score was :—Warring- ton 1 try (3 points), Swinton nil. On resuming, play was in favour of Swinton, but Hallam gathering the ball cleverly saved the situation. ; Then followed several raids on the Swinton citadel, and Morrison picking up, dashed over after good work 'by Isherwood. Preston's kick was unsuccessful. The home forwards were beaten in the closing stages, and subsequently Hockenball got possession near centre and tricking the opposition scored a really fine try. Fish placed a goal. Wallwork, the Swinton [three- quaiter, received an injury to his shoulder, and retired. Result :—Warrington 1 goal and three tries (11 points) Swinton nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. HALIFAX.
div.p: RUNCORN v. HALIFAX.

About 2,000 spectators witnessed the above match at Runcorn. Halifax were short of Little, his place being filled by Albon. The opening stages were in favour of Runcorn, who gained a footing in their opponems' half through smart forward play. Albon cleared, his line with a fine kick into touch, but eventually the visitors were forced back, and a penalty kick being given against them, Price placed a fine goal. Op resumption Rigg, Nettleton and Williams were conspicuous with a fine round of passing, but a dribble by the home for- wards transferred play to the other end, and Halifax were forced to defend for a long time, Albon repeat- edly saving. Just before the interval Runcorn made another effort, Butterworth, Richardson and Moran I getting to the Halifax line. Rigg and Nettleton, how- ever, found relief, and half-time arrived with the score: —Runcorn 1 goal (2 points), Halifax nil. Runcorn had the best of matter in the second half but there was no ' fprther scoring.
ST. HELENS v. SALFORD : PROLIFIC GOAL
SCORING.

This fixture took place at St. Helens before 4,000 spectators. St. Helens won the toss, and Lomas started and after some end to end play Edmunds got hold and threw to Barnes, who after running half the length of the field kicked across to Thompson, who scored in their own half, and Barnes had little difficulty in placing a goal. The Salford backs indulged in several passing , bouts, but St. Helens tackled well. Salford were again penalised, and Traynor placed a goal for St. Helens. Salford after this livened up, and St. Helens being penalised, Lomas added a goal. The visitorsagain made headway, and Maddocks ran round the opposition and i scored under the posts, for Lomas to place a goal. Following this Traynor placed another goal for St. Helens, who led at the interval by 11 points ao 7. Crossing over Salford were penned in close quarters and Traynor just failed at a penalty. Salford then had a turn, and Lomas placed a goal for them from a free kick. Free kicks seemed to be the order, and, for off- side, Salford were penalised, and Traynor placed a goal from half-way. Salford tried desperately hard to cross the line. Richards, Thomas and Parry being held up repeatedly. Lomas, on time, placed lanother goal for Salford, who were beaten by 5 goals, 1 try (13 points) to 4 goals, 1 try (11 points). Teams : St. Helens—Jones, back; Barnes, Traynor, Devereux, and Hunter, threequarter backs • Edmunds and Hall half backs ; Briers, Prescott, Whiteley,Mooney, Mavity' , Wharton, Thompson and Sherwood, forwards. Salford—Lambert, back; Richards, Thomas, Lomas, and Parry, three-quarter backs; Drake and Maddocks, half-backs; Lewis, Rhapps,Williams,Brown, H. Buckler, A. Buckler, Graham and Hindshaw, forwards. Referee, Mr. W. J. Dance, Morecambe. Touch judges Messrs. F. Hancock, Runcorn, and R. Shaw, Wigan.

div.head: BATLEY v. HUNSLET.
div.p: BATLEY v. HUNSLET.

This game, played at Wakefield through the suspen- sion of the Batley. ground, had a sensational start, Hunslet scoring 2 tries in the first five minutes through Jackson and Wilson. Goldthorpe improved the first. Davies later kicked a penaltyigoal for Batley. In the second half, Davies kicked a penalty goal for Batley, and Goldthorpe a dropped goal for Hunslet. Result : Hunslet, 2 goals, 2 tries (10 points) ; Batley, 2 goals (4 points).

div.head: LEEDS v. HULL.
div.p: LEEDS v. HULL.

At Headingley. Hull had the advantage of the wind during the first half, but Leeds did most of the attack- ing. At the interval nothing had been scored. The second half was finely contested. Evans opened the scoring for Leeds, Littlewood failing at goal. This was followed by a brilliant try to Hull by Frear, bat this also was unconverted.Elßesult :—Leeds, 3 points; Hull, 3 points.

div.head: OLDHAM v. LEIGH.
div.p: OLDHAM v. LEIGH.

At Oldham before 6,000 spectators. Oldham played Al'Lean (late bf Cardiff) at centre. The first half was very dull, and it was just before the interval that Owen scored for Oldham after some scrambling play. WLean scored for Oldham in the second half, and O'Brien scored for Leigh, Johnson improving. Result—Oldham, 2 tries; Leigh, 1 goal 1 try.

div.head: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. WIDNES.
div.p: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. WIDNES.

At Hull, before 5,000 spectators. The Rovers had much the better of the play in the first half. West scored by smart following up, for Madeley to kick a goal. In the second half Kemp, Townsley, Carmicluel, and Madeley scored for the Rovers, two goals being kicked from the places. Carmichml dropped a magnificent goal. Result—Rovers, 5 goals 6 tries (28 points) ; Widnes, nil.

div.head: WIGAN v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.
div.p: WIGAN v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.

At Wigan, befqre 12,000 spectators. Leytham placed a goal for Wigan in the first minute, which was equalised by one from Newbold. Bennett scored for Wakefield, the kick failing. Hal f-tirne—Wakefield, 5 points; Wigan, 2 points. On resuming, Hilton got over for Wigan, Mason goaling. Metcalfe placed a penalty goal for Wakefield. Ler,tham also goaled for Wigan. Result— Wigan, 9 points; akefield, 7 points.

div.head: BRADFORD v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: BRADFORD v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

AL Park-avenue, Bradford. before 8,000 spectators. Playing against the wind, Dechan and Turner scored tries for Bradford, Mosby kicking a goal. Dunbavin was injured, and Bradford finished with 14 men. White- head afterwards scored. In the second half Eagers dropped a goal twelve minutes from the end, and this proved to be the only score of the half. Result—Brad- ford, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points) ; Broughton, 1 try (3 points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.

Warrington" A "V. Swinton "A." Warrington "A' team maintained their unbeaten record by severely de feating Swinton" A" on Saturday. The match attracted some three thousand spectators to the Wilderspool enclosure and a good game was witnessed. Although the Swinton team included several players of repute Warrington at once assumed the offensive and practic- I ally attacked throughout the game, the visits of the ' Swinton players into the home half being by no means dangerous. Their defence however, for a time prevailed and when half time arrived only three points had been scored against them' Davies getting over at the corner. In the second half Warrington's superiority was even more marked and tries were scored by Berry, Davies and Short, Knight adding a goal, the home team in the end winning by 14 points to nil.

WARRINGTON ST. BARNABAS v. WARRINGTON ALBTONS RESERVE.

Played at Mill-lane on Saturday. The home team kicked off and the Albions immediately pressed but were easily repulsbd by the backs. Albions again attacked and from a neat pass by Spooner, Gregson scored. The Saints stung by this reverse pressed in fine style and Barrow scored from a centre but was ruled offside.
