div.head: INTERESTING CONFERENCE AT WARRINGTON.- ---- Alderman !Bennett Speaks in Praise of the Town.
div.p: INTERESTING CONFERENCE AT WARRINGTON.- ---- Alderman !Bennett Speaks in Praise of the Town.
SHOULD EDUCATIONAL AUTHORITIES CONTROL MUSEUMS?

Warrington was on Saturday honoured by a visit from members of the Museums Association and others inter- ested in its work, the occasion being a conference arranged for the purpose of discussing subjects of common interest to those concerned in the work of Museums, Art Galleries and kindred institutions. Representatives attended fiona Blackburn, St. Helens, Warrington, Runcorn, Bolton, Rochdale, Manchester, Urmston, Liverpool, Halifax, Huddersfield, Keighley, Stockport. Birmingham, Sheffield, Chester, Bury and Bootle. On arriving at Warrington the visitors pro- ceededjto inspect the museum under the guidance of the staff and the Museum Committee. The many inter- esting collections of relics of bye-gone ages were in- spected with pleasure. The members of the committee and officials in attendance were :—Alderman Bennett (chairman), Messrs. A. J. Jolley, T. May, J. F. Dutton, C. Madeley (curator), and A. Deane (assist- ant curator.) Mr. L. Greening also accompanied the party. At 4.30 tea was served in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, and afterwards the delegates adjourned to the large committee room for the business meeting, Alderm Bennett occupying the chair. Alderman BENNETT said that as chairman of the War- rington Museum Committee he could not adequately express the pleasure it gave him to welcome the visitors to the good old town. He was rather surprised that so many of them had honoured the town by attending, because latterly Warrington had been widely represented as a vary had, wicked, and corrupt old town. They who knew it best—at least some of them—and understood it thoroughly, did notat all recognize it in the caricatures which had been widely circulated through the medium of the daily Press, and they felt that Warrington was a town of which they had no need to be ashamed. To some extent it had hidden its light under a bushel up to now,land had not been regarded !exactly as a pleasure resort. (Laughter.) It was quite a modern develop- ment to have learned gentlemen of the character that ' constituted that 'assembly coming to honour Warrington ' with a visit, and they trusted that as time went on that kind of thing would' develop, and that they would find Warrington was not altogether unworthy of the attention of their friends in the adjacent counties, and from even a wider area. There were many things concerning the town of which they were, not unnaturally proud. They were very proud of the history of the town which went back to very ancient times, and, in fact, originated in the Roman Camp at Wilderspool. Some of the extraordinary discoveries made by Mr. May the visitors had had an opportunity of examining. They .oere also very proud of the mann.- factures of the town. Warrington was called "the town of many 'industries," and the description was not by any means a misnomer. He always lost count when he endeavoured to arrive at a numeri- cal computation of the number and variety of the industries. Many of them were very enterprising and some had a national and even world-wide fame. They were proud, in addition, of their educational institutions—the Grammar School, Blue Coat School, the Clergy Daughter's school (which had recently been removed to Darley Dale) the Training College, and last, and perhaps best of all, the Warrington Academy which won for Warrington one hundred and fifty years ago the ptle of "The Athens of England." They were proud, and he thought legitimately so, of the Town Hall—not only of the building but of the situation. He thought they might almost say it was unique among the towns of Lancashire to find the home of the Civic Parliament standing in a garden, and that right in the thickest part of an industrial centre. To come to matters more immediately cognate to the object of their meeting, they were proud of their museum. —(applause)—and he thought legitimately so. The Roman antiquities contained therein offered many unique attractions, and the collection of reptiles which they owed to the kindness of Mr. Greening was some- thing which he thought was well worthy of a visit not only from the inhabitants of the town but from people from suirounding centres. The Library,he believed,was the first rate-supported library in the kingdom,a,nd they hoped to have that fact recorded on an appropriate tablet. The natural history room was formerly used as the Warrington School of Art, and in it Luke Fildes, Henry Woods—each of them members of the Royal Academy—and Warrington Wood, the sculptor, were educated under the able tuition of Mr. J. C. Thompson, whose portrait now lookl down from one of the walls of the museum. He (Alderman Bennett) was an in- veterate Warringtonian, and although he was not by any means blind to the defects of the old town, nothing could shake his invincible belief in it and his profound admiration for it—all it errors and omitions excepted. In conclusion Alderman Bennett paid a tribute to the work of Mr. Madeley to whom he said, it was in no small measure due that he had the privilege of welcom- ing the visitors to Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. MADELEY explained that as the Museums Asso- ciation had hitherto met only once a year, and did not by any means include in its membership representatives of all the museums in the country, it was decided to hold conferences with the object of stimulating the feeling of mutual interest and making the Association and its work better known. The first conference was held in Manchester and in order to keep the ball rolling the Warrington Museum Committee decided to invite the members of the Association to hold a similar meet- ing in Warrington. Mr. W. W. MIDGLEV, of Bolton,submitted a paper on "The managing authorities of municipal museums." He said the diversity in character and the difference of nomenclature of the managing bodies of municipal museums must have exercised the minds, he thought, of most of those present. At any rate it had often oceurred to him how and why such authorities came to exist, and perhaps, at the end of his paper they would agree with him that, like variety in the animal kingdom, they had originated for the most part through "accident of birth." Mr. Midgley dealt with the various systems of management at present in force, and quoted the statement of Professor Lankester, the director of the British Museum of Natural History—" Nine-tenths, or even ninety-nine tenths of the persons who sit on municipal and other committees concerned in the management of public museums know nothing about the contents of the museums and never visit them them- selves for pleasure or instruction." It might be, said Mr. Midgley, that that was too sweeping an assertion, but in many centres it must be admitted that it expressed, if not "the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth," at least a good proportion of it; and the fault did not fall upon the gentlemen so engaged because of any particular apathy towards museums generally, but rather that their energies were devoted to the other branches of corporate work in which they were engaged. Or, in other cases, they felt—that was where the museum was a real educational centre—that such work as they were doing, belonged to the com- mittee in charge of the general education of the town, and between these two distracting influences the affairs of the museum were left more or less to the permanent staff engaged, whose efforts, however intense, failed unless they were backed up byasympathetic committee. To the example of the recently-established museums, Huddersfield and Lincoln, they must lock -for the ideal of usefulness in museum management, that was where the managing body was the educational authority of the district. (Hear, hear.) Now-a-days museums were not, or should not be, isolated collec- tions of stuffed animals or miscellaneous relics, but, as had been dinned into their ears at conference after con- ference, collections of objects carefully selected to illustrate labels, these labels to tell the history of the rocks, the animal, and vegetable kingdoms, or to lay clearly before the seeker after knowledge some fact connected with the object exhibited which previously was unknown to him. That system of treatment of museum collections was education in its very essence, and such exhibits taught not gnly the scholars from their schools, but thousands of adult visitors, who in their. youth had no such advantages as were now within the reach of all. It was a type of education which could not be carried on in schools with sufficient com- pleteness; but that it was a desirable feature of the ordinary school curriculum, the curators of municipal museums had ample evidence of by the visits of scholars from the public schools. That a museum properly arranged appealed to the minds of upgrown persons was manifested by the care with which descriptive labels and exhibits were studied. Then why shbuld there be any uncertainty as to the constitution of the governing body of a museum? The Education Act of 1902 made municipal or county authorities responsible for the educational requirements of their respective areas. That responsibility did not cease with a child's school life, for it must extend to the technical training of the youth, and in mostcentres the same authority provided for the educational advancement of those of older growth. Museums were aujuncts to that education; their work dovetailed into the teaching in the day schools, the technical and art classes, and to derive the full value from them they must all be under the same authority, so that their development might run on parallel lines. At present they were the victims of the "accident of birth." As the authority for all forms of secular education, museums came naturally within the sphere of the educational committee's work in any borough or county district. (Applause) An interesting discussion followed. Mr. E. HOWARTH, of Sheffield, was not in favour of making the museum a part of the educational system. It ought to be something more, as it should serve a more pleasureable and enjoyable purpose than the ordinary day school teaching and its instruction should not be so much in the nature of a task.

Mr. T. MAY pointed out that the Managing Authority of the IVarrington Museum included both members of the Town Council and the Education Committee so that in that respect, as in everything else, Warrington led the way. (Laughter.) He sometimes thought the bored Town Councillors, with all the business on their hands, had far more than they could properly attend to. They had to rash from one meeting to another, listen to what the permanent ofliciaN told them had to be done, and do

it without knowing anything at all about it. (Laughter) A leading archaziologist had described the museums of the present day as "ghastly charnel-houses of murdered evidence." When that view was taken, it seemed to him (Mr. May) that museums were not fulfilling their proper function which was to collect and preserve evidence and not to mix up too many things. He , appealed to the curators present when they heard of I local antiquities to do their best to make a selection of the valuable evidence these might contain of historical I and artistic matter, and to arrange them in their natural order. The natural history departments ought not to be at the mercy of faddists or men who were here to-day and gone to-morrow and were thoroughly ignorant and I careless of the subject. I Mr. A. J. JOLLEY cordially supported the general idea underlying Mr. Midgley's argument, Mr. L. GREENING did not quite follow the conclusion Mr. Midgley arrived at that the gentlemen who formed an Education Committee were more fit to manage a museum than a specially-constituted Museum Committee, He also took exception to the statement that the chief function of the Museum was one of education, He granted that Museums could play an important part in the question of education, but the most important part of the museum, in his opinion, was the record and store- house of the things that had been. If he were a member of • Museum Committee he should object to the • rarest and most valuable specimens being lent out for educational purposes to any school the Education Com- mittee might desire. He believed the Education COM- ruittee could do a great deal of work by ordering from the museum an educational series of common objects to illustrate their lessons. He felt the Museums Association had done a very good work in removing the jealousy which existed among museums twenty years ago.

- Mr. Mu:waxy, in reply. said he would be the very last to advocate that museums should be purely educa- tional in their objects. He would point out that thousands of children visited the institutions purely for educational purposes, in accordance with a provision of the Board of Education which allowed such visits, while in charge of a teacher, to be 3ounted as school ;time. The closer in touch the officials of the museum were with the permanent officials of the education depart- ment, the better and more effective would be the result of the work of the two institutions.

The CHAIRMAN did not agree that museums should be absolutely under the control of the education authority, but there was something to be said for the idea that the authorities ought to be in intimate touch and work cordially together. Mr. R. NEWSTEAD, A.L.S. (Grosvenor Museum Chester), read a paper on "The,making of plaster casts," accompanying it with practical demonstrations of' various processes. Mr. W. S. LAVEROCK, of Liverpool, spoke on "The aquarium, vivarium and wardian case as adjuncts to the museum." He strongly advocated the introduction of living specimens of animals, fishes, and plants into museums. Dr. W. E. HOYLE, of Manchester' said they could not too carefully bear in mind that the object of the museum was to preserve materials for present and future study, and everything else was subsidiary to that. If, Mr. Laverock's suggestion were adopted on a large scale members of the staffs would have to be told off specially to attend to it.

Mr. GREENING objected to getting visitors to muieums under false pretences. If it was desirable to have a small menagerie in the town well and good, but he did not agree that it should be mixed up with the museum. Mr. E. E. Lowe, of Plymouth, and formerly of War- rington, had prepared an able and interesting paper on "the inductive method tof installation" and in his absence it was read by Mr. Madeley. Votes of thanks were accorded to those who had written papers and to the Warrington Museum Committee for the admirable arrangements,

div.head: DR AGAR BEET AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DR AGAR BEET AT WARRINGTON.

Services and Lecture at Bewsey Road Wesleyan Church. The Rev. Dr. J. AGAR BEET, professor of theology at Richmond College, and who about twenty years ago worked in the Warrington Wesleyan circuit, preached at Bewsey road Wesleyan Church on Stlnday, on the occasion of the anniversary services. The rev. gentleman is a deep thinker and close reasoner and has attained eminence in the world of religious thought. He has many friends in this town and very large congregatio is assembled to hear his discourses on Sunday. In the evening the church was filled in every part, and the, preacher based his sermon on the words In the begia- ning God created the heaven and the earth." Special music was rendered, and the collections throughout the day were in aid of the trust funds. DIFFICULTIES OF BELIEF. DR. BEET ANSWERS QUESTIONS. In the afternoon a service of a unique character was held, Dr. Beet ansßering questions on difficulties of belief which were submitted to him in writing. There was a large congregation, Councillor D. Tinnion presid- ing. The choir gave very creditable renderings of the anthems "Sing 0 Heavens" and " Abide with me," Mr. B. Wadsworth presiding at the organ. Miss Eckersley effectively sang " Jesu, Lover of my soul "and Mr. J. E. Hannan gave a feeling interpretation of" There is a green hill." The first question which Dr. BEET answered was "Is what we term conversion essential to salvation or can we by living a good life inheritehe Kingdom of sod?" In reply Dr. Beet said the question was not what" we termed" but what the Bible said on the point. The Bible did not say a great deal about conversion. In regard to conversion being essential to salvation, much depended upon what they meant by it. If they meant "Must all other people have the same kind of conversion that !we had?" he said No. .God claimed their homage and obed- ience, but it was a wrong thing to think that everybody must have the same kind of inward experience that they had.

Another questioner wrote "I believe in God as a Divine Being and in the Holy Spirit as a power in my life, but how He dwells in me as a personal being, I cannot understand." Dr. Beet said he had reason by studying the New Testament to believe that the Holy Spirit was a person distinct from the Father, and further he found that in his spiritual life it helped him to think of the Holy Spirit as a person over with him. He asked his questioner to try and look upon the Spirit as a companion who knew every- thing and could do everything. The Spirit, however, would not make them infallible—that he thought was a common heresy of good people. Dr. Beet was asked how it was that the four Evangelihts were able to give the actual words of Christ, seeing that the Gospels were written a considerable number of years after His death. How was it possible to remember such discourses as the Sermon on the Mount? —Dr. Beet pointed out that if his hearers read the three synoptic Gospels they had three witnesses who told practically the same tale and gave practically the same teaching. In the fourth Gospel there was another and totally different type of teaching, but if they studied all the Gospels perfectly they would find they were in complete harmony. That harmony told them that all the teaching came from the same source. It was teaching altogether different from all other litera- ture, and what little discord there was, was in trifles. "If God is omnipotent and all-knowing," asked another member of the congregation, "how is that the doctrine of free-will ? "—Dr. Beet said the question really was "Can the Creator create a free agent ?"God was all. powerful and knew all things. Could He create someone else who would be the ultimate source of his own actions? Dare they say No ? He (the speaker)saw nothing in omnipotence or omniscience to interfere with free will. The questioner continued "If anything takes place for which God is not rasponsible and over which He has no control, God is not omnipotent." Dr. Beet said God had control but he might think tit not to use it. If God had not put sin in the world there would have been no character. We would have been neither good nor bad, but mere auto- matoms.

Another query was " Are the small references to future rewards and punishments purposely left vague as it is God's will that what lies beyond death should always be shrouded in mystery ?" Dr. 'Beet pointed out that all around them, in their knowledge of God just as in natural science, their were impenetrable mysteries. They should not therefore be surprised to find that the future state was shrouded in mystery. They had however, a great deal about it in the New Testament, and what was written there they should do their best to understand. The vagueness was rather the imperfection of human understanding than any vague- ness which God had thrown on the subject. _ _

An interesting question was: "One idea is that God and the good shall shut themselves up in the felicities of heaven and that the evil and Satan will be shut up in hell. By the most charitable calculations the evil exceed the good in numbers and if the fitness for heaven lies in cectain beliefs and professions the number of the elect must be almost infinitesimal in comparison with the number of the lost."

Dr. BEET said he was sorry anyone should put the question in that way. Surely the writer knew better than that. No sane man now thought the fate of any person, saved or lost, would be settled by beliefs and professions. Everyone had a light within him—that inborn light of conscience,—and in the long run they might say that he who followed the light within him would be saved. He that trampled underfoot would be lost. That would answeranother question "What is to be done with those who have not good opportunities?" St. Paul dealt with that when he said " They will be judged by the law , written on the heart." .Even the Gentiles who never , had the knowledge would be judged. It seomed to him (Dr. Beet) quite plain that there was a universal standard of judgment. That was true even in the case of the lowest heathen. All the best missionaries told him that the lowest of men knew the difference between right and wrong. In a Christian country he believed that everyone who sincerely followed his conscience would be led to Christ. The questioner continued "Does not this , mean that Satan will triumph ?" He suggested that the larger portion would be lost, but yet he knew nothing about it. The truth was the Bible was not given to us ti teach us what would become of Dick, Tom, Harry or anybody else. He had no right to say that the large majority would be saved or lost. It was quite clear, that when the Redeemer who shed His blood for every child of man saw the redeemed at the end, He would be satisfied. . Later on a questioner suggested that 'All men would

be saved." That, said Dr. Beet, was not the idea of the writers of the New Testament. On a subject so solemn as that he did not want to make any dogmatic assertions. There were two doctrines he could preach without the slightest shadow of doubt. Nothing was more certain in history than that Jesus announced eternal life with God in Infinite blessedness for every- one who put faith in Him and followed in His steps. On the other hand no one could read the New Testa- ment fairly and shut his eyes to the fact that there was a dark counter-part—that for those who rejected Him there was ruin. They might, however, be sure that God loved the lost people more than they did. The question of punishment, unless in the broadest generalities T was beyond their ken. THE OLD TESTAMENT AND MODERN THOUGHT.

There was a large gathering in the church on Monday evening when Dr. Beet delivered a lecture on " The Old Testament and Modern Thought." Mr. R. GARRETT, Liverpool, preLided. and at the outset remarked that he was pleased to identify him- self with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. Tf he might venture to make the suggestion he wouldsay that one of the weaknesses of the Wesleyan Church consisted in her strength. By that he meant that the unity of thought, and power of cohesion, so strongly manifest in the Wesleyan Church might possibly prevent them looking charitably upon those people and organizations outside their own. They should broaden their outlook and get out of the groove into which continual thought in one direction might have led them. They must re- member they were Christians first and Wesleyans after- wards and that there were other churches besides their own and that every human being in the world, good, bad, or indifferent was worthy of their consideration.

Dr. BEET reniarked that athe 17);:i;ea-t-CiWii;e-r-e-Was much which caused unrest among Godly people. Matter about the Bible .which in their childhood they were told were undoubted facts were now contested—particularly matters concerning the authorship and truthfulness of many parts of the Old Testament. Fifty years ago those contradictions were made by persons who reioctel the most conspicuous points of the gospel of Christ, whereas nowadays a change had come over the scene, certain portions of the Old Testament being rejected by men as loyal to Christ as themselves. All this was very puzzling to thoughtful men and women and especi- ally to the younger members of their church. The whole matter hinged upon the question as to whether the picture of Christ and His teachings as given in the New Testament were truth or fiction. Critics of the Bible had a trick of patting the cart before the horse, by dis- cussing Moses before going to the New Testament. There was a wonderful harmony amongst the writers of the New Testament and one harmonious picture of Christ and the account of His teachings, and they knew howthat picture helped them on in their journey through life. That harmony might not settle such questions as to who were the authors of those books, but it proved beyond all doubt that in the main, substantially and really, the picture of Christ was true. When they read the New Testament they would find that Christ pointed back to a Testament older than His own, and it was evident from that that He accepted the Old Testament not as fiction but as fact, and it was extremely unlikely that Christ would be in error in accepting the Old Testament as a correct account of the earlier revelation given by God to mani. Right through the Old Testament they found every- where the clear knowledge of one personal God in a 4orld given to idolatry, and the forecasting of the spread of the Christian religion such as we were wit- nessing to-day, and the foreshadowing of God's revela- tion of Himself to the nations of the world. In con- sidering the Old Testament we had to look, not upon the unimportant details as to the authorship of the books therein contained, and the dates when those books were written. Nit upon the broad principles, propounded by the writers.' What mattered it who were the human writers , when we recognised the broad principals and recognized that the teachings were not the teachings of men but ofGod,who througk human instruments spoke to us in a way we could all understand; teachings which were §upported later by Christ himself, and which enabled us to look up to Heaven and see Him seated in glory. The usual votes of thanks to the sp,saker and chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: Peculiar Incident with South Cheshire Hounds.
div.p: Peculiar Incident with South Cheshire Hounds.
An unfortunate difficulty caused an early
curtail-

ment of sport with the • South Cheshire Hounds on Tuesday. Hounds found a fox in Cox Bank, and there was a burning scent. The fox, however, refused to run. straight, and eventually bolted into a culvert which passes underneath the canal. He subsequently got to ground. One of the hounds stuck fast in the culvert, and Mr. Corbet, anxious to save him—one of .the best in the pack —sent the others home. It was found that some brickwork had collapsed and water was flowing into the culvert,and not until evening was a rescue effected by tunnelling.

At Newcaaile-on-Tyne, on Wednesday, Joseph Stancliffe,a postal clerk with twenty-two years' service, was charged with embezzlement,. It was alleged that for the past three months he had embezzled £1 per week by removing stamps from parcels handed to him, and replacing them with stamps which had been previously used. The accused was remanded for a week on bail of £lOO, and two sureties of £5O each.

The working man to-day gives more attention to the food he has to eat than his forefathers gave, as he realizes that his health—his bank—depends very largely upon the properties of what he eats and drinks. It follows, then, that the popular article of food is that which is easy to digest; but more popular still are prwparations which are found to aid and strengthen the digestive organs, and also to act as an energiser for the whole system. Dr. yibbles' Vi-Cocoa is such a food.

It places a means in the hands of everyone to build up and maintain a strong constitution, which enables its:possessor to travel his life's journey without the aches and pains which are in so many cases preventable. Thus we come round again to sound common sense based on experience.

div.p: Russian Government implicitly condemns itself by I what is virtually an admission that the con- duct of the Fleet and its previous ord3rs offered no safeguard for neutrals. Quite apart from the outrage on the Hull trawlers, the evi- dence of utter recklessness is overwhelming. People who found it difficult to believe the story of the German steamer Sonntag will note that the captain of that vessel has formally lodged a claim for damages. A similar claim is made by the owners of a Norwegian steamer. These incidents show that the Baltic Fleet was no sooner in the North Sea than it I proceeded to treat all neutrals with an absolute disregard for life and property. The natural inferen,c.) is that it did this in compliance with orders from the Russian Admiralty, and that for the satisfaction of neutrals quite different orders have now been issued. It is suggested that the new instructions should be made public, so that all the world may know exactly what they mean. But it is rather too much to expect a Government to tell us pre- cisely what it has done in a matter of this kind. It is enough for the present that by 'giving fresh orders the Russian Government practically aban- dons its own case. Probably the Commission will put some pertinent questions on this point Meanwhile, we shall have opportunities of testing. the reality and efficacy of the Russian Admiralty's new conception of its duties to nations with which it is not at war.

In the letter wkich we published last week, signed J. Keir Hardie, the Rev. H. Dunnico's name was associated with that of Mr. Horatio Bottomley. This Mr. Donnie° resents, and we regret that we should have given publicity to the imputation conveyed in the letter.

berals have reason to be well satisfied with the fesult of the municipal elections in Warrington. Only three wards were contested, but the out- come has been that three Liberals have been re- turned, while two of the defeated candidates are strong Conservatives. Only one, however, of the three contests was fought on strictly party lines, and this was in Huwley Ward where the Liberal and Conservative forces were marshalled in full array. They had a straightforward fight, unaffected by side issues, and the Liberals won. It was like a Parliamentary election on a small scale, and the rout of the Tory forces is the cause of exceeding great joy in the Liberal camp. The two parties have not tried a fall with one another for some time, and we are sure our Con- servative friends hardly expected a stronghold like Howley to be captured at the first onslaught. Councillor Clegg and his merry men are to be warmly congratulated on their performance. It speaks well for the unanimity and enthusiasm with which the workers went into the fray, for there were some heavy guns on the opposite side. The night before the battle,Mr.R. Pierpoint, M.P., and a goodly array of Tory alder- men, councillors, and J.P.'s descended upon the constituency in order to make assurance doubly sure for Mr. Davies. They were said to have settled the issue beyond doubt. Perhaps they did, but not in the direction intended. i'or "our member" particularly, the result is a decided slap, and ought to induce a wholesome fear of his fate at the general election.

Bewsev Ward unmistakably testified its respect for Mr. Skell&nd, the worthy superintendent of the Ragged School. The result here was the surprise of th 9 day, for probably not a single worker on either side exp9cted to see Mr. Rogers in a minority of 132 votes on the declaration of the poll. He was looked upon as a difficult man to dislodge, especially after nine years' representation of the Ward. Councillor Skelland, however, has proved that his opponent's armour was vulnerable, and though he did not represent official Liberalism his political views are so well-known that Liberals may fairly congratulate themselves on the removal of what has always been cmisidered a blot on Bewsey Ward, in the person of so thorough-going a Tory as Mr. Rogers. Bewsey is Liberal in the main, and will, we think, always be so. C )uncillor Ellison had a hollow victory in Latchford Ward, where Mr. Benson the son-Trader was handicapped by a scarcity of workers.

All over the country, at the municipal lections, there was a grand forward movement by the Pro- gressive parties—Liberal, Labour, and Socialist. As far as can be learned from the returns which have been published, the Progressives have gained ninety-seven seats, against a Conservative and Unionist gain of fifty-two seats. Of the Progres sive victories no less than sixty-three were won under the Liberal banner, and we feel entitled to infer from this fact that the flowing tide is once more, and unmistakably, with us. As the " atily News" says "It is easy to attach too much political consequence to elections which are frequently fought on purely local questions, hut local questions are often influenced sympathetic ally by the political temper of the time, and there can be no doubt that the great Progressive gains have a relation to the revival of Liberalism, which has been so pronounced in the last two years." There is little doubt that the country is heartily tired of Toryism as exemplified by this Government of "mess, muddle and make- believe." Even in regard to the recent,—and not yet past—Russian embroglio,though we all thought that the Government was acting with promptitude, firmness and discretion, it appears as if after all our ministers have come off worst in the duel of wits with the wily Muscovite. This is hardly a fair topic to make party capital out of at present —and there is no need for the doings and sayings of the Government and itE responsible members in respect. to Education, LicenEing and Fiscal Reform have sufficed to make obvious the fact that at the General Election the verdict of the country will be far more decisive than at the municipal polls.

At the cancus meeting of the Town Council yesterday it was derided not to recommend for adoption at the andual meeting of the Council on Wednesday the standing orders relating to con- tracts, which were introduced by Councillor Stott. For the time being thaold standing orders govern- ing the fair wage clause have been reverted to, and a committee has been appointed to consider Conn. cillor Stott's suggested alterations. This com- mittee will consist of ConncillorsTinnion,Wilkinson Maginn, P. Peacock, James Evans and Stott. This is a step in the right direction and should go far to allay the unrest caused by the feeling that the standing orders relating to contracts as drawn up by Councillor Stott and the Trades Council would not operate to the best interests of either the Corporation, the contractors, or the individual workmen concerned.

It was a distinct cause for congratulation that so many members of the Mugeums Association should favour Warrington with a visit on Satur- day. The conference was of more than passing interest and the principal subject debated--the managing authorities of municipal museums—is worthy of careful consideration outside the neces- sarily limited scope of the Association. In a well- reasoned paper Mr. W. W. Midgley, of Bolton urged that as the museums formed a valuable part of the educational system, the education authorities created by the Act of 1902 should be responsible for their control. Like some of the members we fail to see why authorities which are already fully occupied in attending to the primary and secondary education of their respective areas, should be better fitted for museum management than committees specially appointed for the purpose. The War- rington museum with its extensive and admirably arranged collections is a striking evidence of what can be achieved under existing methods. With all due respect,we venture to think that there would be little room for improvement even if the Educa- tion Committee took over the reins.Warringtonians are justly proud of the institution which is always considered by visitors to be a credit to the town.

An interesting discussion waged round the sug- gestion to introdur.e living specimens of fishes, animals and plants into museums. Mr. Greening strongly objected to converting the museum into a menagerie and inducing people to visit it "under false pretences." View- ing the matter from a local standpoint, Warrington people are fortunate in having a well- arranged aquarium and aviary in the Park, so there is no necessity to add these departments to the museum. Then again, the committee have recently done much to stimulate juvenile interest by exhibiting varieties of flowers. It is, of course, conceivable that in some toWns the aquarii\m, at any rate, as an adjunct to the museum would supply a long-felt want and afford pleasure and instruction to people of all classes.

Mr. Stead's opinion of Mr. Hall Caine's new book (just issued by Mr. W. Heinemann at 65.) will be much more interesting than his views on the theatre, because on the one subject he is com- petent to speatc and on the other he is not, The problcm which is raised by Mr. Hall Caine's araniatic story is whether the world, and more espeially Christian people, would accept the parable of the Prodigal Son. It is undoubtedly true that in modern days there has been a reaction in favour of the elder son, while at the most charitable of times one might suspect a feeling of repugnance in select religious circles to the prodigal. A fellow who has disgraced the family name, and wasted the family substance so far as his prospective share was concerned, would hardly expect the fatted calf, or that his father would run to meet him when he came back penniless,hungry, and physically weakened. His old mother would have a place in her heart for him, but the father and brother of our generation would probably be disposed to snub him, and the social circle would make it difficult for him to live down his fault. The real underlying question, of course, is whether there be a danger to the moral well-being of a community in a generous forgiveness. Our own opinion is that in this age of education there should not be. Stevenson's belief was that both fools and knaves generally get paid in this world— the fools first. Prodigal sons are a blend in their early career of fool and knave. They find that nature has awarded the punishment in the weakened will, and the difficulty to struggle back to power. In so far as anyone has offended he suffers. It is well for the world to realise the fact. The outstanding thought which the publication of this novel suggests is that from press and pulpit all over Europe and America to-morrow a sermon will be preached simultaneously on the text: "The wages of sin is death."

Coming Events.

The annual sale of work in connection with Emmanuel Reformed Episcopal Church, will be held in the schools over Arpley Station, on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, next week. It will be opened on Wednesday by Mr. John Taylor, on Thursday by Miss Bessie Dutton, and on Friday by the Rev. John Yonge. The Rev. J. Yonge will deliver two special addresses at Wycliffe Church to-morrow. In the morning his subject will be "Doing the Divine Will the real satisfaction of life," and in the evening" The true message of the Christian pulpit for these or any times."

The annual missionary sermons in connection with the Warrington and District Baptist Union will be held to-morrow in the three local Baptist churches. A public meeting will be held in the Latchford Baptist Church on Thursday evening, which will be addressed by the Rev. Cr. Anstie Snitth. The Revs. J. Manning and R. Wilkins Rees will be the preachers at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church, to-morrow. In the evening Mr. Rees will preach on the difficult and important question. What is Unpardonable Sin ? " A concert will be held in the Parr Hall, to-night, in aid of a fund for the erection of a memorial to the men of the South Lancashire Regiment who lost their lives during the Boer War. An excellent programme has been arranged to which contributions will be made by Miss Arline Harrison (soprano), Miss Mary Collin (contralto), Mr. J. Rabbitt (tenor), Mr. E. Pownall (bass), Miss Kate Beesley (elocutionist), the Apollo Quartette, and Mr. J. McDermott and Mr. A. B. Milliard (humorists). The first of a series of lectures on the construction and management of motors and motor vehicles, was given by Dr. Ormandy in the Assembly room at the works of Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, on Thursday There was a good attendance and Dr. Ormandy's address on electrical accumulators was followed with interest. GREAT 'SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now on UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. The Rev. E. T. Reed.

Our readers will be pleased to learn that the Rev. E. T. Reed, formerly of Emmanuel Church, Warring- ton, has been appointed assistant ministeeto the Re'. F. B. Meyer, B.A. of Christ Church, Westminster, road, London. He will enter on his appointment on the first Sunday in December. Since leaving War- rington over two years ago Mr. Reed has been engaged on the staff of the Children's Special Ser- vice Mission whose headquarters are in London and whose operations extend to almost every part of the world. ASK for CONNINGH AM'S HIGH-CLASS MIN ERA WATERS.—Ad vt. Fire at Wilderspool Brewery.

A fire broke out in the "copper stage" at W ilders- pool Brewery about half past seven on Sunday evening, The outbreak was discovered by Mr. Craddock. engineer to the company, who at once gave the alarm. Mr. Thomas lace, captain of the Brewery Brigade and a good number of firemen were soon on the spot and they succeeded in subduing the flames in about half an hour. The damage is not very great. It is believed that the fire, which broke out in a small wooden cupboard,was due to 'spontaneous combustion of some cotton waste.

div.head: St. John's Literary and Social Society.
div.p: St. John's Literary and Social Society.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this society was held in St. John's schoolroom on Tuesday evening The meeting was in the form of a "Hat 'Night " or night of miscellaneous debates, and was in Charge of the secretary, Mr. J. Bennett. Many interesting and amusing subjects were put forward for discussion, among them being the following, viz. : —" Do you favour Passive Resistance ?" "Is public opinion usually right or wrong ? " "Is smoking injurious to eyesight ? " "Should ladies speak in public ? " etc., etc. Most of the subjects were keenly discussed in the short time available, the members being greatly divided in opinion on some 'of the Amore conti ov,.)rsial points. At the next meeting, on Tues- day, November 14th, Mr. W. E. Bindloss will give an address on "The Picturesque East—personal experi- ences."

Ekirglary in Lovely-lane. Early yesterday morning a burglary was committed at the house of Mr. Henry Alinshall, 31, Lovely-lane. The depredators effected an entrance by slippinc, back the window catch and raising the window sash, and turned their attention to the sitting room. Having stolen a smoker's cabinet and other articles they went into the kitchen and ransacked the drawers, appro- priating a quantity of cutlery and several garments. The police have been informed of the robbery. H. M. ASIITON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Social Service League. Morton seconded the following resolution : " That the past record of the Government being one of mess and muddle and its continuance in power detrimental to thc best interests of the nation we here- by call upon it to resign." This was opposed by Messrs. H. E. Hawthorne and William Ince. An animated discussion took place, and the resolution- was carried by a good majority. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS. A. representative number of the Warrington District Officers visited Court " Kidd " at The Horns Inn, Farnworth, on Saturday October 29th. Amongst them were P.D.C.R.'s Thornley, Maybury, Bullock, Chrimes, D.C.R., Hipkiss, S.D.C.R., P. Peacock, P.C.R.'s Dennett, Powell, Healey, Trustee, J. Walsh, and Bros. Roylance and Dr. Stuart. The meeting was held to receive Bro. Thornley's report of the High Court Conference at Southampton, which was linstructive and interesting, showing an increase in funds for the year of the order of £329,142. During ' this period, the sickness experienced averaged 21 days for juvenile members, and 11 days for the adult members. The damaging influence of dividing clubs against registered Friendly Societies was strongly commented upon especially as the former look after the present day only 'instead of the future. Other important matters were dismissed and after the usual vote of thanks, a substantial supper and social even- ing followed. SUGAR IS W. PER LB. DEAKER.—Advt. Popular Health Lectures. There was a decided improvement in the attend- ance at the second of the series of popular health lectures promoted by the Health Committee in conjunction with the Royal Institute of Public Health which was held in Parr Hall last evening. The lecturer was Prof. C. S. Sherrington, M.A., M.D., F.R,.5., professor of physiology of the University of Liverpool, who spoke on "Fatigue of the body and mind : Its causes and consequence." Mr. Charles White presided. The lecture was fully illustrated with lantern slides. The lecturerer was thanked on the proposition of Mr. J. R. Young. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bri dge-street.Warrinqi rm,— Advt. Local Newsagents' Failure. At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, George Morrall, journeyman ironworker, now residing and carrying on business as a newsagent at 40, Bewsey-street, but formerly residing and carrying on a like business at 90, Bewsey-road, and previously at 63, Bewsey-st., attended for his public examination in bankruptcy. The statement of affairs disclosed liabilities of 232 15s. 7d. and assets of £52 S. 9d., leaving a deficiency of £179 6s. 10d.—The bankrupt attributed his failure to short time at the works of his employers, bad trade at the shop, heavy interest on loans, and household and personal expenditure in excess of wages and profits. He commenced business as a newsagent about four years ago, with liabilities exceeding by about £lO the small amount he had in cash. He first became aware of his insolrmey abou eight years ago, but hoped by the profits of the news- agents' business in addition to his wages to 'redeem his position.—The examination was closed.

Death of Lieutenant-Colonel Cornwall Leigh. The death occurred at his residence, High Legh Hall, on Sunday, of Lieutenant-Colonel H. M. Corn- wall Leigh, after .t.t lengthy illness. The deceased gentleman who was born on November 14th, 1839, came of a very old Cheshire family, which has been seated at High Legh since 1250. He had been associated with the regular army, being a retired lieutenant-colonel of the Grenadier Guards. Be joined the Army as ensign in November, 1857, and served in the 25th King's Own Borderers in England and in the Mediterranean until January, 1864, having obtained his company in 1832. He then exchanged into the Grenadier Guards, and joined the first battalion when stationed in Montreal in March, 186 1, and returned to England with them in October of that year. He was appointed adjutant of the 3rd Battalion Grenadier Guards a few years afterwards, and was promoted to lieutenant-colonel in 1871, and retired in 1876. The funeral took place at Rostherne on Thursday.

Girls' Friendly Society Concert. The concert in aid of the funds of the Holy Trinity Girls' Friendly Society richly deserved the largp measure of support which it received. Held in the Trinity schools it was att-) nded by a crowded audience who throughout the evening showed a hearty appre- ciati on of the items contained in the programme. The entertainment opened with a chorus " England and her King " by about. twenty girls connected with the Society. The singing was excellent and spoke volumes for the patience shown by Mrs. Ralph Johnson, who devotes a large amount of her time to the training oF the girls. Later in the evening Mrs. Johnson contributed two items" Mid the hush of the corn " and Braga's Seranade "for which she was en- cored, bowing her acknowledgments. With both of her items there was, a violin obligato, excellently played by Mrs. W. B. Roberts. Mrs. Roberts also gave a splendidly exe- cuted violin solo and was heartily applauded. The character songs and choruses by a number of local young ladies formed the main feature of the entertainment, taking up the greater portion of the programme, and each was deservedly encored. The names of those forming the chorus were the Misses C. Willis, C. and R. Wallhead, E. Whittle, E. Roberts, I. R.owson, Nora, Dora, Molly and Nancy Fairclough, M. Francomb and- Paulina and Mina Johnson. The soloists were the Misses Daunt, E. Whittle, Mabel Henshall and Ethel Roberts, and each without excep- tion sang splendidly. The selections given were from "The girl from Kay's," "The Chinese Honeymoon," "The country Girl" and "San Toy." Mr. Victor Roberts was the humorist and succeeded in creating considerable mirth, being encored for each of his two contributions. Miss Evelyn Young acted as accompanist.

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN AND NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN AND NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY.

The annual general meeting of the shareholders of this society was held in the District schoolroom, Barks- town, on Thursday evening.—Mr. Thomas Haselden pre- sided and there was a fair attendance of members. The report and balance sheet showed that the profit for the year amounted to £2.134 12s. 4d., which with the uudivided balance from last year of £2,846 3s. 10d.. left a disposable amount of £4,980 16s. 2d. From this a dividend at the rate of 5 per cent. was recommended, absorbing £2,152 18s. 4d., leaving an undivided profit of £2,827 17s. 10d. Four members had redeemed their property, representing repayments of capital amounting to £1,302 12s. 4d.— rhe Chairman, in movinft the adop- tion of the report and balance sheet, commented upon the satisfactory conditions,of the society's affairs.—The election of directors and other officials was proceeded with.
