ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATION.

The Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars held their 32nd anniversary on Saturday last. The pro- ceedings commenced with a tea meeting in the Assembly Room, Bridge-street, nicely laid and heartily enjoyed. A public meeting was held after tea, presided over by Bro. James Woods, L.D., supported by Bro. George Clarke,P.D.E.S.—After an opening hymn and prayer the Chairman gave an interesting address, showing the great need for earnest had persistent efforts at this time in spreading temperance principles, and the wisdom and advantages of an active 1, membership in the Good Templar Order. The following programme was gone through very satisfactorily, every item being well received:—Solo, piano" Tarantela" Miss E. Jackson ; solo, " Ora pro • nobis " Miss 0. Booth; recitation, " Mother " Miss M. Watkins; solo, Mrs. Williams; solo, "The two Cities" Miss E. Woods; recitation (humorous),"Doctor " Mr. J. Warburton; humorous song, "Friday" Mr. W. Howl; a selection of sixpieces from an excellent Edison phonograph, Mr. T. Porter; solo, "Twickenham Ferry" Mrs. Williams; solo," Dolly's Revenge" Miss E. Woods; Lancashire reading," 'Seasonable Address " by Ab-'o th-Yate, Mr. George Clarke; duet, piano "The Sleigh Race" Miss E. Jackson and Miss E. Woods. Another excellent selection of six pieces by Phonograph, Mr. T. Porter. An address was delivered by Mr. George Clarke P.D.E.S., in which he referred to some interesting points in the 32 years' history of the Lodge, showing a good record of hard work, under varied circumstances. Bros. E. Newman and John Warburton who joined the Lodge at its inception, were still active workers, whilst his (Bro. Clarke's) member- ship reached thirty years. Two other members Bro.and Sister Willis sen.,joined Earlestown about 25 years ago but their mcmbership dated back from 1871, when they united with the "Hope of Norbiton" Lodge in Surrey. Sisters Miss E. Woods and E. Jackson and Bro. W. Willis were very efficient accompanists. Thanks to all taking' part proposed in very appropriate terms by Bro. W. Rose P.C.T., closed a very happy anniversary cele- bration.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN URBAN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. The plan of the proposed extension of the isolation hospital, at an estimated cost of £4,400, was approved, and it was decided to apply to the Local Government Board for sanction to the borrowing of that sum for thirty years. BETTING PROSECUTIONS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes, on Thursday morning, James Leigh, Church-street; William Bruce, Cholmondeley-street ; Samuel Mercer, Bridge-street; and Harry Beswick, 128, Moorfleld-road, were each charged with street betting on October 27th, 28th, and 29th. Leigh was summoned on three charges, Bruce on three charges, Mercer on two charges, and Beswick on two charges also, and Timothy Cummings on a charge of aiding and abetting. Mr. Knowles briefly outlined the charges after all had pleaied guilty, giving evidence of the betting trans- actions on the various dates. The police had made a clean capture, having secreted themselves in an empty house from early morning, and saw through a hole in the boards which covered the window all that wenG on. Leigh was fined £5 and costs, the costs in the other two cases, and £1 advocate's fee. Bruce was mulcted in the same sums, likewise Mercer and Beswick. Cum- mings was ordered to pay costs in the three cases.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A ST. HELENS CHURCH'S MAJORITY.

Colonel W. W. Pilkington presided on Tuesday night at a crowded meeting held at the Newtown Congrega- tional Church to celebrate the twenty-first anniversary of the founding of the mission. Dr. Best stated that the mission was founded in 1881, in Cyril-street, and in 1888 a church was built on the present site, and it was considerably enlarged in 1900. The Sunday school had grown from fifty scholars to over 700, and the church was correspondingly crowded. It was urgently necessary that they should as early as possible build a larger church. Addresses were given by Professor H. F. Sanders (the first pastor in charge), the Revs. F. V. Clarke, W. H. Jeffries (minister in charge), and William Rawlinson, Mr. C. Sharples, and Councillor Rudd.

div.head: From Joppa to Jericho.
div.p: From Joppa to Jericho.

There was a large attendance at the Parr Hall on Thursday evening when the first series of lectures, held under the auspices of the Warrington Church Society, was delivered by the Rev. Haskett Smith, who gave an interesting account of a journey from. Joppa to Jericho.—The Rev. Morley Stevenson pre- sided and at the outset remarked that in Warrington we were particularly fortunate in the happy relations which had always existed between the different religi- ous bodies in the town, and he hoped that at any rate, so far as the Church of England was concerned they would always endeavour to maintain that spirit of toleration and charity which was engendered by true Christianity. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. Haskett Smith then proceeded with his lecture, dealing with his subject in a most interesting an:: enjoyable manner, showing by theans of limelight views many places of interest and of Biblical antiquity. During the course of his remarks he removed many mistaken ideas as to the character of the country, and destroyed several erroneous impressions as to the exact meaning of passages in the Scriptures. Principal amongst these was as to the feeding of the prophet Elijah by the ravens when he fled from the wroth of his King. The ravens, explained Mr. Smith, were not as were generally supposed, birds, but were a band of outlaw Arabs who were known as ravens, and Who ministered unto the wants of the prophet during the period of his exile.—Mr. Smith, the manipulator of the lantern (Mr. H. M. Houghton) and the Chairman were heartily thanked for their services.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
Annual Meeting of the Council Next Week.

The annual meeting of the Town Council for the election of Mayor and alderman and the transaction of other business will be held at the Town Hall at noon on Wednesday. As we have previously announced, Alderman Bolton has accepted the invitation to occupy the Mayoral chair for another year, and it is intended to re-elect the four retiring aldermen—Messrs. James Fairclough, T. 11. Sutton A. Bennett, and W. Pierpoint. The Council Committees will also be appointed and will undergo very few changes. Councillor Fulton Smith ¶ill be placed on the Finance and Estate. Museuni„ and Water Committees ; Councillor Skelland, on the Museum, Cemetery and Granasium Committees; Councillor Clegg, Health, Cemetery, and Gymnasium, Committees, Coancillor Wright on the Gymnasium, and Fire Engine Committees. Alderman Smethurst retires from the Health Committee, as does also Councillor Maginn who will be given a seat on the Markets Com- mittee. Councillors Stott and P. Peacock have both retired from the Cemetery Committee, and the latter will be placed on the Street Improvement and Lighting and Paving and Sewerage Committees. The Council at a caucus meeting yesterday appointed Mr.,Josiah Longland as a representative manager of St. Peter's school in the place of Sir. E. J. Guest who recently resigned. They also made the following appointments :—Representative on the Lancashire Asylums Board, Alderman Francornb ; representative on the Lancashire Inebriates' Act Board, Alderman Hutchinson: and representative on the County Rate Joint Committee, rlouncillor A. Peacock. By the defeat at the poll of Messrs. W. Rogers and S. Davies, two vacancies have been caused on the Educa- tion Committee, one of which will be if by Coun- cillor Fulton-Smith, who by his elaetion to the Council ceased to be entitled to act as a co-opted member of the committee. CORPORATION CONTRAC I'S CLAUSES. CONFIRMATION WITHHELD.

At a caucus meeting of the Warrington Town Coun cil, held last evening, it was decided to defer the con- firmation of the Corporation contracts clauses recently adopted by the Connell on the motion of Councillor Stott. Pending their confirmation the Counzil viill revert to the old fair wages clause.

Grave disturbances between Germans and Italians marked the opening; of the Itllian faculty of Innsbruck University. The Italians used revolvers, with the result that six persons were wounded, the bullet in one case touching the heart.

div.head: [By Mr. H. Whitham.]
div.p: [By Mr. H. Whitham.]

Some months -ago John Burns startled the House of Commons by asserting that "Industrial America is hell with the lid off." He stated what was, in my opinion, an absolute truth, and when he went on to say. "There will be. a terrible uprising amongst workers in America against barbarous industrial con- ditions unless employers grant shorter hours, and place child labour under proper restrictions," he fore- saw a condition of things that seems to ma to be imminent, and is a result of many more causes than honest John had in his mind's eye. It really needs a cool, far-seeing, judicial temperament to enable one to say just what the outcome of the struggle now going on between Labour and Capital will be. Will it be a sanguinary struggle for a fair share of the spoils, or will those who sit on the seats of the mighty be able with all the power a strong Government has at its command, to reduce labour to the servile condition aimed at?

America is a Republic. Each individual citizen is supposed to be sovereign in himself. Bah ! such clap-trap, one reads it every day. To my seeing America is fast becoming Russian in its methods of government, and the workman's sovereignty a mere shade without even a shadow. Merriman in his novel "The Sowers" says, "If you educate a hungry man, you set a devil loose upon the world.; and a man with mental indigestion raises hell or cuts his owa throat." Is the American workman a hungry man? Possibly not; yet for all that he may be troubled with mental indigestion. These matters have to be looked at com- paratively. I would be one of the last to claim that the workingman is an educated man, or that his employer even ii educated. If he ware educated, if he knew sometaing more than the three R's he would be mentally fit to look around him and take stock of the religious, political, and industrial situation. He would see in the religious world men and women anxious only to get hold of the loaves and fishes an Established Church 'holds in its grasp; he would see , a well defined line drawn between the rich Bishop and the poor curate, he would see enough to convince ' him of the truth of the statement that were He, who had not where to lay His head to visit this Christian world of ours and take a glance towards either Orient or Occident, He would look in vain for those who would take up their cross and follow Him. If He who preached against laying up treasures on earth were to ask the wherefore of all this strife between nations and individuals, what answer could be given Him besides the one that the nations are fighting for markets, and the individuals are struggling fpr the profits? In politics our educated workingman would search in vain for honour, and integrity. He would see a pagan nation fighting a Christian nation. The pagan fitted with the truest patriotism is defending his home and country. Rotten politics have not made his hands too filthy to touch or look at. On the other hand the Christian nation in its lust for territory, in its greed for markets, has opened the eyes of the world upon the low depths of corruption and greed to which so called Christians will descend. The Boer war proved to Englishmen that the ruling classes are the corrupt classes. In America the Spanish war brought to light' the fact that beef-packers would poison the whole army with embalmed beef, if only it were safe. In Washington the statement was recently made that, "During •the first five years of their contracts with the Government the armour plate makers earned enough to pay for all of their plants with interest." And yet during these five years there was no peace between employer and workman. Our educated workingman, in his glance over the industrial world, would soon have his attention arrested by the state of things he would find in the "sweet land of liberty." lam going to say a few words on strikes and I must ask ray educated friends to approach the subject with caution, first noting a few of the possible reasons why there should be and will be strikes. We have in America a Christian family that takes a great interest in Universities and churches. The former it endows, and gags its Pro- fessors should they dare to anproach political economy from a radical standpoint. In the Church the eldest son of this family teaches a very large class of Sunday school scholars. How well this true son of his father, who is known as J. D. Rockefeller, understands what Jesus meant when he said "Give all that thou hast to the poor" is exemplified in the following : The dividend rate of the tandard Oil Company since the re-organization of Ole company in 1899 has been at an average rate of 50 per cent per annum on its 100,000,000d015. capitalization. In other words, Rockefeller, owning 31 per cent. of the stock issue, has pocketed nearly one-third of 50,000,000d015. annually as his share of the company's profit—a tidy sum of about 16,660,666d015. annually, or close to 1,500,000d015. a month. That makes 375.000d015. a week, or over 50,000d015. a day, for Rockefeller's money works on Sunday, even if he does not. During the past five or six years business has been booming and leaping forward to a surprising: extent, and never in its industrial history has America seen such prosperity. At the same time, strikes and lock- outs were never so numerous. With these conditions them has grown up between employer and employee the most bitter feeling. Law is simply ignored and civilization is at a low ebb. While the press publishes reports of business success, it also makes known to the workers, the surprising, nay, the idiotic wages adopted by the rich to get rid of their stealings. In Europe you can have the women folk of the capitalist leading the wildest of lives. At home these men are building mansions as if they had the purse of a Monte Christo to dip into. With his mansion he must have a wine cellar. His wine must be old, or appear so. He therefore spends some thou- sands of dollars on spiders, so that he can have the web and the spider together. The select rich meet at dinner and chairs are, placed for a number of monkeys dressed in evening clothes, and before they separate the dining room is turned into a farm yard, pigs and fowls being brought in to add to the fun. Recently a party of twenty rich men, I cannot call them gentlemen, rode on horseback into the dining room. Each was handed a plate of food guaranteed not to cost less than twenty dollars. The cook in these mansions has a cook and servants to wait on him, same with the valet, he has his servants and suite of rooms. Is it not reasonable for us to conclude that the workman will ask the straight ques- tion.—Where does all this money come from? It is not said that these rich men do any work. No, they simply speculate, earner everything in sight, they are gamblers, thieves and murderers. These are strong words to use. In Bold-street library is a book "Wealth versus Commonwealth" which proves this, and in a few weeks I nuroose sending to that institu- tion another book. "The inside history of the Carnegie Steel Co.: A romance of millions." lb seems to me all this has a str mg bearing on protectidn. The American workman has concluded he will stand it no longer, so he organises. He is persuaded of the truth of the saying "the more profit the em- ployer makes and the more he wants.' To accom- plish his object he makes use of the meanest and most tyrannical methods the wit of man can devise. Recently the Labour party in their efforts to get an anti-injunction bill made law, questioned the em- ployer's lawyer as follows "Do you, as the reoresentative of employers, in opposition to this bill, urge that it takes from you rights which you now have and which you ought to retain ?" "-Certainly," said Davenport. "Do von claim that such rights go with the ownership of the business and that they are rights vested in you as owners of the business ?" "I do," answered Davenport. "When you speak of the destruction of property do you mean the destruction of the earning power of the mine, factory or railroad ? " cc yes:, "Do you claim that any one who interferes with these things interferes with your business or pro- perty in this, and that such interference should be prevented by law or injunction ?" "Do you claim that in order to successfully carry on business you must have absolute control over hours of labour, wages and shop rules ?" Yes." _ .

It has -1)-e-en the practice of the employer and the politician to pat the workman on the back, and tell him he was the most intelligent and the hardest and best worker the world had in it. The workman sees the cat at last and when he reaches out in earnest for the cat's tail, something will drop. The Chicago strike made a fairly good rumbling noise. A. bigger noise may grow out of it yet. The ways of these men do not average 30s. a week. Their work is so arranged that three and four clays a week make their time. They asked for a minimum wage of IS cents ail hoar. They also asked for the recaz.lition of their ifeion. All they asked for was refused. They determined to strike, did so, and lost.
A strike in the meat packing bminess means a

great deal to those immediately interested as well as the general public. In the first place it is the stop- page of the meat supply. Again, it means a distur- bance in the homes of thousands of families. Added to these features is the attraction of thousands of lawless roughs, known over the country as strike breakers. These men pose as law-abiding citizens and willing workers. They are simply the scum of the cities, and the lazy ne'er-do-wells of the number- less villages that are scattered over the various States. When a big strike is on, these men are gath- ered in by the employment agencies, and many of these agencies are controlled by the Citizens' Alliance which in its turn is but an employers' association. Five dollars a day, bed and board, is the bait that tempts the strike-breaker. I have just gone through a strike that lasted four weeks, and I am likely to suffer the rest of my days through it, although I opposed the strike as much as I could, As soon as the strike was declared the above conditions were advertised through the country, and hundreds of the toughest customers lever saw turned up as if by magic, and let me say it is just here where the trouble will come in, that everyone is expecting. These strike breakers will fight for the p -mad a day of eight hours and bed and board thrown in. They are, as a rule, men who, under normal conditions, do not work. I listened to their conversation, and am satisfied that when the struggle comes the struggle will be as keen between organized and unorganized labour as between the Capitalist and the Trade Unions. The Labour leader of America does not look with favour towards a strike, but as a weapon of defence he intends to hold to it. The strike at Chicago was forced upon the employees in the first place by the packers, who insisted upon reducing a rate of wages already down to the life line. Circumstances obliged the packers to compromise, but their compromise was only a pretence. They purposely forced a renewal of the strike by treating the returning men in a manner which made its instant renewal inevitable. The true meaning of it all is that a well-planned war upon labour unions is on foot, of which the forced packing- house strike is the first battle. When unionism in the packing-houses is broken up, unionism somewhere else will be attacked in a similar manner, the ultimate object being to place workingmen at the mercy of the employers' organizations. What these einployers are capable of doing in their eagerness to get rich quickly is beyond all conception. in Colorado there are large districts which have been under martial law for over a year,and I give here only a sample of what has been the game. Forty men working in the Parkland mina were arrested by the military on Thursday. The prisoners were employed as engineers, firemen, master melhanics and skilled men .in other depart- ments. The citizens taken into custody by the soldiers were guilty of the crime of preferring to belong to ono union rather than to another; that is, they were members of the Western Federation of Miners and had not taken out cards from the Mine Owners' Association."

' This breaking up of the Unions is a serious matter. It would mean placing the workman at the mercy of the wildest competitive gambling system the modern industrial world has yet seen. lam not alone in foreseeing and, in a poor fashion describing " labour conditions of the present, and the possibilities of the future. Professor Goldwin Smith has just said, "He thinks he sees in America the signs of decadence, or at any rate of revolution—the revolu- tion which shall swamp the constitution and bring the good wsrk of the Fathers to a disastrous close." 'Talk of doing away with Unions, and allowing these men of force to "do as they please with their own!" A. Mr. Jerome addressing the Bar Association of Colorado with reference to the condition the State said :—" Ideals amount to nothing: you have got to have steam at the back of them. A masterful devil from hell is a much more inspiring spectacle than an angel suffering from nervous prostration." I fear this is the spirit that now ills the breasts and guides the labour policy of the wealthiest body of em- ployers and investors the industrial world has in it. Take the following as a sample of man's inhumanity to man, and I could give a score of them "FIRE ALL MEN OVER TEITRTY-FIVE." ORDER AFFECTS MANY IN SONIE DEPART- MENTS OF CARNEGIE PLANTS.

Pittsburgh (Pa.), September 25.—The Carnegie Steel Company has issued a circular letter to the superintendents of the different plants and to the heads of departments in the plants, instructing them to employ no men over thirty-five years of age in certain departments, and extending the age limit to forty years in others. The rules do not apply to labourers. The order affects a large num- ber of the most expert steel men. It is said that the announcement was made over a month ago, but great secrecy was observed in its enforcement, and it has only now become known. OLD MEN ARE LIKE OLD HORSES. [Special Dispatch to "The Examiner."] Redding, August 12.—The Mountain Copper Com- pany of Keswick has established fifty years as the age limit for its employees at the mine at Iron mountain and smelter at Keswick. No men over that age will be taken into the service, and it is gradually weeding out old time hands who have passed the limit and putting younger men in their places. DISMISS ALL MEN FIFTY YEARS OLD. New York, August 9.—With the curt explanation that "men over 50 years old are all mossbacks" Philip Childs, general manager of the Barrett Manu- facturing Company at Shadyside, N.J., has issued a general order removing from the pay-rolls all employees who have passed the half-century mark. The only explanation of the company has been that "old men were mossbacks. "The men themselves have been almost too stunned by the order to protest. To come across an exception to the rule of the inhuman is rare, but I give it with pleasure because it is suggestive of another feature of the later question. Herbert E. Walmsley of New Bedford, Mass., is a man among Americans. He is the president of the New England Cotton Manufacturers' Associa- tion. That body was in session the other day, and Mr. Walmsley, in the course of his remarks, went thoroughly into the difficulties of his line of mann- facturmg. Among other things he said: "If again the cotton industry of New England or any particular section of the industry has arrived at such a pass, such a stage in its history, that all that can be done in the endeavour to make ends meet is to reduce wages below a legitimate standard, below what is fair, equitable, humane or expedient, by all means let such portion of the industry leave us and go elsewhere. We want none of it." If all men would approach the wage question as fairly and hs free from prejudice as Mr. Walmsley the problems confronting the wage payer and the wage earner would be easy of solution. HENRY WHITHAM. October 3rd, 1904.

div.head: BRITISH COTTON GROWING ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE BRITISH COTTON GROWING ASSOCIATION.

The subject of cotton growing within the British dominions has occupied much thoughtful attention of late,in view of the shortages which have caused so much distress,and the prospectus of the British Cotton Grow- ing Association which appears in our advertising columns to-day will doubtless be studied with interest. The Association was founded in .1902 with the object of extending the growth and cultivation of cotton in the British Colonies, Dependencies,and Protectorates, and therefore the prospectus can be claimed to appeal in quite a different way to the usual applicatioss for capital. It is undoubtedly a national scheme, and the Government having fully recognized the imperial nature of the Association are cordially co-operating in the work. Au important working arrangement has been entered into with the Secretary of State for the Colonies, whereby in consideration of the work which is being carried on by the Association the Governments of Lagos, Southern Nigeria, and Sierra Leone will during the ensuing three years make grants to the Association amounting to £6,500 per annum. Several of the large steamship companies are at present lending assistance towards the extension of cotton cultivation by parrying freight free or at nominal rates. Should the hopes of the Council be ulfilled, the operations of the Association will ulti- mately develop into a business not only remunerative o itself and of advantage to the grower and user, but one which will be of lasting benefit to the country by providing ample supplies of cotton and by enriching our colonies, who will consequently become better customers for out manufactures. For seven years no dividends can be paid. The list of share- holders, which includes many influential firms, is evid- ence of the importance attached to- the s cheme in Lancashire and Yorkshire, no fewer than 125,332 shares having been allotted. The subscription list will open on Monday next.

A Renter's telegram from Berlin states that at a !performance at the opera on Thursday, at which the lEmperor was present, many ladies were turned back, as 'they appeared in high-necked gowns instead of ' decolletees, in accordance with the Royal command. ' Many ladies in order to obtain admittance improvised low-cut dresses by borrowing scissors from attendants and cutting out the offending portions of their frocks. Amusing and painful scenes were enacted in the corridors, and much millinery littered the floor. At an inquest at Hackney on Thursday on Alfred Millard Lucas, 80. an architect and surveyor, late an inmate of the Hackney Workhouse, it was stated that he was ruined 'by a famous Glasgow bank failure, ohrough which he lost £4,000.

div.head: MR. HENRY ROBERTS J,P., AND WHITECROSS WARD.
div.p: MR. HENRY ROBERTS J,P., AND WHITECROSS WARD.
Address to the Ward Committee. TWO VERSIONS OF THE PROCEEDINGS.

-- We have had two versions of the proceedings at the private meeting on Wednesday of the Wiaitecross Ward Liberal Committee sent in this week, which differ considerably. We append both for the consider- ation of our readers. The first report reads as follows : A meeting of the Whitecross Ward Liberal Committee was held on Wednesday last in the Thewlis-stre?t schools. There was a very good attendance including Councillors James Evans (chairman), Walter Brough, and Thomas Barton, Mr. H. Roberts J.P., and others. The CHAIRMAN in opening the meeting referred to the penalty clause lately discussed by the Town Council and asked the meeting to express its opinion on the subject, in order that his two colleagues and himself may thoroughly represent the views of that committee on this most important question. The meeting unanimously decided to leave their three representa- tives to deal with the matter as they thought best. Mr. Evans thanked theta for their confidence and at once called upon Mr. Roberts to make a statement. Mr. Roberts then delivered an address dealing with the whole question of the recent agitation, in reference to the promoters of it, their objects, their change of front from time to time, their methods of attack and failure. The address was very cordially received, and the various spbakers afterwards were unanimous and very severe in their condemnation both of the agitation itself, and of the manner in which it had been conducted, strong opinions being expressed as to the serious effect the agitation had had upon the good name of the town and upon its material prosperity. Before the close of the meeting the following resolutions were carried unani- mously and with considerable enthusiasm : (1) Resolved—That this committee desires to express its unabated confidence in Mr. Henry Roberts and heartily thanks him for his past services to the town. 12) That Mr. Roberts be asked to address a public meeting of the electors of White cross Ward upon this as early as convenient. After Mr. Roberts had acknowledged the resolutions the meeting terminated.

The second report reads : A meeting of the'Whitecrosi; Ward Liberal Committee was held on Wednesday evening to hear a statement from Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P. There was a good attend- ance and the chair was occupied by Councillor James Evans. After some introductory remarks by the Chairman,he was asked whether the meeting was held under the auspices of the Warrington Liberal Association or whether it was a private meeting. The questioner understood that the secretaries of the ward knew nothing about the meeting till it was called. Tau CHAIRMAN replied that he himself took full responsibility for the meeting. He had consulted several of his friends, and they were of opinion that it would be better to allow Mr. Roberts to explain his position. Mr. Roberts had asked him to call the meet- ing so that he might place his views before the Ward Committee. After some further discussion on this point, during which it was clear that many members of the Com- mittee objected to the meeting being called an official meeting

Mr. "RoßsinTs delivered an address, in which he alluded at length to the Non-Trading agitation and criticised both its inception and methods. At the close of his speech a number of questions were put to Mr. Roberts, and some little heat evolved. A resolution was put and carried thanking Mr. Roberts for his statement. He explained that he had thought it advisable to put his position before the electors of the ward, and would call a public meeting if necessary. The opinion of those present appeared to be that such a. meeting was desirable, but that it should be held inde- pendently of the Liberal Association and a resolution was passed to that effect. [lf any of our readers who were present at the ward meeting thus differently reported would like to give us their own version of the proceedings we should be glad to hear from them.—Ecl."Ex"l,.

div.head: CASUAL VACANCY IN TOWN HaLL
div.p: THE CASUAL VACANCY IN TOWN HaLL
WARD.

Polling to fill the casual vacancy in Town Hall Ward occasioned by the resignations of Councillor Dodds will take place on Tuesday next. Two candidates_ Messrs. A. J. Jolley (C), and W. Benson (Independent) are in the field, and as the trading question is the main issue before the electors, considerable interest centres in the contest. In his address Mr. Benson says he has been in entire sympathy with the movement for the purification of the administration of the municipal life of the borough, having all along been in full accord with the Non-Trading agitation so ably and -tlis- interestedly led by the late representative of the ward, Mr. Dodds, and he will do all in his power to prevent the re-introduction of illegal and immoral trading of any kind. On the other hand, Mr. Jolley repudiates the agitation as a" campaign of calumny ;'which he considers quite unjustified. Both candidates are working hard and the fight promises to be a keen one. The polling station will be at Kendriek- street schools.

MR. DODDS' ADVICE TO THE ELECTORS. Mr. James Dodds has issued a long address to the electors of Town Hall Ward and it appears in full in our advertising columns. He points out that his desire has not been to secure a seat in 1 the Council but to kill improper trading which had been so extensively practised for many years past. His sole object in retiring from the representa- tion of the ward was to prevent Mr. Henry Rolvrts from creeping back into the Council before the issue of the inquiry reports and before he had satisfied the rate- payers that his company would never again trade with Corporation while he was a member of it. Immediately spon Mr.Dodds'nomination for the recent casual Bewsey vacancy Mr. Henry Roberts retired. "He has not so far been nominated for any other ward" continues Mr. Dodds "but it is not unlikely that had I now stood and been returned for your ward, one of his many " com- pact" friends still in the Council would have at once retired in his favour, and thereby necessitated a second resignation on my part. In view of this and of the honour you so generously conferred upon me two years ago, I have felt that while you would appreciate and approve my recent action, it would not be fair to you to run any risk of the inconvenience of a second con- test in your ward, and so I have felt it best to stand aside in favour of Mr. Benson and to wait and watch developments." Mr. DODDS "with respectful sincerity, but without any hesitation "asks the electors to return Mr. Benson who, as a large ratepayer,and a well-known and respect- ed tradesmen, has come forward as a loyal supporter of those principles which the voters so signally endorsed two years ago. He points out that Mr. aolley was "ignominiously defeated" on the purity issue in November 1902, when out of 1,096 votes recorded in the Fairfielek Ward, he only received 158, the balance of 933 votes being given to Non-Trading candidates. Alluding in detail to the trading question Mr. Dodds challenges Mr. Jolley to give a single instance of an incorrect statement in regard to any charge he (Mr. ,Dadds) ever made. "I have made the most definite charges" he states "in regard to the considerable trading of John Buckley and Co., and the enormous trading of the Warrington Slate Company, and every charge I have made has been proved to the hilt." Mr. Dodds proceeds to give reasons why he asks the rate- payers to specially oppose Mr. Jolley,and in conclusion assures them of his profound gratitude for the too kind and generous way in which they have supported him, and for the willing acquiescence in the policy which the other day necessitated his retirement.

div.head: "BELOW THE BELT."
div.p: "BELOW THE BELT."
- - We quote the following from the current issue of the "Dawn." with reference to the" Observer." The com- ments are interesting as coming from a Conservative quarter.

"BELOW THE BELT." "We are a little surprised that our usually fair and always interesting Conservative con- temporary should have used the brave and able article by Miss Pruda Crosfield which appeared in our last issue as a means of prejudicing her distin- guished brother, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, in his fight for Parliament. We want Mr. Pi3rpoint to win, but we do not think it necessary to resort to tactics of this sort to enable him to do so. Nobody could possibly read the article and dream that the writer had any other motive than to serve the best and highest interests of the town. A glib-tongued stranger comes to Warrington and calls it the corruptest place in England—a downright untruth—and thousands cheer him to the echo. A gentle lady, daughter of a family who have for genera- tions been amongst the old town's truest benefactors obviously animated solely by the wish to make it better, brighter, happier. is bold enough to bluntly say that it is ignorant and dirty—which nobody can honestly deny—and straight- way our chivalrous citizens fling mud at her. The Rev.R. J. Campbell lately dared to pen some home truths re the working-classes,and they promptly mobbed him for his pains. He answers their attack by asking them to meet him face to face and reading to them every word in the obnoxious article. Miss Crosfield tells the people of her native town some home truths, too, and like the London mob they squirm at it. She answers them by asking our contemporary to kindly print her words in full. No more in either case is needed, for no fair- minded man or woman can deny that both of them were practic Jly right. When shall we begin to understand that those are our best friends who have the courage not to flatter and lie to us, but just to tell us the plain, homely truth ?"

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

WASTING THE RXTEPAVF,RS' .M 4 )NEY- At the orough Police Court, on Saturday. before Mr. Birchall and other magistrates, Thomas Cullen. of no settled abode; was charged with running away from the borough on April 30th. 1903, and leaving his five children chargeable to the Union.—Mr. Shearer, reliev- ing offic:er. said Cullen was sent to prison for three months in January, 1903, for n3gleoting his children. He afterwards appeared before the Guardians, and they gave him an opportunity to send his children to the institution. He did so and paid a little money for their keep. In July, 1903, he disappeared, did not pay for his lodgings, and had not been seen since. The youngest child had been sent to a relative in Glasgow, and the keep of the children had cost the Guardians 12100. Paisoner was a rubber worker and bad a good situation before he went away. He had not !paid anything since July, 1903.—Cullen said he had only been able to get worklon Messrs. Crosfield's boats occasionally, and when he had money he bought his children a few packets of sweets. (Laughter.)—Cullen was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

Minor Cases.
MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair) Alderman Francomb,Smethurst,C,onncillor Wilkinson,aml Nlessrs Thornton, Hayward, Wright, Burge3; Birchall, W.

Roberts, Pilling. A SING CLAR. CASE.—On the name of Herbert Plump- ton. 23, Jollev-st beingicalled the Cnief Constable stated. that on Saturday night Plumpton was found in an in- sensible condition and as he smelt strongly of drink he was taken to the police station. Dr. Smith was called and applied the stomach pump. This failed to restore Plumpton to consciousness and a galvanic battery was applied to which,after some considerable time, Plumpton responded. He was then taken to the Workhouse Infirmary and there detained. He the(Chief Constable,) would like to withdraw the charge as Plumpton was in no way disorderly. The magistrates allowed the case to be withdrawn. ANOTIIF.R YOUTItIFUL WRECKER.—Peter Aynes (9), 11, Richardson's-row, wis summoned for doing wilful damage by breaking windows in St. Luke's Church, on the 19th October.—P.C. Woods stated that on the date in question he went to St. Luke's Church and there saw the defendant and some other little boys throwing stones. They broke six squares of glass in one of the church windows.—The Chief Constable stated that he had received many bitter complaints from the vicar of St. Paul's so many in fact that he was compelled to do somethinc, very special in the matter and therefore appointecfP.C..Woods to watch the church. The result was he found that the damage was done by little boys like the defendant in the prosecution of whom he received a certain amount of criticism. The vicar of St. Paul's had declined to come forward and prosecute when he learnt the age of the defendant, though he (the Chief Constable) thought that if a man made a complaint to the palic'3 he should have the courage of his opinions and be prepand to come forward and back them up.— The Mayor, in inflicting a fine of ss. said be thought parents should do more to prevent their children doing wilful damage.

TWSDA.Y.—Before Dr. Pox (presiding), Alderman Hutchinson, and Messrs. C. Jackson Elolmes and W. Richardson. WIND) V. Asa Esc.% —Frederick Thomas Spencer, 3, Ohorley-street, was charged with having been chunk in Chorley-street early that morning and also with wilfully breaking ten panes of glass the property of Messrs. Platt, Wilkinson and Cornpany,fustian cutters,Lythgoes- lane, and doing damage to the amount of £l.—Sergeant Smith said he heard a smashing of glass and immediately after he met the prisoner at the end of Chorley-street. He told the officer that he had had a bothar with his brother and was going to his sister's house. Seeing that he had nothing in his possession witness let him go The officer afterwards noticed that ten panes of glass had been oroken at Messrs. Platt, Wilkinson and Com- pany's and afterwards went in search of the prisoner. When he found him he took him to the works and asked him what he had done it for and prisoner replied" for revenge." There were sixty panes of glass altogether broken around the shop.—Prisoner said he only broke three panes, so that his friends would hear him as he wanted to get into the house.—He was fined 20s. and costs. WANTED TO BE LOCKED Up.—Edward Slattery, shoe- maker, last from Stockport, was charged with wilfully breaking a plate glass window, the property of .11r.John Gerrard, Sankey-street, early that morning, dnd doing Jamage to the amount of £S.—P.C. Burton said he was on duty in Sankey-stra.t when he heard a noise. Prisoner went up to the °Meer and said he had broken a window, and wanted to be locked up, as his feet were sore.—Sl attery was sent to gaol for six weeks with hard labour.

Alderman Hutchinson,

div.head: KILLED WHILE OILING MACHINERY'
div.p: KILLED WHILE OILING MACHINERY'
Jury Suggest Automatic Lubrication.

A shocking accident occurred at Whitecross Works on Saturday morning. At about 7.30 Arthur Poole (27), a fitter's labourer, 48, Hulme-street, Warrington, was oiling a patent wire coiling machine when he was caught between the belt and pully wheel of the nvlhine. The accident was not witnessed by anyone, but a man named Charles Stringer heard Poole shout and at once stopped the machine. It was then found to h) impossible to extract Poole from under the pulley wheel NvAhout partially taking the machine to pieces, and when this had been done life was extinct. Poole leaves a widow and three young children. The inquest was conducted by Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, at the Warrington Police Station on Wednes- day. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared on behalf of the White- cross Company, Ltd., Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, on behalf of the relatives of the decease, Id Mr. Clarke, H.M. Inspector of Factories was also pr .ent. Charles Stringer, labourer,' said he was with the deceased at tile time of the accident Poole went down the pit to oil the machinery, and shortly afterwards he heard him shout, and at once had the machine stop r )d. Life was extinct when Poole was got from under the machine.
ln answr to the Coroner, witness sa,id he a 3rsonally oiled that particular machine while it was in motion. He had had no instructions not to do so.

Henry Baines, foreman mechanic, st :tad he had verbally ordered the deceased not to oil the machine whilst it was in motion. Deceased had special hours for meals, so thit he could not oil theta-id other machinery whilst it was stopped during the ordinary meal hours. Mr. Brighouse said he thought it would be better if notices a.boat the oiling of machinery were plap3d in the works. He had always found that verbal instructions on such points were absolutely useless. Mr. Steel pointed out that with regard to the pit similar pits existed in Warrington and other tow.,s. The jury returned a verdict of " Accident I delth " and attached no blame to anyone. They suggested that automatic lubrication shon'd be used in the future, and that printed notices should be placed in the works giving notice that no one was to go down that and similar pits whilst the machinery was in motion. Mr. Steel mid he would convey the jury's recommen- dation to the company. On behalf of the firm he expressed his sympathy with the widow and rels.tives of the deceased.
Mr. Jenkins remarked that he had every reason to believe that the company would treat the widow and children with kindness. THE FUNERAL.

The deceased was an active member of the Moss Rose Lodge 1099 of the Natioral United Order of Free Gardeners, and the organization was well represented I at the funeral which took place at the cemetery on Wednesaly. The se3retery (Bro. William H. Parkes) and a nu:nber of present eqd rlst officers of the lodge attend( 1. The loss of so young and ardent a worker is deeply regrett3d by local Free Gardeners. Brother Poole had been connected with the lodge from youth and since his transfer into the adult section had ablyel filled many offices in Lodge and District. He had gained the esteem of all his co-workers,and a vote of con- dolence expressing the members' deepest sympathy has been forwarded to the bereaved wife and children. As an additional mark of respect an artificial wreath was sent bearing the Lodge inscription.

div.head: Crimean Veteran's Funeral.
div.p: Crimean Veteran's Funeral.

I At the Warridgton Cemetery oa Monday the I remains of the late Sergeant William Bodle, a well- known and respected Crimean veteran, of 118, Wilderspool-road, were laid to rest. A large number of townspeople witnessed the last rites, the service in , the chapel and at the graveside being conducted by the Rev. G. H. Carnson. The lesson was read by the Rev. B. Weaver, of Swinton. The chief mourners were the widow (Mrs. Bodle), Mr. and Mrs. W. Bodle, Mr. and Mrs. James Bodle, Mr. and Mrs. R. Bodle, ' Mr. T. Bc. lie, Mr. B. Bodle Mr. W. Bodle, jun., Mr. An d Mrs. Martin, Mr. and Mrs. Jackson, Mr. H. ; Martin, Mrs. Gartland, Mrs. A: Galand, and Mr. Gartland. There were also present some old heterans ; I —Colour-Sergeant H. Corney, Colour S3rgeant H. B. Bowers, Colour-S)rgeant Sp3ndelow, S3rgeant Arm- strong, S3rgeant Catchpole,S3rgeant-Major Nunnerley, I and Quartermaster-Sergeant Lake —Corney and Nunnerley being two of the few remaining Crimean heroes. Others at the graveside were the Rev. John Gunnell, Messrs. W. Fletcher, H. Landon, T. Bowers, Foster Jackson, and J. Peters (from Messrs. Fletcher, Russell's works), Francis Dixon, A. E. Ashley, George Weaver, James Weaver, G. Jones, T. Gritchley' Harding, Nunnerley, Page and many others. Floral tributes west sent .bv the following ;—" Will," "Richard and Maggie," "Kate," (Tenbury), directors and staff of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Mr. W. Fletcher, Miss Fletcher, Mr. Harding and family, Mr. and Mrs. J. Robinsbn, Mr. and Mrs. -Bilsborough, Mr. and Mrs. G. Weaver, and Mr. P. Harrison.

CANON MAITLAND WOOD'S NEW APPOINTMENT. Canon Nfaitland Wood, who has been appointed by the Bishop of Chester to the archdeaconry of Maccles- field, in succession to Archdeacon Woosnam, has been vicar of Runcorn since 1886. Apart from his parochial work, in which he has shown capacity as an organiser, he has taken some considerable part in diocesan affairs, and, in addition to holdinc, an honorary canonry, he has served as rural dean of 6 Frodsham, proctor for th e diocese, and examining chaplain to the Bishop. He has been in orders close upon forty years, and his ministerial experience has all been gained within the diocese of Chester.

PLEASANT PAPLAGRAP lIS
WHAT is sauce for one may make a goose ut another.

• You can't tell how valuable a girl's affections are antil you are sued for blighting a set of them. ENGAGED.—Tramp : "Is missus in, please ? " Servant: "Yes ; but she's engaged." Tramp : "Well, I don't want to marry her." "So you know Frau Dr. Wolff ? She's a very talented .woman—she's mastered three languages, and also her husband." • IT isn't much to the worm's credit to turn when trod upon; any old barrel-hoop will do the same thing. "CAN'T understand how Mrs. Smiley can waste so much of her time with her pet dog." " Well,. you would if you had ever met her husband." " FALSE-HEARTED beauty," he sobbingly said, "I shall never love again." " No? " asked the heartless one. " ;-I shall start now to save money."
CRUEL FATS : "Miss Oldly- is one old maid who doeSn't try to conceal her age." " Yes ; but she knows it's no use." " Why ?" "Her twin brother lives with her."

TOMMY told a policeman that there was a person in the next street tearing up the pavement. The policeman hastened round the corner, to see a man energetically running after an omnibus. "1 SUPPOSE," he said, as they undulated round the hall, "that -my mother would be awfully worried if -she knew was here. She thinks it is a terrible thing to danqe." "Oh, never mind," the girl Said ; "site wouldn't know you were dal-tang, even if she saw you."

A WOMAN living in the north of England, not being able to tell the time by the clock' was asked one day by a friend how she knew wheu it was time to get her husband's dinner ready. She answered : When the big finger points to the pantry door and the little finger to Mrs. 's meaning her next-door neighbour then I know." _

Biggs : There you quite make a mis- take, my dear fellow ; my misfortune is really worse. I never catch my proper train. You al- ways see me waiting patiently for the next. •

As a famous comedian was travelling on a steam- boat he seated himself at the table and called for some beefsteak. The waiter furnished him with a small strip of the arliele, such as travellers are usually put off with. Taking it up on his fork, and turning it over, and exivnining it with one of his peculiar, serious looks, the comedian coolly re- marked, " Yes, that's it ; bring me some." "1. say, said he, softly, " have you been a prisoner lung in this—this menagerie?" " Inn," said the lady, " prisoner' isn't exactly the word in my case. You see, fin the landlady, and it's 1 who feed the animals." GENTLEMAN to dog-dialer "I gave you a high price for this dog last week because you warranted it to be a good house-dog. My house was baokea into last night, and the dog never even barked." Dog-dealer: " No, sir ; I quite believe yer. He was too busy lookin' 4t the burglars, so as to be able to identify 'ern, to even think of barkin'.. If you was out with this 'ere dog, and was to meet them burglars, he'd kmow 'ern in a minute. He ain't no common barking dog;-- he's a regair 'tective. an' worth 'is weight in gold, he is."

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Plans for tile New Building Passed.
LIVELY DISCUSSIONS.

A meeting of the Warrington Bortrd of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on NVednesday, Mr. A. Brooks presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkirson, Miss Broadbent, Rev. Father Mercer, Dr. Murray, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. W. Houghton, A. J. Jolley, J. Payton, W. Hickman, J. Billinge, T. Ritchie. R. Forshaw, G. Mather, G. Thompson, J. Talton, M. W. Seton, W. Flannagan, NV. Bolton.J. C,Sutton,(clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schools),
APPLICATION FOR INCREASED SALARIES
At a meeting of the Padgate Schools Committee, an application signed by several officials for an increase of salary was submitted. The consideration of the mat- ter was deferred for six months.

div.head: SKELETON PURCHASED.
div.p: A SKELETON PURCHASED.

At a meeting of the House Committee it was repor- ted that the Masters and Dr. Braide had purchased the skeleton and other articles required for the proposed lectures, and the cost totalled £ll is. Gd. They had, however, successfully pressed for a 15 per cent. reduc- tion. It was decided to pay the expenses of the depu- tation out of petty cash.—The Committee instructed inquiries to be made as to whether certain afflicted persons could be received into special institutions dealing with such cases.
EXTRAORDINARY INCREASE IN THE COST OF VACCINATION.

A letter was read from the Clerk to the Ashton- under-Lyne Union pointing out that on the 13th inst. that Board passed a resolution to address a petition to the Local Government Board with a view to the re- ductioni of the minimum fees payable to the public vaccinators under the Order of 1838. He had been directed to request that the Clerk to the Warrington Board would place this communication before his Board and inform him of the decision arrived at. He (the clerk) forwarded for the information of the War- rington Guardians a copy of the return of the cost of vaccination for the four years prior and subsequent to the Act of 1898 for which it appeared that from 1894 to 1897 the cost was £637 7s. 3d. and from 1899 to 1992, £3,974 Os. 11d. Mr.HICKMAN : Shame! Does that increase apply to this Union?
The CLERK said the charges for the Warrington Unioa had increased to about the same extent. The letter was not discussed. A TENDERING FIR' COMCLA.INT.

Messrs. PENDLEBURY and Co., Warrington, wrote pressing for a reply to their letter complaining that their tender for coal was not accepted although it was the lowest. The Clerk said he had informed the firm that he had no instruction from the Board to give them a reply. The CHAIRMAN said he was not present at the meet- ing of the House Committee when the matter was dis- cussed and he could not say what arguments were used He believed one or two of their Newton friends could enlighten them on the subject. He understood they were of opinion that Pendlehury's coal at Pendlebury's price was not as good a bargain as Evans's coal at Evans's price. The, Board were not bound to reply to the letter. The question was whether they considered it anact of courtesy to do so. Mr. FoßsHew moved that the letter lie on the table. Mr. JOLLEY seconded.

- - Mr. HICKMAN moved an amendment that a reply be sent to the effect that a majority of the committee thought they were accepting the best tender. There was a difference of opinion on the question, but he was not present when the tender was accepted. Mr. THOMPSON seconded. The amendment was defeated by nine votes to eight. THE PROPOSED NEW BUILDING. WARM DISCUSSION.

Messrs. WILLIAM and SEGAR OWEN attended to explain the plans which they had prepared for the pro- posed new building,to accommodate 104 infirm inmates. It was reported that the Building Sub-committee had approved the plans and estimates, together with the site suggested by the Local Government Board. Mr. WILLIAM OWEN informed the Board that the new block would contain beds for 104 inmates, and there would be sitting room accommodation. Mr. JOLLEY moved the confirmation of the sub-com- mittee and observed that if there was to be any difference of opinion, they had better have a clear issue before them. They had not to consider the propriety of erect- ing the buildingsbecause the Board had already decided that matter and had instructed the sub-committee to report as to the best way of carrying out their wishes. The committee had considered several alternatives and that morning they recommended the acceptance of the plans prepared by Messrs. Owen. The acceptance of the planCanct estimates vould commit the Board to an expenditure of £6,900 on the building, but the question of furnishing and other extras was a matter for further consideration. The Board would be getting slightly more accommodation for considerably less cost than many members seemed to imagine would be involved when the scheme was fully discussed. The Board decided to erect a building to accommodate not less than 100 inmates, and some of the members sug- gested that the expense would be anything from £lO,OOO to £15,000. They had before them a scheme which had already received informally the approval of the Local Government Board and they had an opportun- ity of securing a building with 104 beds for just inside £7,000. He ventured to think that showed the committee had tried to carry out the instructions of the Board to secure the erection of an inexpensive building as faithfully as possible. Mr. FORSHAW seconded. He was agreeably sorprised to find that the cost was not higher. The Board knew how necessary the extension was, and he hoped the members would support the adoption of the minutes. Mr. THOMPSON pointed out that when several Guar- dians expressed the opinion that the cost would be £15,000 they did not refer to the skeleton of the build- ing, but to the completed and furnished erection. They would find, before they got to the end of the under- taking, that they would not be clear with £7,000 or £B,OOO. He, however, thought that the Board could not do better than support the committee. Mr. HICKMAN moved an amendment that the matter be deferred for twelve months. He said the arguments previously used against the scheme had not been met, and to his mind they were stronger now than they were before. He did not see that there was any immediate need for the new buildings. They hadalready buildings I which might be utilized to answer their purpose for Isome considerable time. He would ask the Board to bear in mind that there'were buildings which could and ought to be used, but which were not being utilised at present. On the last occasion he opposed the scheme, they were told that they were likely to have a great influx of inmates. He would , point out that that influx had not occurred, but on the I contrary there had been a considerable reduction. Last week there was a reduction of twenty-six and the week I before the numbers showed a• decrease of sixteen. I From a statement prepared by Mr. Jenner Fust, he found that from 1885 to 1895 the expenditure of the Union increased by about £l,OOO. In 1895 it stood at £17,370, but at the end of last year it had risen to £25,276. The Guardians were supposed to be economists and yet they spent money at that rate. Mr. JOLLEY : I rise to a point of order. What has that to do with the plans before the meeting. It may be relevant to a discussion of the principle, but that has already been settled. Mr. HICKMAN • lam moving an amendment.

Mr. JOLLEY : It is out of or-der. It is not really an amendment but an attempt to raise the whole issue which has been settled by the Board. Mr.lliciotAN :It is not the first time I have been ruled out of order, and I know what to expect if I:differ in opinion from some of you. U know what I have suffered for differing in opinion, but I shall maintain my right to free speech and private judgment for all that. We have been going the pace and it is time we utilized all the buildings we possibly can. We shall do no harm by deferringlthe matter for twelve months. I am doing my duty to the ratepayers who have to bear the burdens. If the ratepayers had to decide it,they would not accept the plans. • I Mr. RITCHIE seconded. He strongly protested • against this reckless expenditure of the ratepayers' •, money, bspecially considering the bad state of trade. He spoke for the workingmen and it I was not fair to thrust that burden upon them at the present time. The scheme could afford to wait. As Mr. Hickman stated some time ago,they were known throughout the country as the spending Board land they were still trying to go on in that way. It was about time the curb was put on. Considering the high rates and taxes, it would be most absurd to spend £lO,OOO or £12,000 on a new building. Miss BROADBENT said some of the Guardians did not ' seem to realize that it was never economical to encour- age pauperism. If they did not have a Workhouse • sufficiently large for the size of the union, pauperism would increase by leaps and bounds. Mr. BILLINGE said the buildings which were un- occupied had been condemned ten years ago.if the Guar- dians practically used them, it was only by the courtesy I and consideration of the Local Government Board in- spector. It was absolutely necessary for the Board i to erect a new building. The more buildings they had the better would they be able to administer the Poor I Law, and, if possible, to minimise paup3rism in the Union. I Mr. JOLLEY said he regretted very mi,ch the difference ' of opinion, and still more did he regret the tone in which Mr. Hickman had seen fit to move what he called an amendment but what was an attempt to re-open I alseparate question. In his (Mr. Jolley's) judgment I that was not a fair thing. To quote statistics of twenty years ago, without any explanatory observa- tions was grossly misleading and unfair. Mr. Hickman failed to state theta number of additional duties bad I been put on the Union during that time and naturally , they had increased the expenditure very considerably. I The Board were entitled to expect better things from i a gentleman who had held the post of Chairman of the • House Committee than the statement he had made as to there being a large amount of accommodation in the institution which was not in use. Mr. Hickman, if he did not know, ought to know that that statement was I inaccurate, and a very small amount of trouble would

have tihow n him that it was both inaccurate and unjusti- fied. Mr. Hickham had the opportunity of serving on the sub-committee and declined to do so. If he had served on the committee and ,riven the time and atten- tion which the members of the committee had given to the matter he would have understood the real bearings of the question. He (Mr. Jolley) objected to any mem- ber of ttiat Board or of any public authority getting up in the presence of reporters and making a clap-trap speech Mr. HicKmAN : I rise to a point of order., I hope you will withdraw that. Mr. JOLLEY . I shall not withdriw it.
Mr. THOMPSON : I think Mr. Jolley ought to with- draw the remark.

Mr. HICKMAN : I shall claim the right to reply. zq Mr. JOLLEY (continuing his speech) : about subjects with which he is imperfectlyacquainted, and with which he ought to be fully acquainted. Continuing, he said Mr. Hickman had the opportunity of assisting in carry- ing out what he (Mr. Jolley) hoped would be an impor- tant progressive step in the administration of the Poor Law in that Union, but he refused and then threw unfair criticisms on the action of the committee who were absolutely unanimous in their recommendations. Mr. Jolley expressed surprise at Mr. Ritchie's speech, and remarked that out of respect to his chairman at Newton (Mr. Billinge) who had been an active member of the committee, and had given a great deal of time and attention to the work, Ur. Ritchie might have employed more courteo us adjectives. He (Mr. Jolley) had spoken so:uewhat warmly, but he felt warmly. He did not think it was fair treatment for members of public bodies to accord to their colleagues who had given time and energy and such abilities as they possessed to the Work when all that was offered in reply was a subterfuge. The CHAIRMAN: May I ask Mr. Jolley to withdraw one word?
31r. IircKMAN: I aaa not in the habit of using clap- trap. Mr. JOLLEY withdrew the remark.

The CEIAIRMIA.S, in alluding to the increased expendi- ture, said they were constantly complaining of the in- creased vaccination charges, and they alone raised the estimates by thousands of pounds per annum. On a vote being taken the amendment was declared lost.

Mr. RITCHIE pressed for the names to be taken and after some discussion this course was agreed to,although Mr. Jolley protested that it was against the standing orders. There voted for the amendment :—Mrs. Wilkinson Messrs. Hickman, Ritchie, Sutton. Payton and Bolton The other members opposed the amendment which was declared to be defeated by a large majority. Mr. BILLINGE moved that the Board approve the additional expenditure of £5O on asphalt and £250 on tiling in the bath rooms and lavatories. Mr. JOLLEY seconded and pointed out that the esti- mates made no provision for furniture wnich, in a similar building at Burnley cost £5OO. 'Mr. °WWI said an enlargement of the electrical plane would be necessary. . The proposition was carried, and the Board rose.

div.head: lOW
div.p: lOW
THOSE NERVOUS WOMEN.

Half the letters daily laid upon the writer's tableare from nervous women. Poor souls! What shall be done with them, or for them? Used as lam to the tales of invalids of every sort, it is the complaints of nervous women that most strongly appeal to me. They suffer throughout their whole being. To them no day is brigiat, and June is dreary as November. It is not the fault of these women that they are as they are. They would have things different if they could. Bad health is the sole cause of their trouble, and from bad health they perceive no way of escape. But there is a way of escape ; and Mrs. Mary limes, of Five Ways, Bourneheath, near Bromsgrove, once an almost helpless invalid, was fortunate enough to find it. Writing on July 21st, 189 S, Mrs. Helms says: "It was in the early part of 1890 that my illness began. I felt tired and weak, and had no energy or spirit for anything. My appetite was poor, and the little I ate oppressed my chest terribly. My heart, too, acted very strangely, and seemed to flutter as I moved about the house.

'After a while," continues Mrs. Hemes, "my legs and feet became so swollen that I could hardly walk. For weeks together I got but little sleep, and was too worn out to do my usual housework. Most of my time was spent lying on the couch. "As time went on I grew worse. I was deadly pale, and so extremely nervous that any uncommon event or sudden noise grely excited me. "In this way I passed three wretched years, being attended by a doctor most of the time. He took great pains with my case, doing his best to relieve me; but though I took his medicines, and faithfully followed his directions, I made no real progress towards recovery. "It was in July, 1893, that I received a pamphlet, wherein I read how other women who had been troubled exactly like me had been cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup. I believed the statements in the book, and re- solved to try the effect of that medicine in my own case. A few days after. I began to take it my con- dition improved. I could eat without subsequent dis- tress, and what I ate strengthened me. Continuing to take the Syrip I fought my way back to health step by step. Gradually my nerves ceased to trouble me, and eould work by ay and sleep by night as well as ever before in my life. Thanks to Mother iSeigel's Curative Syrup, my health is now perfect." Many things have happened during the last eleven years, but in all that time no illness has come to Mrs. Hemes. Writing again on March 22nd, 1904, Mrs. Hemes says: "I am not in the least nervous now. In every respect my health is excellent—could not in fact, be better. To be nervous is to be afraid of one's own shadow. It is intolerable misery ; but it can be evaded as Mrs. Hemes evaded it.

div.head: ST. HELENS COLLIER'S SHOCKING DEATH.
div.p: ST. HELENS COLLIER'S SHOCKING DEATH.

Mr. Brighouse, county Coroner, investigated the St. Helens drowning mystery at the Town Hall on Tuesday when Mrs. Hart, of Stubshaw Cross, Ashton, identified the body which was taken from Ravenhead Dam on Sunday morning as that of her brother, William Simm, who had lodged at 6. Dorothy-street, Thatto Heath. Simm was thirty-six years of age, and a collier. About two years ago, he met with a serious accident at the Lea Green Colliery, and after being in hospital soma time he was awarded compensation. He had not worked during the two years.—Mrs. Chisnall, the deceased's landlady, said that six weeks ago Simm received £23 from the compensation funds and £l2 103. from his own club. He wes always a very heavy spender, and the money went very quickly in drink. A fortnight ago he borrowed some money from her and left the house say- ing he was going to cash a cheque, and would be back at dinner time. She never saw him alive again.—The Coroner: What money was found on the body?— Sergeant Stewart: One penny.—Tbe Coroner: So he had gone through the £37.—Mrs. Chisnall : Yes.—The jury returned a verdict of" Found drowned."

A London telegraph clerk who committed suicide through over-study and consequent breakdown thought he was responsible for the Russian war and the weathe It is stated that the Tiverton labourer, Arscott, wh died suddenly last week, has left £4OO to the Wesleya Chapel in the town. Arscott was for many years in th employ of the Council as a roadman at 15s. a week.

Nowadays all good tables, instead of being Fitted with moulded rubber cushions (which sooner or later get very hard) are fitted with cushions built up of strips of very yielding rubber, and on all such tables the eccentric angle at which a very fast ball rebounds after striking

„ a cushion at no great angle, has to be reckoned with. A double at Pool or Pyramids, if played with any speed, is quite a different stroke on a fable with fast resilient cushions from what it is on a tablwith slow, hard cushions. In certfiin positions this fast ball eccentric angle is of the greatest assistance in keeping a ball out of baulk when playing an in-off. In fact, it is not too much to say that many a stroke whi(.T) played on a table with hard cushions sends the object ball into baulk to remain there, would, if played in exactly the same way on a table with very • yielding cushions, not only not send the object ball into baulk, but actually keep it in the upper half of the table.

Diagram 23 shows such a stroke—an ordinary powerful forcing shot easily within! the com- pass of any fair player. On a table with cushions that give very little, the object ball taken half-ball would rebound off the first cushion at an angle which, though owing to the great strength of the stroke is less acute than the angle of incidence, is sufficiently acute to cause it to travel into baulk (as shown by the thick intersected lime in the diagram. On a table with. very yielding cushions, if the stroke were played in an exactly identical manner (that is to say, catching the object ball with only the same degree of fulness) there would be no fear of driving the object ball into baulk, and it might even remain in the upper half of the table a 4 shown by the thin intersected line in diagram 24 In such a case the object ball behaves in exactly the same manner as the ball struck with thv? cue in the stroke illustrated in diagram 22 (given last week.)
DIAGRAM 24
A stun stroke cannon.—By playing very full on to the red it may be prevented from going down the table.

Diagram 24 showes a stroke often played by profe6sionals and good class amateurs. If the ordinary player will place the balls in a posi- tion similar to the one shown on the diagram and play the screw cannon in the way ,he is accustomed to play such a stroke, be will find that although he can make the cannon easily enough the after position will always be uncer- tain, for the simple reason that in making the cannon he drives the red down the table. A. good player, on the other hand, keeps the red in the upper part of the table by playing almost full on to the red. In playing full on to the red, if any considerable screw be imparted to the cue ball the ball will screw back to a certain extent, and the cannon will be missed.. The correct way of •playing the stroke is by playing moderately strong and very nearly full on to the red, and hitting the cue ball only just slightly below the centre, the stroke being what is knoWn as a "stun stroke," the slight screw and the nearly full impact with the object ball stunning the cue ball so that it travels comparatively slowly on to, the second object ball. • If in the stroke shown on diagram 23 the cue ball be struck .with right hand side, a slight amount of side will be transmitted to the red ball, and. as already shown in an earlier article this transmitted side will be the reverse side on the object ball (left hand side on the red ball in diagram 23), so that .the tendency of this trans- init;ted side will be to keep the ball up the tahle-.• Many good players have, however, an exaggerated idea of the effect of transmitted Side in a stroke of this nature. Occasionally in Playing such a stroke, the object ball after hav- ing struck the side cushion at an angle slightly towards baulk will be thrown straight across tli‘ table. and from The second cushion the re- bound vill actually be to the upper part of the Transmitted side could never account for such an eccentric angling of the object ball (shown on diagram 24). The effect of the side Which the object ball undoubtedly carries is only noticeable when the second cushion is k. and if, any transmitted side remained after the contact with the first cushion the ten- dency 'of this side would be to take the ball dowr. and not up the table. Instead of the side on the object ball being transmitted side, it is Side imparted by the cushion to the ball which - has been imbedded in it.

The reason that such a stroke as shown in diagram 24 is occasionally noticeable by a keen observer of the play of leading professianols, is simply because all big matelis are generally Playe4.l on brand new tables with cushions in the best possible condition.
