div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 5, 1904.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I THE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. I THE FREE CHURCHES.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at 'Dutton on Tuesday, when
THE WELSH REVOLT.

there were present: Messrs. A. R. Norman (presiding) The eyes of the Free Church world are now T. Baxter, T. Wright, J. B. Chadwick, 3. 3lounfield, J. Douglas, W. M. Morris, C. Roylance, J. Spruce, J. T. directed to Wales and the gallant stand the Collier, J. Temperley, A. G. Guest, G. Egerton, Welsh nation is making against the Govern- Warburton, G. Pilling, J. L. Jones, H. Eyes, H. M. "lent and its education policy. The great Davies, J. H. Davies, J. Bolshaw, J. Whitley, J. Hallows, S. Horton,_ J. Whitlow, C. E. Linaker, Welsh Convention at Cardiff showed the A. Mounfield, W. Harrison and Admiral Jones wonderful unanimity which prevails• among all Parry, with G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. Hough. (assistant, clerk), J. Cook, J, Riles,W. DePrez (relieving officers), the Welsh Education Authorities, and which is J. Cunnah (master). backed up by the nation at large. As the WORKHOUSE CHILDREN'S BIRTH CERTIFICATES. . Welsh correspondent in the "Free Church The Registrar General wrote stating that on the application of a number of Boards of Guardians Chronicle" says: "One cannot recall within supported by a deputation from the Association of Poor living memory any occasion on which the Law Unions he had applied for and had obtained the sanction of the Local Government Board to alter the nationalist spirit in Wales has run so high as at regulations issued for the guidance of registrars of present. All petty jealousies and divisions births in such a manner as to authorise them to omit have been swallowed up in the one idea of as- all direct reference to the Workhouse in future in the interests of children born in the Workhouse. The. sorting national rights against a Government Registrar General asked for the Runcorn Guardians to ! which has wantonly trampled upon them. At furnish them with their proposed description of the address of their Workhouse. • the outset of the controversy I ventured to 1 Upon the suggestion of the clerk it was decided to suggest that the Government, in its desire to describe the workhouse for the purpose of the register- buttress up Church interests in Wales, had ing of the births of children as Northwick-road, Dutton. , overleapt itself. That is turning out to be the case. The Government in their blindness have forced the Welsh people, out of a sense of self-respect, into revolt, and upon them , and their backdoor advisers must rest the conse- - quences."
THE UNEMPLOYED.

_ The Clerk to the Poplar Union wrote asking the Runcorn Guardians to support the following resolution which had been passed by his Board. "Seeing that the question of the unemployed although 'host acute during the winter months, is a widespread, constant and national question,this Board of Guardians consider that all local efforts to meet the case are only temporary and merely touch the fringe of the question. The Board there- fore considers that the question should be taken up and dealt with on a national basis, and hereby requests the Government to at once summon a special session of Parliament to deal with this grave and pressing question." Mr. PILLING pointed out that thelPrime Minister had intimated that if strong enough representation were made he would call a special autumn session of Parlia- ment to discuss the question of unemployed. Person- ally he thought that the sooner the question was gone into the better. (llear,hear.) Mr. Collier moved that the resolution be supported.
SUPPORT OF ENGLISH CHURCHES.

Meanwhile the Welsh people will. have the hearty support of English Free Churchmen in their struggle. At a recent meeting of the General Committee of the National Free Church Council a resolution was passed assuring the Welsh leaders that they would support their policy. If necessary, financial aid would be afforded in case of a deadlock, to provide education in Nonconformist schools in Wales.

Mr. Pilling seconded. Admiral Jones-Parry moved that the resolution be not supported. He thought the calling of a special sitting of Parliament would be involving tremendous expense for nothing. . Mr. Horton seconded the amendment. On a vote bein taken, the Board decided to support the resolution.
THE TAXATION. OF LAND VALUES.

A letter was read from the Glasgow Corporation, ask- ing the Board to support tie action of the Corporation in seeking to bring about the taxation of land values. Mr. Collier moved that the action of • the Glasgow Corporation be supported. The present system, he said, of grouping land and buildings together for the purpose of taxation was very unfair. Mr. Morris seconded. Mr. Hallows objected to the taxation of land values. He thought that as soon as land was taxed rents would go up. Upon a vote being taken, the action of the Glasgow Corporation was supported by 12 votes to 11. THE COST OF PAUPER LUNATICS.

The Clerk to the County Asylum Committee wrote stating that the cost per head for the maintenance of pauper lunatics in the asylum had been fixed at Bs. 9d. per week for the quarter ending 31st December next. Mr. Baxter remarked upon the increase in the cost as compared with the cost last year. This he thought was due to the building operations which had had to be undertaken in order to increase the accommodation at the asylum. The Chairman thought some means could be devised whereb_y harmless lunatics could be treated at a less cost. It was not necessary that the same elaborate arrangements should be made for them as were made for more dangerous patients. (Hear, hear.) The matter dropped. RETIREMENT FROM THE VISIT IN' (; COMMITTEE. Miss Eliza Andrews wrote stating that as she had removed from Runcorn she felt compelled to resign her position on the Workhouse Visiting Committee. Mr. Baxter moved a vote of thanks to Miss Andrews for her services in connection with the committee. The Chairman said Miss Andrews was always pre- pared to help forward any good work. He had pleasure in seconding the motion. The vote was heartily accorded. THE GIRLS IN THE PANTASAPH HOME. At the last meeting of the Board, a discussion ensued upon the question as to whether any girls from the Runcorn Union in the Pantasaph home were kept in the home when they were old enough to work, and the clerk was instructed to obtain information on the subject. On Tuesday, Mr. Ashton reported that one girl aged 18 was still in the home, but was being kept there because she was not physically fit to go out to work. Situations were being found for two other girls who were 16 years of age. Those were the only girls from Runcorn who were in the homes and who were old enough to work. Mr. Hallows thought every child above a certain age should be taken out of the home and sent to work, and that they should not be kept in the homes and there educated at the expense of workingmen who whilst pay- ing for them could not afford to give their own children a very good education. If a good many workingmen were not Englishmen they would give way to temptation and send their children into the workhouse in order that they might receive a better education than they were getting at home. The Chairman said he did not see that Mr. Hallows' proposal was at all necessary, as he did not think there were any girls in the home who might have been earn- ing their own livings. He was sorry those remarks had been made, as it might give the public the impression that they were keeping children in luxury when they ought to be working, whereas they were doing no more for the children than was necessary. Mr. Hallows said he failed to see why they should keep girls of 16 in the homes. The Chairman pointed out that in the home the chil- dren had a means of learning a trade. When the chil- dren were kept in the workhouse they had not the opportunity and had to be sent out as apprentices, whereas in the homes they learnt a trade, and when sent out of the home were able to take up fairly good posi- tions. Sometimes when they sent children out as pprenticea,the employer did not prove satisfactory, and the children hag to be taken bacic again after an absence of a few months. Moreover, the farming out of children was often unsatisfactory, and they had had instances afforded recently where children had been farmed out and improperly treated. He contended such homes as the Pantasaph Home were a protection as in them the children were properly cared for, and he certainly would rather they sent their children to such homes, than that they should,be sent out and left to the mercy.of individuals who perhaps only took them for pecuniary reasons. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Spruce: I contend that when children reach tho age of 16 years they ought to be earning their own living.

div.head: ILLNESS OP MR. JOSEPH STOKES.
div.p: ILLNESS OP MR. JOSEPH STOKES.
- A vote of sympathy with Mr. Joseph Stokes in his long illness and an expression of satisfaction at his recovery, was passed.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.

WARRINGTON ROYAL v. ORFORD BARRACKS. Played at Walton; The teams were equally matched, and the result was a draw of three goals each. For the Warrington Royal, Bailey (goalkeeper) played a first class game. WEST DERBY v. STOCKTON HEATH.

At West Derby. Stockton Heath, in the first half had most of the game, R. Pierpoint scoring two goals. In the second half West Derby struggled vigorously to get on terms, but the Stockton halves held them in check, and the visitors resumed the attack to the close, R. Pierpoint adding two more goals. Result: Stock- ton Heath, four goals ; West Derby, nil.

STOCKTON HEATH 2ND WEST DERBY 2ND. At Grappenhall. After some give. and-take play Smith fed Longdin, who raced away nicely, and passing to Skelton, the latter opened the scoring. West Derby soon made their presence felt, and were not long in making the score equal. From now till the interval the visitors held the upper hand, and mis-hitting among the Stockton backs enabled them to add two more goals to their score.

111111 SALE "B" V. LATCHFORD "A." Played at Sale on Saturday. This game ended in an easy win for the visitors by three goals to one. All the goals were scored in the first half. Banks netting the ball in each case for Latchford.

div.head: GOLF.
div.p: GOLF.
THE WARRINGTON CLUB.

The fourth and final qualifying round for the Captain's (Alderman Fairclough) prize in connection with the Warrington Golf Club took place on the links at Hill Warren on Saturday. A large number of cards were taken out and the lowest net score was returned by Mr. Fred Pendlebury, who thus wins the silver button. The following gentlemen have now qualified for the prize: —Mr. T. E. Jackson, Mr. Homer, Mr. William Richard- son, snd Mr. F. Pendlebury.

div.head: HOME-COMING OF GIPSY SMITH.
div.p: HOME-COMING OF GIPSY SMITH.

After a wonderful series of missions in South Africa, Gipsy Smith, Missioner of the National Free Church Council, has returned to England. A very stirring welcome awaited him at Exeter Hall, when the Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., President of the National Council, extended a hearty welcome home and the congratulations of all Free Churchmen on the results achieved. The audiences addressed by Gipsy Smith in South Africa amounted to some 300,000 persons, and 13,000 or 14,000 entered the Enquiry Rooms at the various missions. This is a marvellous result, considering the small population in South Africa. Gipsy Smith, while resting prior to commencing his winter campaign in England, is revising the diary which he wrote in South Africa. This, with numerous illustrations of scenes in connection with the missions, will be published almost immediately by the National Free Church Council.

div.head: DR. CAMPBELL MORGAN'S INTENTIONS.
div.p: DR. CAMPBELL MORGAN'S INTENTIONS.

Dr. Campbell Morgan, who has returned to this country from America after three years' work there, made his first public appearance at the Gipsy Smith home-coming. His pastorate of Westminster Chapel commences at the end of October. Dr. Morgan intends devoting three days a week next autumn to conducting missions in various parts of the country under the auspices of the National Free Church Council.

div.head: WORK OF THE GIRLS' GUILD.
div.p: THE WORK OF THE GIRLS' GUILD.

An interesting little gathering has just taken place at the Memorial Hall consisting princi- pally of women workers in connection with the N ational Free Church Girls' Guild. Mrs. Burnett Smith (" Annie S. Swan ") presided and made a charming little speech. She con- fessed that her work lay more at the desk than on the public platform, but she felt that the most interesting subject in this world were the young women. Mrs. Percy Bunting, who read a paper on "The Work of the Guild," related experiences she had had in visiting the music- hall. She had been surprised to hear the girls of the Guild visited music-halls, and she felt that she should be acquainted with anything which touched the life of her girls. Accordingly she visited a music-hall, and, whilst she did not see much harm in it, she felt better able to give the warning word where necessary. Accounts from various towns were given showing the progress of the work. Mrs. Charlotteßenliam, organising secretary, reported that there were 400 Guilds, and 12 Permanent Homes devoted to the work of the Guild.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

November is the month for a great number of Municipal Elections. The Free Churches are taking more and more interest in these contests. Under the Education Act, Borough and other Council became Local Education Authorities, and from these Councils members of the Education Committees are chosen. It is of great importance that those who have .in their charge the machinery of the Education Act should be men who will carry out its pro- visions without injustice. Free Churchmen should use their votes in the highest interests of education and the children. The main in- justice of the Act can only be remedied at the next General Election, but the choice of the administrators of the Act is in many cases now to be decided, and every effort should be made to secure justice.

USEFUL AID TO CHURCH EXTENSION. Localised magazines as aids to Church work are coming more and more to the fore. The National Free Church Council, recognising the importance of counteracting the sacerdotal ; tendencies of many of the Anglican publications, issues the "Free Churchman" as a means of spreading Free Church principles and giving the Gospel message in a bright and attractive form. I An advance issue of the January number, with j the programme for 1905, has just been brought , out, and is indeed a handsome production. Practically all the Free Church writers of note contribute to the programme, which is one of the thost varied and interesting issued. Pre- sented with every copy of the January issue is a handsome portrait gallery printed by a special process. All interested in the question of localising should send to the Publication I Department, National Free Church Council, Memorial Hall, London, E.C., for full particulars.

div.head: SCOTTISH CRISIS.
div.p: THE SCOTTISH CRISIS.

The United Free Church of Scotland has the deepest sympathy of English Free Churchmen in the deadlock at which they find themselves, owing to the failure of negotiations with the " Wee " Church. The conviction is growing stronger and stronger that the matter can only be settled by Parliamentary intervention. It is difficult for the ordinary English mind to appreciate the subtleties of Scottish theological differences. The National Free Church Council has just published an admirable little guide to the question. It is written by Mr. W. Grinton Berry, M.A., and is entitled, "Scotland's Struggles for Religious Liberty." It forms one of the series, "Eras of Nonconformity."

div.head: YOUNG FtEE CHURCHMEN'S AUXILIARY.
div.p: YOUNG FtEE CHURCHMEN'S AUXILIARY.

'Considering the short time the Young Free Churchmen's Auxiliary has been established, its progress is satisfactory. Mr. George S. Hirst, of the Memorial Hall, London, who is Acting- Secretary for the Auxiliary, has issued five or six interesting leaflets by such leaders as Dr. Clifford, Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., Rev. C. Silvester Horne, M.A., ttc., explaining the work of the Auxiliary and how it may be undertaken. There should be a great future before this new branch of Free Church work.

LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday.

Town Hall Ward Election. Sir,—When I proposed Mr. Benson as a candidate for Town Hall Ward it was not because I had It more friendly feeling for him than for Mr. Jolley whom I have known mach longer,but because I believe that the Inquiry will prove a lasting benefit .to the town, and Mr. Jolley is of quite a different opinion. Therefore I desire and hope that the electors of Town Hall Ward will back up the Inquiry by returning Mr. Benson,—Yours truly,
S..KENN'ON.

div.head: Rev. H. Dunnico and Mr. Keir
div.p: The Rev. H. Dunnico and Mr. Keir

• Hardie, M.P. Sir,—l beg to state that the manifesto, a copy of which appeared in your issue of the 15th does not "purport" to be but is an accurate copy of an Independent Labour Party manifesto with special pre- face by Mr. Keir Hardie, M.P., that appeared in an edition of the " Workingmen's Times" some years ago and was reprinted in Reynold's Newspaper for July 24th,1904. I pass over the personal.' imputation which Mr. Keir Hardie has thought fit to make against me. That will be dealt with at the proper time. Yours truly,
HERBERT DUNNICO.

"The Observer "and the Inquiry. Sir—For kreeks, rather months, I have watched your contemporary, the Observer, and made a mental note of the editor's comments on the Trading (capital T please) and Non-Trading agitation. His sympathies have been with the Traders. He said there never would be an Inquiry,the Non-Traders didn't want it,there never would be a report ecc., Ste. He opened his columns to special articles on the subject, written by persons evi- dently in the know, letters, ditties. and rhymes that suggest the atmosphere .of a bar-parlour, and the mental calibre of its habitues. But now that we have had the Inquiry and the Report, what does he say? Scarcely anything last week and this week,—not a word! The little he did say didn't carry conviction with it—it was disappointing. Can it be that the report has opened his eyes and he daren't say so for fear of offending his erstwhile friends? It is too important a matter. to be dismissed with a few words, but it is on a par with his "lack of courage" with regard to Mr. A. H. Crodield's letter. lam thank- ful that it doesn't require the" Observer " to help me to make up my mind re Trading or Non-Trading. When I was a youngster I used to hear my father deprecate anyone with" an axe to grind" going into the Town Council. Axe to grind—l used to wonder what it meant in that connection. But now I know, thanks to the Non.Tmders, and as long as I live I will never give my vote for a man who has an axe to grind. —Yours truly, October 29th, 1904.
"CONVINCED."

The Pealth of Warrington. —Our Markets. Sir,—ln your issue of the 29th ulto, under the 'above heading, I read with great interest a letter signed "L.W.E." in Which the writer made some very good and reasonable suggestions. The letter ended with the words "I trust then that what I have written has not been written in vain, and that something will be done. Again, I ask where are our Labour men and Social Service Leagurers? Where, oh where are these aspiring people, anxious for the welfare of the common classes?', Our friend "L.W.E." is undoubtedly aiming in the right direction, and I should think from the tone of his letter he is a progressive. Now, as a member of the Social Service League, I should like to remind your correspondent that this organization is only in its infancy, a few weeks old, and needs feeding and nourish- ing for a time in order that it may grow and become a power for good. "L.W.E.' seems to be a person of intelligence and I invite him to join our league where he ,will have every opportunity to state his views and also see what the brotherhood is trying to do to educate the people and bring about those reforms which are so sadly needed. I have not much patience with people who hold aloof, doing nothing but criticise the efforts of those who are working. Let our friend throw in his lot with us and do his best to obtain the realization of his hopes, so that what he has said in his letter may not be in vain, but that something shall he done.—Yours &c., E. W. EVANS. 30, Norris-street, Warrington, November 2nd, 1904,

Sir.—l was very pleased to see in your issue of Saturday last that the serious condition of our markets has been noticed by at least another person than myself your correspondent L.W.E. has hit the right nail on the head in drawing the attention 'of the ratepayers to the clumsy method adopted in the removal of the refuse from the markets. It has been my misfortune to be passing the fish market when the refuse bins were being emptied and the stench arising from the cart was more than I could stand. I have had to beat a hasty retreat What kind of a committee can we have to allow the bins to be emptied in that fashion?- As your corres- pondent says the bins ought to be carried bodily away and empted where the st ench will not annoy anyone and clean bins brought to replace the ones that were full. lam not at all surprised at the death rate in Warrington being so high. In regard to the arrangements of stalls (as one whose business takes him to many markets,) I can safely say that not in any market in England will you find cheese stalls next to fish stalls with only two feet of apace separating the two. lam told by a hawker calling at my house that there is a great demand for fish stalls in the market. If that is so can the committee be doing their best for the ratepayers? Why I wonder is a cheese stall (and sweet stall also), taking up space that ought to be devoted to fish. Cannot the empty stalls In the beef market be utilised for cheese and sweets? These are all matters for the Medical Officer, who I hope will act with a view to pressure being brought to bear on the committee, compelling them to do some- thing in these matters.—Yours A RATEPAYER.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PRESENT AT lONS.—A very interesting gathering took place in the Wesleyan School on Friday night last, when the friends and wellwishers of Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Smith, gathered together to present to them a token of their regard, upon their leaving Penketh to take up their residence at Helsby. The gathering was of a social character, songs and music being rendered, and refreshments were also partaken of. The gathering included all the prominent Wesleyans in the neighbour- hood, Mr. Smith having been connected with the Chapel since his boyhood, and having held most offices in con- nection therewith. He has also, up to the time of his leaving the village, occupied the arduous posts of Choirmaster, and Superintendent of the Sunday school. The present consisted of a splendid mahogany writing desk, and silver inkstand, bearing the inscription "Pre- sented to Mr. and Mrs. J. A. Smith on their leaving Penketh, as a token of affection and esteem. Mr. G. Withinshaw made the presentation in a few well chosen words. and said how hard it would be to fill the place of Mr. Smith. Mrs. Garnett, Mr. Dodds, Mr. James Watson, the Rev. John Gunnell and others also spoke of the good work done, and their regret at the departure of Mr. and Mrs. Smith. Mr. Smith was much affected and thanked the gathering for himself and his wife for the beautiful present, and for their kind expressions.—Mr. Within- shawl also on behalf of the gathering, presented; the Misses E. and A. Hughes with a Bible and Hymn Book respectively. The Misses Hughes are also leaving the village, and have been for many years earnest workers in the Chapel and Sunday school, and their services will be much missed. The singing of the hymn "God be with you till we meet again," concluded a very pleasant gathering. MUTUAL bieIIevENIENT ASSOCIATION.—The usual weekly meeting of the above, was held in the Wesleyan School on Wednesday night. The night was taken by A Bennett Esq.,of Warrington,who gave a very interest- ing paper entitled 'A glimpse of Garden City." Mrs. R. Garnett was in the chair, and at the conclusion, the lee turer was cordially thanked for his efforts.

div.head: FOR WORKING MEN.
div.p: FOR WORKING MEN.
BY JOHN TAYLOR Author of " Search Lights on Lana, Labour awl. Social Problems."
TALKING IT OVER WITH THE PUBLICAN.

"The caution with which investment in licensed premises is at present regarded seems to be chiefly due to doubt as to how the compensation scheme will work out in practice.—" LICENSED VICTUALLERS' GAZETTE." During my recent election campaigns I have made many attempts to interview the average publican, and get him to say what he honestly thinks about the Brexvers'Endowment Bill, and what benefit he expects to get out of it personally. Everybody knows that the licensed victuallers as a whole have declared that "their trade is their politics," ' and they will vote for that party in the State that will ,do most for them. And when the Compensation Bill was first introduced into the House of Commons they welcomed it as a wise, and just, and statesmanlike I measure, that would give them peace and security in their calling. ' But a closer acquaintance with that measure has opened some of their eyes, and they are talking very differently about it to-day. I.—HOW DOES THE FREE HOUSE PUBLICAN REGARD IT? A short time ago I was sent to a large agricultural village in the Midlands, and one of the innkeepers there was engaged to drive me round to all the neighbouring villages, so I had plenty of opportunities of finding out what he thought about the measure. I said one day, 1" Driver, what is this new Licensing Bill going to do for you ?" He said "It is going to take about thirty pounds a year out of my pocket that I shall never see I again." I must not tell you who this man was, or where he lives, for if I gave his show away like that he would , never give me any more information. I may tell you that this big village was once a prosperous little market I town, and though its population has declined it has kept 1 alive nearly all its licensed houses. There are fourteen public-houses for only twelve hundred people, and my driver is the owner of the only free house in the place All the rest are tied houses, belonging to big brewers and their tenants have to take and sell whatever the brewers choose to send them. We pulled up to speak to a man on the road, and when we drove on again I said, "Driver, does your friend keep a public-house?" He said, "You bet he does, for the public-house does not keep him. He came into my house one night in a bit of a temper, and threw a two- shilling piece down on my table, and he said the •com- pany might as well have it, for it was all he had taken that day. I know for a fact that his house had been a dead loss to the brewers ever since they bought it, for nobody will drink their ale, unless they are very hardened topers indeed, and the licence would have been surrendered long ago if there had been no prospect of compensation. And why should I pay thirty pounds a year more than lam paying now to buy out a rival like that? I have a free house. I can buy whatever the people want, and my customers know that I shall never poison them with bad beer, or kill them with raw spirits. I do a good and prosperous business, and I shall never want to surrender my licence or claim compensation for it, and I know the licensing authorities will never shut up the only free house in the place without some very weighty reasons. So my thirty pounds a year will go to cover a risk that is never likely to happen to me, and if it closes one or two of my tied house rivals their loss will be no gain to me." But what about the scale of compensation and the apportionment of the compensation money?" T asked. Oh, there will be plenty of law suits and trouble about those things shortly," he said, "and I have no doubt the lawyers will reap a rich harvest over these quarrels?' The Act of Parliament says that" a sum equal to the I difference between the value of the licensed premises, including the amount of any depreciation of trade fixtures and the value those premises would bear if they were not licensed premises, is to be paid as com- pensation to the persons interested in the licensed premises." In other words, if the premises were worth five hundred pounds without a licence, and fifteen hundred pounds with the licence,the compensation money would be a thousand pounds. "But how are these values going to be ascertained, and who are the persons in- terested in the licensed premises ?" I asked. The driver replied: "Now you have hit on the weakest points in ' the Act. It gives no protection whatever to the barmaids and waitresses, and servants, who often have to work from six in the morning till eleven or twelve at night. These unlucky slaves can be dismissed at short notice, and cast adrift without any compensation whatever, and in nine cases out of ten the landlord whose name is on the licence can be got rid of just as easily. And so far as the scale of compensation is concerned I can tell you what will happen in our village as soon as there is any compensation money to be had. One or two of the poorest houses in the place will be offered, because it does not pay to keep them open, and they will expect as much money for their worthless property as I should get for my house, that is doing ten times the business. There will be no end of lying, and cheating, and roguery as soon as there is a bit of money to handle. The Bill is all right for the brewer with plenty of worthless tied house property in his hands, but it is all wrong for such folks as me." IL—WHAT DOES THE TIED HOUSE TENANT SAY ABOUT IT?

Well, it is very difficult to loose his tongue and get him talking freely, because he is a poor filave who dare not say all he thinks. My driver introduced me to a village innkeeper who has suffered many things at the hands of the brewers. They send him beer that no free house can sell, and this man could not sell it if he had not a monopoly of the trade in the village. During the harvest time there was a little mutiny among the labourers about the vile stuff that was served out to them, and one workman who happens to be a teetotaller turned the laugh on them by telling them that "if the beer were any better they would not get a chance of it, and if it were any worse they would not drink it, so they ought to be contented." My friend the tied house tenant is a monopolist in the sense that he has the only licensed house for miles round, and yet he frankly confesses that no man can make a living out of it under present conditions. He has a bit of land and a few cows,and I have no doubt he makes more by farming and trading than he does by selling beer. When the Licensing Bill first appeared his brewer called on him one day and urged him to Use his influence with his customers in favour of it. "But where do I come in for aishare of the compensation? " he asked. " Ob, it would pass the wit of man to devise a scheme that would compensate everybody all round, and those who ought to be compensated are the men who have risked their money and who own the property," was the reply. He says the new Compensation Act will raid his pockets to the tune of nearly twenty pounds a year, and he is not going to pay it. His task-master, the brewer may pay it for a year or two, and as soon as there is any compensation money to be had he will sell out and sacrifice the licence. "And where do you come in then?" I asked. "Oh they can get rid of me any time by giving me three months' notice, and if they give me notice before they offer to surrender the licence I shall be gone before the money is paid, and they will get the lot. The Com- pensation Act is about as respectable as highway robbery. It turns adrift the landlord whose name is on the licence, and the waiters, and boots, and servants, and it hands over the money to the brewer who owns the house."

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
KEEN CONTEST AND A LIBERAL VICTORY IN HOWLEY WARD.
Mr. Skelland's Return for Bewsey.

With contests in only three wards—Howley,Bewsey, and Latchford—Lgeneral interest in the Warrington Municipal elections on Tuesday did not run high. Each election, however, was keenly fought, and the candidates had the assistance of an energetic band of workers. In only one instance was the vexed ques- tion of Municipal trading prominently introduced, Councillor Luke Ellison for Latchford Ward being opposed by Mr. William Benson, the nominee of the Non-Trading Association. By the heaviest majority of the day, Mr. Ellison succeeded in retaining his seat. There was a straight party fight in. Howley Ward and it speaks volumes for the organiza- tion and enthusiasm of the Liberals that Mr. William Clegg was able to wrest the seat from Mr. S. Davies, the retiring representative. The surprise of the day came in Bewsey Ward, for although Mr. James Skelland and his supporters were confident of success, the most sanguine hardly anticipated such a decisive majority oVer a strong candidate like Mr. William Rogers. In six wards the candidates were unopposed and ,were returnld as follow :
Ton Hall Ward Councillor Forshavr (C). Whitecross Ward Councillor Brough (L). Orford Ward Councillor Wilkinson(L)

St. John's Ward Mr. J. Fulton Smith (C)'. Fairfield Ward Councillor Duncan (L). St. Austin's Ward Councillor Burton (L). Polling during the greater part of Tuesday was far from brisk, but in the evening there was a rush of voters. The arrangements for the elections were admirably carried out, the following being a list of the polling stations andlofficials together with the number of persons entitled to vote : RENtEY WARD.—Polling booth No. 1, 98, Hoyle- street; presiding officer, Mr. Joseph R. Williams ; poll clerk, Mr. E. Lockett; number of voters allotted to the station, 481. BEWSEY WARD.—Polling booth No. 2, St. Ann's School, Dannett-street ; presiding officer, Mr. Roger Pierpoint •P poll clerk, Mr. S. Wright; number of voters 321.

HOWLEY WARD.—Two polling booths at the National School, Church-street. Presiding officers, Mr. F. Timperley and T. H. Spinks ; poll clerks, Mr. W. Longdin and Mr. Arthur Wood; number of voters, 1139. LATCHFORD WARD.—Two polling booths at St. James's school, Old-road ; presiding officers, Mr. Arthur ,B. Fox and Mr. F. England; polling clerks, Mr. W. Sumner and Mr. G. Rice; number of voters, 1,131. LATCHFORD WARD.—A third polling booth at Christ Church! school, Wash-lane; presiding officer, Mr. F. H. Wilson; polling clerk, Mr. C. J. Newton ; number of voters allotted to the station, 419. To deal with the respective wards, the struggle at Howley was an exceptionally interesting one. Mr. Samuel Davies, the retiring councillor, had the help of the Conservative organization, whilst the Liberals rallied enthusiastically round Mr. William Clegg, who from the commencement showed that he was deter- mined to put forth every effort to change the represen- tation of the ward. While Mr. Davies pointed to his past record as an evidence of his interest in the ward, Mr. Clegg announced his intention of advocating the erection of a new bridge to connect the Howley and Latchford Wards, the abolition of gas meter rents, and the utilizing of a. large proportion of the gas profits in reducing the price to consumers. The electors were asked to "vote for Clegg, the workingman's friend and the business man" and for "Clegg and progress." On the eve of the poll a public meeting was held in further- ance of Mr. Davies's candidature, and Mr. Robert Pier- point, M.P., delivered a speech. Both the candidates in Bewsey Ward described them- selves as "Independents" though of opposite political colour, and here, also, the campaign was entered into with zest. Mr. James Skelland is well-known and respected throughout the town as the founder and superintendent of the Ragged school, and in asking the voters to support him, he expressed himself in favour of free breakfasts for school children during periods of local distress, so that every poor child can have a meal before going to school, free baths for children as being a sanitary necessity in Warrington, and anything that would tend to better housing of the working classes Mr. Rogers asked the electors to bear in mind that during his nine years' continuous service in the Council he had attended almost a thousand meetings of the Town Council and Committees. He claimed that he had advocated true economy and fought for Warrington work for Warrington people. There were numerous workers for both a indidate3and although comparatively few votes were recorded during the day the officials were kept busy in the evening when many workingmen availed themselves of the privileges of the ballot. The question of trading figured largely in the appeals of both contestants in Latchford Ward. Mr. Luke Ellison, who again came forward at the request of the Liberal Committee, informed the electors that when returned two years ago the Non-Traders promised lower rates and purity in the town's affairs, but they had not fulfilled their promise as the rates were higher thanever. Moreover "the name of Warrington had become a bye- word in neighbouring towns since Mr.Norbury Williams called it 'the most corrupt town in England except one." Mr. William Benson issued a handbill con- taining the following questions :—Why are your rates so high? Ask the traders. Who arelibuilding big mansions just outside the borough? Ask the Traders. Who are thereby avoiding the rates which you have to pay? Ask the Traders. The Non-Traders are only a small minority in the Council: how can they be responsible for the high rates, or for the bad state of trade all over the country? They have always told you that rates were bound to go higher owing to the past extravagance and mismanagement of the traders. The burgesses were requested to " vote for Benson independence arid economy."

THE RESULT. 'lie rolling stations were closed at eight o'clock and the ballot boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall. The counting was expeditiously carried out in the presence of the Mayor (returning officer for the Latchford Ward), Alderman Fairdlough (Deputy-Mayor),(returning officer for the Bewsey Ward), Alderman Francomb (returning officer for the Howley Ward), the Town Clerk, the Deputy Town Clerk, and other officials and the candi- dates.
The votes were all countel in about h%lf-an-hour and the results were declared by the respective Returning Officers as follows :
HOWLEY WIRD. Mr. W. Clegg (L.) Mr. S. Davies C.)
Majority for Mr. Clegg `2l, 1314 WSFX WARD. Mr. J. Skolland (Ind.) Mr. W. Rogers (Ind.) •-)G0
Majority for Mr. Skellancl 132 L ATCHFORD WARD.
Mr. Luke Ellison (L.) . Mr. W. Benson (1.N.T.) 297

Majority for Mr Ellison ... 293 Councillor CLEGG said it gave him great pleasure to express his thanks to Alderman Francomb for his ser- vices as returning officer, and to the Corporation officials for the very straight and orderly way in which the election had been carried out. He was deeply grateful to all who had rendered assistance. Alderman IigRANCOMB thanked Councillor Clegg for the compliment. He remarked that a more orderly election and a quieter street than Church-street he had not seen for a long time. Councillor SKELLAND moved h, vote of thanks to Alderman Fairclough and the officials who were res- ponsible for the pollinn, arrangements in Bewsey Ward. The courtesy shown 'to him by all had exceeded his expectations. Mr. ROGERS seconded, and endorsed every word Mr. Skelland had said. Everybody had conducted himself in a most gentlemanly manner. The DEPUTY-iVIA.YOR, in reply, said he was glad the election had been fought, as all elections should be fought, in as good-humoured a manner as possible. He congratulated the winner and still he was sorry for the loser. (Hear' hear, and laughter.) Councillor ELLISON, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor for his services, said he also felt indebted to all who had helped in any way to carry the election through in such a splendid manner. The expeditious way in which the work had been done was a credit to all concerned. Mr. BENSON seconded, and the motion was carried, the NIA.YOR briefly returning thanks. ANNOUNCING THE VICTORIES.

The returning officers then proceeded to the top of the Town Hall steps and declared the results before a large and enthusiastic crowd. When Mr. Skelland's splendid victory was announced there was a round of loud and prolonged cheering, in which a contingent of smiling children who had come under Mr. Skelland's care played a vigorous part. Mr. Clegg had also a great reception. There was very little speech-making. Councillor CLEGG thanked the electors of the Howley Ward for the splendid manner in which they had backed him up having returned him at the head of the poll by 24 votes. (Cheers). He should do all that lay in his power on behalf of the ratepayers of whatever colour or party at all times. (Cheers). Councillor SKELLAND declared that the victory he had achieved was a great one, the greatest that had been won in Warrington for years. (Cheers). He was, he said, suffering from a severe cold, and he must be ex- cused making a speech on that occasion, but he would express his thanks to the electors through the public press. He thanked all the returning officers for the courteous manner in which they had conducted, the elections. He had never thought they could have been conducted in such an amicable and straightforward manner. His election had been won without the aid of

strong drink. (Cheers). It had been a pure election. He had never given a farthing. He hoped they would all go home contented. (Cheers). The crowd then dispersed. COUNCILLOR CLEGG AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. Councillor OLEG G was accorded an ovation by a large number of workers on proceeding to the Liberal Club. , In the course of a short speech he expressed his thanks , for the magnificent way he. had been supported by ,the workers. He never worked, he said, with a better set of men, and never had better results for the work. The canvassing had been most satisfactory. Some three or four years ago he took up the chairmanship of Howley Ward Committee, and they had had several vacancies. They had made several attempts but failed to get a candiaate to champion their cause. The Committee approached him and asked him to stand, and as no one else came forward—and he felt there were better men in the ward—he determined the fight. (Applause aud cries of " None better.") Something like twelve years ago they had a fight in Howley Ward, when Mr. Arthur Browne tied with Mr. Arthur Bennett. They knew the result and he might say that before the polling began that day he (Mr. Clegg) said that he hoped in the event of a tie—had there again been:atie—the presiding officer would give the seat to his opponent. He had no desire to sit on the Council if only by the casting vote of a presiding alderman of his own colour. (Hear, hear), He hoped the victory that day, was but a beginning and the forerunner of a great Liberal success right through. the Borough. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfteld would be de- lighted to hear.the result of the day's contests, and would take heart, and he hoped that next year the Gown would be called upon to again record their votes and would return Mr. Crostleld as their member. (Applause.) He again thanked them heartily. (Applause.)

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE'S PROPOSALS SUPPORTED,
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE'S PROPOSALS SUPPORTED,
"A Fool's Paradise of Illusory Strength,"

The proposals of the National Service League were expounded and supported at a largely attended meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Thurs- day evening under the auspices of the Warrington branch. Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P., presided and was sup- ported on the platform by Mr. E. P. Warren (of the London Executive Committee), Captain G. R. Crosfleld, and Dr. Markel. The Apollo Male Voice choir was in attendance under the able conductorship of Mr. T. Brough, and opened the proceedings with a spirited rendering of "Crossing the plains." The CHAIRMAN said he belonged to what one might perhaps have to say nowadays was the older school of Liberalism, and he remembered well the time when as a much younger man it was an accepted article of the Liberal creed, that anything which savoured of a military 'spirit was necessarily condemned before it was heard. A great many things had happened during the last twenty-five or thirty years. The expansion of our own empire had brought with it very greatly added res- ponsibilities; and the commercial competition of the continental nations had added to the responsibilities which we as a nation of shopkeepers ought to realize. We found from the experience we had only three years ago that our army was not, at any rate, more than sufficient to protect those vulnerable points which a magnificent empire like ours, with its vast ex- panse of territory, must necessarily have. These facts had convinced him that it was necessary for the safety of the homeland that our people should be trained in what was needed to enable them, should ever occasion arise, to defend our own citadel. (Applause.) To illustrate the argument Mr. Roberts *led his hearers what they would think of a man who acquired a business worth £2,000 and although by dint of energy and enterprise he increased the value to £20,000, he had it insured for only the original amount of £2,000 ? If a disastrous fire happened most people while they would deeply sympathise with the man in his loss would say what a fool he had been. (Hear, hear.) That was practically their position to- day so far as this question was concerned. He must confess that he saw no reasoa whatever why the youth of this country should not be put into a position to share properly and efficiently that responsibility which might come upon thqin under circumstances which he hoped might never occur in our lives, but which were possible at any time and might have happened even during the last few days. We had had a serious warning in connection with the circumstances of a fortnight ago as to what might possibly occur and he thought we had to be extremely grateful to the good officers of a neighbouring nation that we were not at this moment embroiled in perhaps the most serious war of modern times. (Applause.) Mr. E. WARREN moved the followinn. resolution : "(1) That this meeting of the inhabitants of Warring- ton is of opinion that a short period of military or naval training for the youth of this country would minimise the risk of war and wouldigreatly improve thelraorate and physique of the nation; (2) that all present who sym- pathise with the aims of the National Service League should assist in the endeavour to educatepublic opinion by joining the league,by inducing others to do so,and by supporting it with all energy and enthusiasm. He wished every success to the Warrington branch of which the Executive Committee were very proud. They heard constant reports from Warrington of more energy and progress than from any other branch in the country. (Applause.) He proceeded to advocate strongly the principle of compulsory service on lines similar to those existant in gwitzerland and said he considered the present voluntary system an injustice because the willing and patriotic men had to do service for the apathetic. Everybody should be .made to do his share by being trained to arms and taught to serve his country. The volunteers' experience had shown , the impossibility --'of really efficient training for oCiicers or men under the system, which for well nigh half a century had kept this country in a fool's paradise) of illusory strength. The question of compulsory ser- vice was above all a citizen's subject, because it con- cerned the safety, honour and welfare of the empire. Surely if a country was worth living in, it was worth fighting for. If our liberty was what we boasted it was, ought not we to be prepared to defend it? Were Englishmen so far behind the rest of the world in devo- tion to their country and willingness to self-sacrifice that they would not, like every, other nation in Europe, put in some period of military service? As an English- man he would be ashamed so think that was the case. He did not believe it. The training advocated would do much to redeem the deterioration in the physique and moral qualities of a large proportion of the people of England. It would also, he believed, bring about the, death of Jingoism—the irresponsible, foolish, light- hearted way of hoping for war which only existed in the United States and England. the two countries which had not compulsory service. If we had had a complete national system of service he did not think it likely that there would ever have been a Boer war, nor did he believe that we should have had these events in various seas with Russian volunteer cruisers and the recent event in the north sea. (Applause). Captain CROSFEELD seconded and said the training would make young men stronger in their bodies, more alert in their minds, and better disciplined in their characters. They would never get compulsory service carried except by means of the league. (Applause). The resolution was carried unanimously. Mrs. EDELSTEN then gave an effective and appealing recitation of Kipling's "The Islanders" and was very cordially thanked. It wasimentioned that Mrs. Edelsten had most energetically formed a ladies' committee to further the objects of the league. At this stage an interesting series of lantern views illustrative of military training in Switzerland was exhibited, Mr. Henry Taylor manipulating the lantern. Colonel EDELSTEN pr )posed a vote of thanks to Mr. Warren for his address. To his mind, no State or Empire could endiire unless every member of it was prepared to take his fair share of the national burden. Dr. ADAMS seconded and the vote of thanks was heartily accorded. In responding• Mr. WARREN asked the audience to take every opportunity of driving home their views on the question to their member of Parliament. He found members of Parliament to be a peculiarly timid race. (Laughter.) When he spoke to them about the League's proposals they admitted they were the right thing and would have to come someday.but they said"the country was not ripe for them." When was it going to be ripe. When fruit was ripe it fell, and they did not want the country to fall before they began to take measures to save it. (Hear, hex.) He believed the statement that the British workingman. would not stand the system was absolutely false. The Rev. W. BRACECA.MP moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and expressed himself in favour of the league's proposals on the ground of their educational value and the improvement the service would mean to the physique of the nation. • Mr. DALE seconded the motion which was heartily agreed to. The programme concluded with an admirable minter- pretation of" Spartan Heroes" by the Apollo Male Voice Choir

That Den of Humbugs." At a meeting of the Orford Ward electors on Monday evening, which was addressed by Councillor Stott, gr. G-avan Duffy and others, Mr. Duffy alluded to Councillor Stott as the worker's standard beare r in that den of humbugs —the Town Council."

At the Liverpool City Council on Thursday, a proposal to limit the speeches of members to ten minutes was rejected by a considerable majority. It was pointed out that the minute sand-glasshad been success- ful in the Glasgow Town Council. Mr. Taggart though t t hat five minutes was long enough for any Scotchman. (L aught er). SUGAR IS D. PER LB. DEARER.—Advt.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Outbreak of Scarlet Fever.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rura District Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present: Messrs. Halton (presiding), Houghton, Thompson, Forshaw, Knowles, Backho use, Longton, Brooks, Mather, together with Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer).

div.head: OVERSEERS TO BE SUMMONED.
div.p: OVERSEERS TO BE SUMMONED.
The CLERK announced that in no parish Lad the last call, payable in October, been met. It was decided to summon the overseers of every parish for the amount of the call.

div.head: UNEMPLOYED QUESTION.
div.p: THE UNEMPLOYED QUESTION.

'Me CLERK reported that die Local Government Board had written asking for information as to the probable state of employment in the district during the coming winter. After consultation with the persons likely to know, he had written to say that it was prob- able that during the ensuing winter there would be sufficient work for resident labourers, but that it was not probable that there would be employment for out- side labourers. _ _
Nothing further was done in the matter.
THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
OUTBREAK OF SCARLET FEVER.

Dr. SEPHTON reported that during the month there had been_2s births and 27 deaths. The death rate was equal to 28•4 per 1,000, as against 350 the average for the past three months, and 37•8 for the corresponding period of last year. Seventeen deaths bccurred at the County Asylum exclusive of which the death rate proper for the district was equal to 10.5 per 1,000. Twenty- two casesof scarlet fever hail been reported. Mr. BR*KS asked what was done in the way of deal- ing with infectious disease by means of isolation. Dr. SEPHTON explained that the Warrington hospitals were full and that the cases which occurred had to be isolated as far as was possible at home. In families where there were five or six children there was practi- cally no isolation though the children were kept off the highway as much as possible. Mr. MA.THER : Would it not be better, as was done in the old days, when a child was taken ill to put the other children in bed with it and let them have it all at once.
Dr. SEPHTON : That was Dr. Sherratt's opinion, but it is not mine. Mr. HOUGHTON asked what was the cause of the out- break at Winwick.

Dr. SEPHTON explained that one child which had scarlet fever was, through the ignorance of the parents, allowed to attend school and this probably spread the disease. In that case no medical man was called in as the parents were very poor. Mr. KNOWLES expressed the opinion that had the first case been properly isolated the desease would not have spread as it had done. Mr.J. C. StrnoN did not agree with Mr. Knowles and pointed out that Warrington had a hospital for the isolation of infectiou3 disease and that at the present time that hospital was full, in spite of the fact that the first known case of scarlet fever was isolated. lie had always found and always would find that if there was a disease which was prevalent children would have it. Mr. KNOWLES : You will always find that where buildings are erected they will as a natural sequence be filled sooner or. later.

Mr. SUTTON: The Medical Officer has done the best he could under the circumstances. Dr. SEPIITON said he could not recommend the clos- ing of the schools as the epidemic was confined to eight or nine houses. Nothing further could be done, unless the District Council could obtain a house to be used as a temporary hospital.

_ _ SANKEY BROOK. Mr. KERFOOT reported that Messrs.Crosfield Ltd.,had not removed the obstruction in Sankey Brook caused by refuse falling in the brook from their tip. The water was still being held up. Mr. Longdin had said he was going to have the obstruction removed but had not as yet moved in the matter. 'Mr. NEWCOMBE explained that Messrs. Crosfield had promised to remove the obstruction but had not done so. It was decided to serve a notice upon Messrs. Cros- field calling upon them to remove the obstruction.
FEARNHEAD SEWAGE SCHEME. ALTERATION NECESSARY.

Mr. NEWCOMBE reported that the field in which it was proposed to place the sewage system' was being set out for building purposes and that the Council would be compelled to carry out the system much further down the brook to be a safe distance for health pur- poses. "This means," continued Mr. Newcombe, "that our system would have to be either at or below the junction of the badly polluted ditch containing all the sewage from above Bruche Hall Avenue, which means that we should have to put down a much larger system suitable to treat the whole sewage of Padgate-lane. If this scheme is adopted I should suggest that the sewer at Mr. Houghton's be carried along the present ditch but in his garden to obviate crossing it. In fact it would perhaps be better that I should thoroaghly amend the scheme first put forward, which of course is not feasible if the site as proposed cannot be obtained." The report was adopted.

div.head: GIAZEBROOK-LANE IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: GIAZEBROOK-LANE IMPROVEMENT.

The SURVEYOR reported upon an interview Messrs. Farrington's surveyor Mr. Banks with regord to obtain- ing land for this improvement. Mr. Banks would sell the land at building price. Mr. Knowles remarked that the improvement would greatly inhance Mr. Farring- ton's property in makinc, good building lines &c. At times he (Mr. Knowles) had been glad to give land for road improvements. It was well worth people's while to do that to have good roads through their property. After discussion it was decided that the improve- ment should be dropped.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

It is not gsnarally kno Ara thlt hailei el ges o motor cycle tyres should be rubbed with pure vaseline as a precautionary measure before the winter season sets in. By this means, the edges of the tyres make a good water- proof connection with the rim, and so, during a long ride undertaken in bad weather, prevent any moisture penetrating to the inner surface. Every cyclist knows that directly the wet gets through, the canvas backing is apt to rot and rotting of the canvas spells ruination to the tyre, so the simple preventive just referred to will doubtless be appreciated by those who have not hitherto made use of it.

A writer in a weekly journal declares that no puncture upon any motor tyre can be satisfactorily repaired unless it is vulcanised. This is quite wrong, although we are willing to admit that when a patch is vulcanised there is usually far more chance of the repair proving satisfactory than if it is merely adjusted in the Ordinarily adopted manner. If the following directions however, are carefully followed, the job will be found to prove eminently satisfactory.

When the puncture is located and—if the Irishisin be permitted—found to be a nip, as nine out of ten alleged punctures really are,do not attempt the ordinary rlopair before first putting a patch inside. Your friends will tell you that this cannot be done; they have failed because they have solutioned the patch first and so caused it to roll up and become unmanageable. Insert it, quite dry, in through the hole, and so manipulate itinto position that it lies, so far as you can tell, quite evenly all round. Now work in a little solution with the point of a lucifer match, taking plenty of time and using plenty of patience for the operation. When this is :lone, you will see that the cut closes over the patch, and, as the tube is blown up, apparently holds together well.

Over this closed cut now place a patch in the ordinary manner. See that the edges are nicely trimmed and bevelled, and be sure to wait until the solution both on the patch and cover is quite tacky. Half the failures to hold arise through the solution not being sufficiently dry when the two surfaces are brought together. When this is done, take a piece of fine canvas and cut a length sufficient to go right round the tube when fully inflated, and wide enough to comfortably take in both ends of the outside patch. Solution this neatly over the whole, and you will then have a serviceable repair which will be guaranteed to give you thorough satisfaction.

It is well worth while to find out the best way to make a tyre repair, for pneumatic tyres, as, at present made, are the cause of a large percentage of motor car stoppages on the road. Now that certain patents have expired, we can hardly hope for anything better to be produced, for the various companies which will rush I into breach will rather aim at reducing the price for the public than getting out a pneumatic which will I stand reasonable wear and use. To a certain extent this is the public's own fault. They are agitating for cheaper tyres, and there is no doubt that they will get them; but it does not follow that the goods will be exceptionally reliable as well.

A great many drivers are so disgusted with their ex- periments and troubles with pneumatic tyres that they are disposed to abandon them alto gether—certainly,so far as the driving wheels are concerned—and revert to solids. But, unless some means be taken to reduce the excessive vibration caused by this older type, their use will hardly prove successful. Mr. Moffat Ford, the energetic Managing Director 9f the Motor Car Co.,Ltd., believes he has discovered the solution of this difficulty by means of an anti-pneumatic suspension invention in which he is interested. The initial trials made with it have proved eminently satisfactory and should the more severe tests succeed, as he believes they will,there is no doubt that he will be in a position to supply the public with an excellent substitute for the pneumatic tyre.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
(By " Ovalist.",

For the first time this season Warrington have won two matches in succession. Their performance on Saturday at Swinton was full of merit, for titey caught the " Lions " while on the improve and fairly and squarely defeated them. It was thought locally that Warrington would have more than an outside chance, for the style of play affected by Swinton is one at which Warrington are admittedly their superiors. If all the teams in the League played open football then Warrington wguld soon find their way to the top, but they occasionally have to contend with different tactics, and on those occasions they generally come off second best. In the fast open game at Oldham, Warrington recorded a moral victory, and on Saturday they managed to win outright ,by superior speed and cleverness.

Once more magnificent weather favoured the game, and there was a fine crowd of Swinton and Warring- ton followers at the alleged "colliery village." War- rington were compelled to make three changes in the forward line, but the substitutes all played with energy and there was no weakness in this department. The opening stages of the game were not very flattering to the Warrington people, for the Blues attacked with a persistence which seemed bound to succeed. Nevertheless the defence prevailed, though more than one aspiring scorer was pulled down inches only from the Warrington line. Then Warrington changed the venue with a rush, and Davies getting cleverly away gave Harris a pass which the right-winger turned to the full account, and Warrington crossed over with a lead of one try to nil.

During a greater portion of the second half, Wall- work, one of the Swinton centres, was" cracked," and Warrington gained the upper hand completely. Isherwood led the way to the line and Morrison got over with the second try. Before the close liockenhall smartly picked up and dodged in beautiful fashion right through the Swinton defence to score the best try of the afternoon. Fish had no difficulty in adding. a goal and bringing Warrington's total to eleven points.

This victory by 11 points to nil is Warrington's best performance at Swinton for a great many years. Time was when neither team could defeat the other away from home, and when the Blues succeeded at Wilders- pool only three or four seasons back it looked as if Warringon's equality with Swinton was lost. But last season Warrington played Swinton four times, drew twice at Swinton and won easily at Wilderspool, so that the tables were effectually turned. Saturday's performance sustained Warrington's position as "top dogs," and there is no fear as to the ultimate issue when the Blues come to Warrington again.

A great deal of Warrington's superiority on Satur- day was due to the half backs who both played a magnificent game. Hockenhall has been coming to the front for some time, but his partner Davies has appeared to be under a cloud: At last, however, the Welshman seems to . have found his feet, and he was cleverness itself against Swinton. Both men were a long way ahead of the Swinton pair and it was a treat to see the way they got through the opposition. I must congratulate Harris on opening his account again. He started the season with a couple of tries, but since his injury he hap. only played in one match prior to Saturday. Now that he is gaining confidence in his knee we may expect more points from the right wing than has been the case lately. Fish is getting more closely shadowed than ever, and if Harris gets back into form it will increase the effectiveness of the threequarter line by 50 per cent.

Warrington's success lifted them considerably in the league table, and they now occupy the respectable position of 6th. Leeds dropped a point owing to the visit of Hull, and Oldham now hold a clear lead. The championship could not be more open, however, for no team has shown any marked superiority over its neighbours. There is as much danger from Bradford as from any side in the Competition, the shield-holders appearing now to have got into a winning vein. A glance at Warrington's scoring average shows it to be about the best in the League. Only one team, Halifax, has had fewer points scored ag, inst it.
The League table up-to-date is as follows :- -For— —Against—. _ _ _

Last week I commented on Warrington's combina- tion being of a stereotyped order, but matters were apparently better on Saturday. Rather curiously, "Im- pressionist "in the " Umpire " alludes to the same topic, but blames the Swinton threequarters and praises the Warrington men. Perpend : "A.mongst the three-quarters the uniform passing, etc. of the Swintonions was in marked contrast to the more go- ahead methods of the opposition, and at half too the visitors showed both more resource and originality. Combination is good, but even a good thing can be overdone; and if I may suggest it the Swinton men are much too orthodox."

Warrington " A." continued their victorious career and made short work of the strong side representing Swinton "A," though such experts as Chorley, Morgan and Lewis were operating for the " Blues. ' The score was 14-0 at the close of a fast and inter- esting game. J. Davies played brilliantly at half- back, and seems likely .to be a splendid reserve for the first fifteen. Pace ls the one thing he lacks at present. Berry is proving an acquisition at centre, while Knight, Duckworth, and Short are all shaping well. The victory carried the Warrington juniors to the top of the table, and they mean to stay there I can tell you. Combination medals would be very acceptable.

Yorkshire easily defeated Cumberland at Batley on Tuesday by 18 points to three and subsequently the following team was selected to oppose Lancashire at Oldham a week to-day: Gunn (Bradford) ; Dechan and Mosby (Bradford), J. Riley (Halifax), Davies (Batley) ; Marsden and Surman (Bradford) ; Starks and Osborne (Hull K. R.), Kilburn (Hull), Brooke (Hunslet), Laidlaw (Bradford) and J. Riley, Morton, and Langhorn (Halifax). Reserves: Taylor (Hull ; Gover (York), Avans (Leeds), and West (Hull K. R.) ; Bradshaw (Bramley) ; Wilson (Hunslet), and Stead (Leeds).
The inglorious display given by Lancashire against Cheshire has naturally resulted in several changes. 'Here are the selected players:

Poole (Broughton Rangers) ; Hogg (Broughton Rangers),Taylor (Widnes),Harry (Broughton Rangers) Fish (Warrington) ; Lomas (Salford). S. James (Broughton Rangers) ; Boardman (Warrington, Ferguson (Oldham),O'Neill (Leigh),Thomas (Oldham, Prescott (St. Helens), Cheetham (Swinton), Trotter (Broughton Rangers), and Buckler (Salford).
Reserves : Gifford (Barrow), Leytham. (Wigan„ Hockenhall (War rington), Preston (Warrington), Wilkinson (Oldham), Thomas (Warrington), and McCabe (Widnes). Referee : Mr. J. Bruckshaw, Stockport.

The weakest spot in the team appears to me to ber at centre. Taylor of Widnes is hardly class enough. for the style of game usually associated with •Lomast James, Fish and Co. He has pluck and resolution, but at Runcorn he frequently spoiled the passing. The team generally is stronger, but the men will have to put their backs into their work to get the better of the sturdy Tykes. Warrington have Fish and Boardman selected, while Preston, • Thomas, and Hockenhall figure on the reserves. I am glad to see that Hockenhall's improved play has earned him recogni— tion at headquarters. There are few half-backs in Lancashire to-day playing a better game.

It is unfortunate that the county match coincides with the date of Warrington's visit to the Hull Kingston Rovers' ground, for the locals will have to take a weakened fifteen for the encounter with the "Robins."

Warrington have an off day to-day, and the "A " team will thus have everything to themselves. They will entertain Rochdale Hornets who are also in the combination, and ought to strengthen their position.

A Rugby Club has been formed in connection with- Robertson's Morris Brook Works and fixtures have been secured in the Cheshire Junior League. To-day Robertson's play Widnes Rangers at home, and their other home and away fixtures are with Walkers', Widnes Rovers, Runcorn Reserves, Castner Kellner, Runcorn Fertilizers and Runcorn Juniors. I hope the new club of which Mr. W. Humphreys is secre- tary will have a successful career.

"A Spectator" writes to congratulate the Warring- ton team on its last three performances. He adds I have come to the conclusion that the team was a little disorganized with the three new forwards not knowing each other's play, but now they have got to combine more together. I hope they will keep it up as we have got a set of forwards now that will want some shifting.' lam sorry to see the three-quarter line is not playing up to its past reputation and I hope they will get back to their old standard. I think if they will all work with a will they will not be so far from championship honours. There is no one that would be more pleased than the old evergreen Harry Ashton, and there is no one works harder for the club and men than he does. I must also cmgratulate the A' team on their splendid performance this, season, as I think there was never a brighter prospect of two league championships beSides the West Lancashire Cup coming to Warrington than there is this season if the players will only ,put their heads together and work with a free will.'
Hockey. [By R.G.'.]
A SITUUTOR.

The Stockton Heath first team travelled to West Derby last Saturday minus a goalkeeper, so it was decided to adopt the three back game. The experiment worked admirably, E. E. Woods, E. Pierpoint and L. Fairclough being altogether too good for the home forwards.

The team played well to a man, and defeated the home side by no less than 4-0. Although to mention any special individual would be unjust to the rest of the eleven, nevertheless R. Pierpoint must be praised, for his really brilliant exposition of how to hold the wings • together, and also for scoring all the four goals.

The second eleven were at home to West Deiby 2nd, and were very unlucky in being defeated by 3 goals to 2. It was certainly not the fault of the forwards that the home side suffered defeat, although H. Smith at centre half played a fine eamedet the other two were off fo rm, and to this weakness in the half back line must be attri- buted the want of success.

Time and time again Ferguson, Howard and Longdin showed good combmation, and only the want of support caused their attacks to be fruitless. D. Skelton at out- side right was very badly fed, and had really only one good pass all afternoon, from which he scored a beautiful goal. The second goal for Stockton Heath was scored by W. G. Longdin, with a shot that hit the top of the net.
This afternoon Stockton Heath play Latchford, and as both teams are confident of victory, a good game should result.

div.head: Cross-Country Running
div.p: Cross-Country Running

Warrington Athletic Club had 23 members out last Saturday from headquarters (Bridge Inn). Messrs. Fort and Matthews laid trail over six miles of country. The remainder were divided into two packs, the first of the slow pack to finish being, G. Cooper, D. Bibby, W. Gibson and T. Wareing and of the fast pack, S. Parsonage, C. J. Straw and J. Parsonage. This was Straw's first run since his accident and he is apparently none the worse for it. Forty-six new members have been enrolled and with all the old members again available the pros- pects for a successful season are very bright.

On Saturday next thefixture is an inter-club race with Winnington Park H. from the Bridge Inn and it will no doubt be interesting to Warringtonians to hear that A. Shrubb, who is staying for a few days in Warrington on his way back from Glasgow, will run for the home team.
The club members have had a very successful summer on the path. Prizes to the value of over £l9O have been won during the season, these representing 20 firsts 26 seconds, 21 thirds and 5 fourths.

div.head: LOCAL OBITUARY.
div.p: LOCAL OBITUARY.
MR. W. BELLIA ‘T.

. . The death took place on Thursday morning at his residence, Cawdor-street, Stockton Heath, of Air. W- Bellian, at the age of 66 years. The deceased, who had been ill for some considerable time, was in his earlier days a well known singer, and figured with success at many local concerts. He was also a well known local cyclist, riding sire the time of the old " boneshaker machine. In politics he was a Conservative, but did not take a prominent part in local political life, thou4ll he was on two occasions unsuccessful in contests 10 Whitecross Ward as a sandidate for municipal honours • In business he was a fllesmith and tool maker in Cart' wright-street, retiring some years ago. He leaves three sons.

div.head: MR. JOHN HEDGECOCK.
div.p: MR. JOHN HEDGECOCK.

A well-known local gentleman passed away on ThurS- day in the person of Mr. John Hedgecock whose death took place at his residence, White&ld-road, Stockton Heath. after an illness extending over several monthS• Mr. Hedgecock. who was in his 68th year, for fort 9 rears carried on the business of a plumber and decorator in Mill-street, retiring six years ago. In 1884 be sought municipal honours, unsuccessfully contesting till North-West Ward. He was well-known amongst Wag Freemasons, being for many years a member of Lodge 1250, though he always declined to accept office 10 connection with the Lodge, preferring to see youngt3r men in harness. He leaves five daughters to mourn y_is loss. The funeral will take place at the Hill Chu° graveyard this afternoon.
