MUNICIPAL ELECTION. 1904. TO THE ELECTORS OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I beg to tender you my sincere thanks for the honour you have conferred upon me by electing me to represent YOU again for the fourth time in the Council. I shall always endeavour to merit your confidence by strict attention to duties and the best interests of our Ward and Borough. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, LUKE ELLISON.

TO TEIE ELECTORS OF BEWSEY WARD LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— I heartily thank you for returning me as your repre- sentative in the Council by such a handsome majority. It is especially gratifying to me that I gained the victory by pure methods. I also thank the kind friends, many of them anknown to me, who worked so hard on my behalf. Whilst my efforts will be primarily directed to the betterment of the poor children of the town. I shall not forget my obligations to the burgesses of Bewsey Ward. I am, Ladle and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, JAMBS SKELLAND.

TOWN I.I.ALL WARD. BYE-ELECTION, NOVEMBER BTH, 1904, TO THE BURGESSES. LADIES IND GENTLEMEN, In asking for your votes, I hope El may, reithout immodesty, appeal to my record of public work, religious, educational and social. I have already received gratifying offers of support; irrespective of party or creed. Al gone of the Commission of Inquiry I can speak with knowledge, and am satisfied that the so-called Non- Trading Agitation, which has so seriously injured the Town. was unjustifiable ; this will also be clear to you if -von rem, the evidence which is now published. If you honour me by sending me to the Town Council, itewill be a pleasure to me to help, so far as lies in my power, to place Warrington in the front rank of pro- kressive and well governed Borough.. Yours respeztfully, ALF. J. JOLLEY. 16, Arpley-street, November 2nd, 1904.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1904. TO THE ELECTORS OF TOWN HALL WARD. LAI,/ 4 AND GENTLEMEN, havt- been n)minated and have consented to stand as an Independent Candid ite for the vacincy in your Ward. I believe that politics are entirely out of place in municipal matters and that a man shou'A not be re- turned because he is either blue or red,buc he is honestly and fearlessly determined to work unselfishly and untir- inely far the Economical Management of our Local Affairs. I have been in entire sympathy with the ra Nement for the purification of the administration of the Municipal life of the 80-ough. having all along been in full accord with the Non-Trading agitation so loyally and disinterestedly led by your late representative, Mr. Dolds, and I slasll do all in my power to prevent the re-introduction of illegal and immoral Trading cf any kind. As a native of Warrington and a large ratepayer my, interests are entirely yours, and I leave myself con- fidently in your hands. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your faithful servant, WILLIAM BlitibON. 11, Sankey Street, Warrington, November 2nd. 1904.

called upon to pass or reject material that has been supplied by a man who is practically their employer, especiplly when such employer retains his seat in the Counc.l by means of a cmapact which disfranchises the town. I am to-day more than ever convinced that the whole thing is altogether wrong, and that as a result our rates have gone up and are bound to go up. In Manchester and in other towns, the drastic con- demnation of all contracting and sub--iontracting what- ever, direct or indirect, either by members or by companies in which members of the Council were shareholders to more than a merely nominal extent, has been so thorough that not only have the pockets of the ratepayers in these places been saved and safeguarded but the standard of exactness, of moral rectitude, and of honour in public and municipal life, than which noth- ing is more vital for our social well-being and our national liberties, has been distinctly raised. In conclusion, I must once more assure you of my profound gratitude to you for the too kind and generous way in which you have supported me. and for your willing acquiescence in the policy which the other day necessitatad my retirement. I shall never forget you, and if ever I can render any service in any way to any- one connected with your ward I shall be ready and proud to do so. Your faithful servant, JAMES DODDS.

aCpossible, and the experiments which have been carried on since 1902 have proved that all the cotton that Lancashire requires and of suitable quality, can be produced in the British Colonies, Dependencies, and Protectorates. The work has passed beyond the experimental stage, and the time has now come when the results obtained should be utilised, and operations extended on a large Beale and on a commercial basis For this purpose large funds are needed, and it is incumbent on everyone who is dependent on the cotton trade, or affected by it directly or indirectly, or interested in the welfare of the Empire, to further the work of the Ass ociation by applying for shares. The following steps. among others, have been taken by the Association before incorporation, or are now contem- plated 1. INDIA. —The association is in consultation with the Government as to the best means of increasing the quantity and improving the quality of East Indian cotton. Considerable sums,to which the Indian Government have contributed, have already been devoted to large experi- mental plantations,more especially in those districts where the Indigo industry is dying out. 2. WEST INDIES, BRITISH GUIANA. —Advances have b een made to cotton growers, and seed, machines and im- p lements supplied. Ginning centres have been established, and arrangements are now being made for the establish- ment of buying and other agencies. The finest qualities of cotton have been obtained from Sea Island seed, and the industry is now in many districts established on a commercial basis. 3. Haar An/res.—Similar action has been taken here, and with ample funds, in Nyassaland alone considerable quantities ot cotton equal to t• Good Par" Egyptian can le., produced and :thewsl the steps that are be-lug taker. to establish cotton grow'lng es a native industry prove suc- cesstul, even larger te ulr's will be attained. Important work is also being carriechen in the Soudan, and in British East Africa there is a large and promising field, which is as yet entirely undeveloped. 4. WEST AFRICA.—The Association has now a large staff of experts at work distributing seed and instructing the natives. Baying and ginning centres have also been established. Three large model planations have been corn- menc.ed,and it is proposed, should funds be availab e, to establish others, to each ot which there would be a buying and ginning centre attached. Excellent cotton, similar to American, has already been grown by the Association. Vast suitable territories are available, and labour is cheap and abundant, and almost unlimited quantities of cotton , could be grown. From Lagos alone it is estimated that from 6,00) to 10,r00 bales will be obtained next year, as compared with 2,603 bales last season. 5. The Association is actively at work in Australia, South Africa, and other parts of the British Empire. 6. It is proposed to urge the Government to do all that is possible in opening up various Colonies by the construc• tiou of railways, roads, and other means of transport. The Government have fully recognised the Imperial nature of the Association.and are cordially co-operating in the work. An important working arrangement has been entered into with the Secretary ofiState for the Colonies, whereby, in consideration of the work which is being carried on by the Association, the Governments of Lagos, Sout tern Nigeria , and Sierra Leone will, during the ensuing three years, make grants to the Association amounting to £6,500 per annum, Several of the large steamship companies are at present lending assistance towards the extension of cotton cultiva- tion by carrying freight free or at nominal rates. Arrangements are being made, as far as is eonsistent with the objects of the Association, to establish everything as soon as posssble upon a commercial basis. Should the hopes of the Council be fulfilled, the operations of the Association will ultimately develop into a business not only remunera- tive to itself and of advantage to the grower and user; but one which will be of lasting benefit to this country by pro- viding ample supplies of cotton and oy enriching our Colonies, who will consequently become better customers for our manufactures. The management of the business of the association is vested in the Council. The present Council was appointed by the Charter, but all the members thereof are to retire at the first general meeting of the Association, which must be held within four months from the date of the Charter, when a new Council is to be appointed. The Association has power from time to time to make bye-laws as to the terms and conditions upon and subject to which the shares will be held It is inteucied shortly to submit these bye-laws to the Association in general meeting for confirmation. In accordance with the powers contained in the Charter, the Association has taken over the assets and liabilities of the unincorporated Association as on the 31st August 1904. Under the Charter the Association has power to repay any moneys advanced or paid on behalf of the unincorporated Association, and to credit sums given or subscribed to the unincorporated Association :previous to the date of the Charter against or in anticipation of calls on shares in the Association to be allotted to the donors or thetr nominees. Up to 31st August 1904 there had been received in dona- tions and instalments of donations to the guaran- tee fund of the unincorporated Association the sum of £27,91 3s. 2d., and shares of the unincor- porated Association, fully lor partly paid as the case may be (except fractions of £1), have been or will be on application I allotted to the donors or their nominees In respect thereof. UP to the date above mentioned the unincorporated Also- elation had expended £/8,914 12s. 7d. for general purposes, and the balance of the above-mentioned sum of £27,59/ 3s. 24. was represented as to £3,049 us. id. by cash at Bankers, and as to the remainder by advances against crops and advances for machinery. Accompanying the Prospect-is is a list of the present shareholders, or those for whom shares are held, and their holdings, which includes such of the donors as have applied for shares, and also certain others, no:, being donors, who have applied for shares since the incorporation of the Association. Applications for shares must be m rde on tbe form accom- panying the Prospectus, and sent to any of the said Banks, or to the Offices of the Association, together with a cheque made payable to such Bankers or to the Association for the , amount payable on application. If no allotment is made the application money will be returned in full. Where the number of shares allotted is less than that applied for, the surplus will be credited in reduction of the amount of the future instalments. The Royal Charter may be seen at the Offices of the Association, and prints thereof at the Offices of the Solicitors in Manchester, Liverpool, and London. Prospectuses and Application Forms may be obtained from any of the said Bankers and Solicitors, and at the Offices of the Association. 13, St. Ann Street, Manchester, 4th November 1904.

In order to interest the children, who are such eager and devoted consumers of "Provost' Oats, a Grand Christmas Prize Competition ha been organised for their special benefit. This will take the form of an easy Drawing Competition 00 5 • Moneg Prizeo will he given. First which . First Prize £5 50 Prizes of 101- each Second Prize mi £3 100 95 7/6 „ Third Prize 100 Y. 5/. 99, Fourth Prize 250 SS 2/6 „ The prizes will be awarded to those who send in the best pencil, pen and ink, or coloured drawing in which a " PRovosT " Porringer shall be a feature. Competi- tors may introduce any additional features they please, and may represent the porringer in small or large form. But the whole drawing must not be more than 8 inches wide and 6 inches deep, and when sent in must be accompanied by the front part of a " PRovosT " Oats 2-Ib. packet, or the drawing will not be considered.
